    `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB`'s "none host-wide" clause excludes, and a hardlink is the same
    inode the operator can rewrite mid-run, which forfeits the pin the copy exists to provide.
  - *An env var telling the runner where the injected root is* — a second source of truth that can
    disagree with the filesystem, silently and in the expensive direction (a variable set, a directory
    that did not land, a job running without the skills its flow was written for). The worker creates the
    directory only when the trigger set the field, so PRESENCE is the signal and `existsSync` is the whole
    detection. `CONST-NO-CONTEXT-FILES-MANDATORY`'s "no env knob for this, deliberately" is the same
    instinct, and `PI_PACKAGES` is not a counter-example: package paths are operator-chosen and variable
    in count, so they must be told; this root is a fixed constant whose only variable is existence.
- **Traces to**: `REQ-PER-TRIGGER-SKILLS`, `INT-CONTAINER-JOB-INPUTS`, `INT-TRIGGERS-FILE-CONTRACT`,
  `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB`, `DES-OPERATOR-GLOBAL-OVERLAY`

## DES-OPERATOR-GLOBAL-OVERLAY

- **Decision**: Reuse an operator's existing host `pi` setup across every job through a single **global
  overlay dir** (`PI_GLOBAL_PI_DIR`), bind-mounted `/opt/pi-global:ro` into each container and layered as a
  new trust **tier 2** between the baked floor and the per-repo `.pi/`. It supplies custom models
  (`models.json`), global skills, and a global persona; the runner reads them (models path selection,
  `additionalSkillPaths` with the repo path first, a global persona entry in `appendSystemPromptOverride`).
  A host-side `pi-dispatch import-pi` stages the **credential-free** subset of `~/.pi/agent` and `doctor`
  re-verifies it. Extensions are staged and loaded **by default** — `--no-extensions` is the escape hatch,
  every staged extension is **printed by name**, and `PI_GLOBAL_ALLOW_EXTENSIONS` survives as an opt-OUT
  (`"0"`) — with the admin extension hard-blocked. A runtime **mount**, not a rebuild, so it works with the
  pulled image.
  The overlay carries a fourth thing: **operator-staged pi packages** at `packages/<dir>/`, installed on the
  host by `import-pi --with-packages` from an exact-pinned `pi-packages.json` and handed to the runner as
  `PI_PACKAGES` — absolute container paths, appended **last** to `additionalExtensionPaths`, for every job
  except one whose trigger set `run.packages: false`.
  **The overlay's `extensions/` is passed as its entries, not as the folder (issue #544).** pi reads an
  explicit directory path as a package root (a `pi` manifest, else `extensions/ skills/ prompts/ themes/`
  subfolders, else the folder itself as one extension), so a folder of loose files failed to import and only
  `extensions/index.js` ever loaded, with the failure only in `getExtensions().errors`. The runner lists the
  entries by pi's own rule for `~/.pi/agent/extensions` (`collectAutoExtensionEntries` at the pin, restated in
  `discoverExtensionEntries`, pinned by needle and hash in `pinned-api.test.mjs` and checked against pi's own
  discovery of the same folder in `loader.test.mjs`), so the overlay loads what the operator's machine loads,
  with one difference: a `pi.extensions` entry naming a DIRECTORY is skipped and logged as `manifest-dir`,
  because pi's own discovery imports it as a module while a directory PATH handed to pi is read as a package
  root, a different load. An ignore file with pi's matcher unloadable withholds the overlay's extensions
  (`overlay_extensions_withheld`), failing closed. A layout that loaded as a package before and loads nothing
  now, or loads differently, is named once per job (`overlay_extensions_layout`): `extensions/`, `skills/`,
  `prompts/` or `themes/` subfolders the rule loads no extension from, a root manifest's non-empty skills,
  prompts or themes fields, and a root `pi.extensions` with glob or override entries, or none that exists.
  The rule's gitignore matching uses pi's own `ignore` package, resolved from pi's install. The
  `PI_GLOBAL_ALLOW_EXTENSIONS=0` opt-out applies unchanged. The recursion guard is AMENDED: besides each
  entry's own name it tests the first folder under each root, so an admin package placed as a manifest
  subfolder is dropped. One change from before issue #544 is accepted: a root `package.json` with a `pi`
  manifest now contributes only its `pi.extensions`, as on the operator's machine, and those entries are
  read as plain paths, without globs, excludes or folder entries; before, it was a package root that
  expanded them and could also bring skills, prompts and themes. Load errors are now reported as
  `extension_load_failed` (entry path relative to its root, the root, and `load` or `conflict`), never with
  pi's error text; an error for a path that does not exist is left out, so the absent `/job/pi/extensions` on
  every job logs nothing.
- **Why**: Four trust tiers, each refining but never removing the one above — baked floor (immutable) →
  operator overlay (deploy-time, operator-authored) → per-repo `.pi/` (trusted-by-merge) → adversarial input.
  The overlay sits at the operator's own trust level, which is why it may carry a persona (unlike the
  admin-editable settings overlay) yet must stay `:ro` and credential-free (it rides into an adversarial-input
  container: `CONST-TOKEN-SCOPED-PER-JOB`). Skills are **first-path-wins** in pi, so listing the repo path
  first makes repo skills override global ones — the "project refines global" semantics operators expect.
  **The packages tier is a fifth tier inside tier 2, and it carries gates the overlay's own extensions do
  not.** Overlay extensions are the operator's *own* code, vetted by having been run in their `~/.pi/agent`
  and staged from a printed list, so they load by default and `PI_GLOBAL_ALLOW_EXTENSIONS=0` is the
  opt-out. A staged package is *someone else's* code, so it adds an exact version pin at declaration time,
  an all-or-nothing host-side stage, runner-side path validation, and a **per-trigger** `run.packages`
  switch that no env flag can express — a deployment can run one flow without a package while every other
  flow has it. That per-trigger switch is finer-grained than any env flag on purpose: the decision belongs
  to the capability-consumer, not to the host. It defaults **open** for the same reason the overlay's
  extensions do — the operator pinned and staged the thing deliberately — which makes it a withdrawal
  rather than an arming, and leaves the pin, the stage and the runner's refusal as the gates that still
  refuse by default. Staging happens on the **host** because pi resolves a
  non-`npm:`/`git:` spec as a **local path**, in place, with no install, no network and no writes — which is
  the only shape that loads under `PI_OFFLINE=1` inside a container with adversarial input.
  **The finding, and where it is actually fixed: on the raw load a staged skill beats the repo's.** pi
  builds `skillPaths` as `mergePaths(cliEnabledSkills, additionalSkillPaths)` — the **package-contributed
  paths first**, ours after — and `loadSkills` is first-path-wins, so a package's `deploy` is the one pi
  keeps and the repo's is dropped to a `{type:"collision"}` diagnostic nothing reads. That would **invert**
  `REQ-GLOBAL-PI-OVERLAY`'s documented "repo wins on conflict", and **path order cannot fix it**:
  `additionalSkillPaths` cannot be placed ahead of the package paths. (Ordering *does* work for extensions,
  which is why the package paths are listed last there.)
  **The ordering is pi's; the result is ours.** `DefaultResourceLoaderOptions.skillsOverride` is a declared
  option on the pinned loader, invoked with `{skills, diagnostics}` the moment `loadSkills` returns and
  before the loader stores anything — so precedence is re-imposed on the *result*: any kept skill under a
  package root whose name also exists under `/job/pi/skills` or `/opt/pi-global/skills` is replaced by the
  protected one, protected roots consulted in order so the repo still beats the overlay. The substitute is
  produced by pi's own public `loadSkillsFromDir` with `source: "path"` — the loader that `loadSkills` would
  itself have used — rather than by parsing `SKILL.md` here, which would be a second, divergent reader of a
  format we do not own. This is not a workaround for a missing lever; **it is the lever**, and using it is
  what makes the requirement true rather than merely asserted.
  **So a name collision is reported, not refused.** An earlier draft of this entry refused the job on the
  grounds that there was no reordering lever; that premise was **false**, and refusing a conflict we have
  already resolved the documented way would have cost an operator a run for nothing. What survives is the
  *visibility* half: pi's unmodified collision diagnostic is read after load and logged (the winning root,
  never a file path), because a package whose flow was written against a procedure that is not the one now
  running may quietly do less than it claims — and the operator should learn that from a log line rather
  than from behaviour. That detector doubles as the tripwire on the pin: a future pi that reorders
  `skillPaths` so the repo already wins makes it go quiet at exactly the moment the override becomes a
  no-op.
- **Rejected**:
  - *Copy `~/.pi` wholesale* — drags `auth.json` and MCP-credentialed extensions into the box. The curated
    subset is the point: what reaches a job should be a list someone chose and `import-pi` printed, not
    whatever accumulated in an operator's home directory.
  - *Bake the overlay into the image* — a per-operator image defeats the pulled prebuilt image; the mount
    delivers the same content without a rebuild.
  - *Keep overlay extensions dormant until a second env flag arms them* — **superseded**; this is what
    shipped first and it was the wrong default. The arming flag was a third gate behind two the operator
    had already passed (running the code in their own `~/.pi/agent`, then staging it from a list
    `import-pi` prints), and its failure mode was silent in the expensive direction: an overlay present but
    dormant is a deployment quietly missing the setup its flows were written against, with no error to
    read. It survives inverted, as `PI_GLOBAL_ALLOW_EXTENSIONS=0`. The admin extension must still never be
    among them, and that is enforced by a refusal at stage time rather than by a default.
  - *A separate `/opt/pi-packages:ro` mount for staged packages* — it would buy nothing the overlay does not
    already carry, and it would cost an amendment to `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB`, whose acceptance
    **enumerates** the mounts a job may see. Widening a constitutional enumeration for zero new capability
    is the wrong trade; `packages/` rides the mount that already exists, and the mount list is unchanged.
  - *A third env flag (`PI_GLOBAL_ALLOW_PACKAGES`) for them* — redundant and coarser than what ships.
    Three gates already refuse by default between an npm package and a job (the exact pin, the
    all-or-nothing host stage, the runner's pre-spend path check), and the per-trigger `run.packages`
    switch is **finer** than any env flag could be: an env flag decides for the whole deployment, which is
    precisely the granularity a third-party-code switch should not have.
  - *Route packages through pi's own `settings.packages`* — that is the supported path for an interactive
    pi, and taking it would mean giving the runner a `SettingsManager` that reads a project file. The
    runner uses `SettingsManager.inMemory()` **deliberately**, so a serviced project's `.pi/settings.json`
    can never override our spend controls (`INT-SDK-SESSION-OPTIONS`); re-opening that to carry a package
    list would trade a real protection for a cosmetic one.
  - *`npm:` sources resolved in-container* — a live network install of third-party code, at agent runtime,
    inside an adversarial-input container, on **every** run, into a writable `~/.pi/agent`. `PI_OFFLINE=1`
    exists to make that branch unreachable rather than merely unused.
- **Discovery of the host's own packages (issue #102), and the four calls it turned on**:
  - *Read pi's `settings.json`, do not walk `<agentDir>/npm/node_modules`.* pi installs with plain npm and
    default hoisting, so in that tree an installed package and a transitive dependency are
    **indistinguishable**; a walk would stage third-party code into every job container because it happened
    to be hoisted next to something the operator did ask for. Settings carries intent, git sources and
    enablement. The one thing it lacks is a trustworthy version — it stores the spec verbatim, which may be
    a range — so the pin is read off the installed `package.json`, the same field pi itself reads. We
    **capture** a version, never inherit one, which is how `CONST-PI-VERSION-PINNED` survives a road the
    operator did not type. When settings is absent or malformed, discovery yields nothing and explicitly
    does **not** fall back to the walk: inferring intent from a hoisted tree would be worst exactly when
    the operator's config is already broken.
  - *A package with no `pi` key but a convention dir IS a pi package.* The issue proposed requiring the
    `pi` key. At the 0.80.7 pin `collectPackageResources` falls through to `extensions/ skills/ prompts/
    themes/` when the manifest is absent (still so at the 0.99.1 pin, issue #509), so requiring the key would have silently dropped a legitimate
    class. The stager already had the right predicate; discovery reuses it rather than restating it.
  - *On by default inside `--with-packages`, rather than an opt-in flag for one release.* A flagless
    `import-pi` still stages no packages, before and after, so the only run whose behaviour moves is one
    that already asked for "the packages" and until now silently got a subset excluding exactly what
    `pi install` had put there. An opt-in release was **rejected** for the reason this entry already
    records for extensions: an overlay that is present but dormant is a deployment silently missing the
    setup its flows were written against, and it costs two behaviour changes instead of one. What makes
    that defensible is that the printed list now carries provenance per entry, and that `doctor --fix`'s
    restage offer was narrowed to `--no-host-packages` in the same change — the one automated path stays a
    **repair**, so importing is always something the operator typed.
  - *All-or-nothing scoped to the declared set.* A declared pin that fails still refuses everything. A
    discovered one is dropped with a printed reason, because discovery multiplies the entry count from two
    pins to twenty and one bad host package must not zero an overlay that was working. This does not
    weaken the original rule, which was about **silence**: a named drop is not a silent skip.
  - Rejected here too: *reproducing pi's enablement state for skills, prompts and themes.* Only
    `extensions/` is the sharp edge (it runs code in every job), and every additional mirrored internal is
    another thing that can drift out from under us. A glob in an enablement pattern is **not evaluated** at
    all — we carry no matcher — so the extension is copied and the command says it could not honour the
    pattern. Fail open, and say which. That reach, together with git-sourced packages and project-local
    installs, is `OQ-019`, recorded rather than glossed.
  - **What this design buys with an unexported dependency, stated as a cost.** `worker/src/host-pi.mjs`
    reimplements two pi internals that have no public equivalent: the user-scope install-path lookup and
    the enablement grammar. Two pins at different distances bound it — a contract test against the resolved
    artifact, a canary against `latest`, sharing one needle list — but neither catches a mirror that was
    reading the wrong lines from the start. The residual is `OQ-018`, and it is the reason the bullet above
    resists widening the mirror further.
- **Traces to**: `REQ-GLOBAL-PI-OVERLAY`, `INT-CONTAINER-RUNTIME-CONTRACT`, `INT-SDK-SESSION-OPTIONS`,
  `INT-PI-PACKAGES-FILE-CONTRACT`, `INT-TRIGGERS-FILE-CONTRACT`, `INT-CONTAINER-JOB-INPUTS`,
  `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB`, `CONST-TOKEN-SCOPED-PER-JOB`, `CONST-PI-VERSION-PINNED`,
  `DES-FLOWS-ARE-DATA-PERSONA-IS-CODE`

## DES-MCP-OPERATOR-ONLY

- **Decision**: The MCP servers a job may connect are one operator file, the overlay's `mcp.json`, in pi's own
  `mcpServers` shape and a strict subset of pi 1.1.0's keys (`INT-OVERLAY-MCP-CONFIG`), read by pi-dispatch on the
  host (`worker/src/mcp-config.mjs`). `import-pi` REWRITES the host's file into the overlay, keeping only the servers
  a job may connect, each in pi's shape, and lists every server it left behind with the reason; the overlay's file
  follows the host's, so `--no-mcp` or a host without one removes an earlier import's file. Doctor reads the overlay
  with the same parser as the pickup will, and checks streamable HTTP servers against the egress allowlist and the
  declared endpoints the way the proxy reads them (`worker/src/egress-allowlist.mjs`: an allowlisted name on 443,
  or a declared endpoint's exact host and port, since the runner sends every request as a CONNECT).
  - **A credential is a reference, and references are resolved by pi-dispatch, never by pi.** A reference may sit
    wherever servers take a key: a header value (`${NAME}` or an auth scheme before it, from a fixed list, so the
    word cannot itself be a key), an env value (exactly `${NAME}`), a url's query value (exactly `${NAME}`), and amid
    literal text in a url's path or an argument. Header, env and query VALUES are never literal: a rule that wanted a
    reference only under credential-like names was measured letting `X-Goog-Key`, `GH_PAT`, `PRIVATE_KEY` and
    `DATABASE_URL` through, and a list of names always has a next one. A literal argument or url path is written as
    is: a second rule, refusing the argument after a credential-like flag, was measured refusing `--max-tokens 4096`
    and `--token-file` while passing `--api_key=sk-...` and `-H "X-API-Key: sk"`, so the defence there is a reference
    to write instead and docs that say plainly that every job reads the overlay. A url's host takes no reference,
    since the egress check reads it before the job starts; the url is read whole by a URL parser, never cut as text,
    and must be written exactly as the parser writes it back, because the parser also takes `https:/h`, a backslash
    and a tab as the start of a host, and two readings of one url were how a reference reached the host. pi's resolver (`core/resolve-config-value.js`) runs a
    value starting with `!` as a shell command and expands bare `$NAME`, with no switch to turn either off, and it
    resolves only headers and env; so the job resolves every reference itself, and a secret value that starts with
    `!` is sent as text.
  - **Refused per server, not per file**, except for what makes the file unreadable as a whole (not JSON, a
    duplicate key, not an object, an unknown top-level key, a non-object `mcpServers`, a non-boolean
    `autoEnableCodemode`). A host file built for interactive pi often holds an OAuth server; one such entry should
    not cost the deployment every other server. Nothing refused reaches the overlay, and the JSON parser's own
    message, which quotes the file around the error, is never shown.
  - **A stdio command runs from the image or the overlay**: a bare name on the image's PATH, or an absolute path
    under `/usr`, `/bin`, `/sbin`, `/opt` or `/app`. Named roots rather than excluded ones, since the job's root
    filesystem is writable and a list of the folders it writes (`/workspace`, `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/dev/shm`)
    always has a next one. Nothing starts with `~`, which pi expands to the job's home. A package runner (`npx`,
    `uvx` and the like) needs `allowPackageRunner: true`, because such a server is fetched at the start of every job
    at whatever version the registry serves, and reaches the registry only if it is allowlisted.
  - **`import-pi` replaces, never writes through.** A new file is written beside the overlay's and renamed over it,
    so a link from it to the host's own `mcp.json` cannot make the import rewrite the host file, and a write that
    fails leaves the last good list; a host file that is not a regular
    file is not read (a pipe would block, a device would never end); a host file that cannot be read whole changes
    nothing in the overlay, since the last good list should stand while the operator edits.
  - **The allowlist is read as squid reads it**: one entry per line, so a line with two words admits neither, and an
    allowlisted host that is the proxy's own machine (`to_host_local`) is not reachable.
- **Rejected**: a credential-name heuristic and a credential-flag heuristic (above); copying the host's `mcp.json` verbatim (a literal header, an OAuth server and pi keys a job cannot
  honour would reach every job); refusing the whole import over one bad server (above); reading a repo's
  `.pi/mcp.json` for a job (the repo is not the operator, and pi would connect what a merged change names, with the
  job's secrets); a per-trigger server definition in `triggers.json` (the same server would be written once per
  trigger, and a trigger edit could then point a credential at any host); letting pi resolve references (above).
- **Residuals**: a credential written as a literal argument or url path segment is written in the overlay, which
  the docs say plainly; the command rules read the command, not what it runs (`node` with a script, a
  launcher such as `env` or `sh`); a server's own code is the operator's choice and runs with the references its
  trigger maps, which the job's agent can read anyway (`run.secrets`, `SECURITY.md`); doctor reads no DNS, so an
  allowlisted name that resolves to the proxy's own machine reads as reachable; doctor reads the allowlist in this
  folder, which is the file the proxy mounts on both venues.

## DES-MCP-EGRESS-PREFLIGHT

- **Decision**: A job's MCP servers are judged at pickup by one function (`worker/src/mcp-preflight.mjs`,
  `makeMcpCheck`) that reads the overlay's `mcp.json` once for the job and either refuses before anything is spent or
  returns the per-job document, which `prepare` writes to `/job/mcp.json`. One read serves both, so the servers the
  job connects are the servers the check passed; an overlay edit between the two cannot change them. It sits with the
  free refusals, after the skills folder and before the secrets resolver (the one pre-spend gate that spawns), the
  mint, the clone and the budget (`CONST-BUDGET-BEFORE-TOKENS`). In order:
  - the job's own list is one the loader writes: 1 to 8 unique valid names (`mcp-list-invalid`), since queue data is
    not always the current receiver's, and a list that is not one must neither pass as none nor reach the comment;
  - the file reads whole (`mcp-config-invalid`; an errno that may pass, such as EIO, is retried instead);
  - each name is offered as the file's own entry, enabled and accepted (`mcp-server-unknown`);
  - no reference, of any server, is one this deployment writes or pi reads for the job itself: a credential the job
    is set up to spend with (the builtin key variables of its own provider and of each provider on its model list,
    the trigger's else the deployment's, or of every builtin provider when there is no list, since the runner then
    guards no call; and every variable the overlay models.json references in any value, since
    pi reads a custom provider's key and headers from them), a minted forge token, the egress and runner variables
    (`mcp-secret-reserved`). Asked of every reference before the next rule, since a server must never be handed the
    job's own credentials. A builtin provider the job's list keeps it from calling is not counted, as in
    `run.secrets`: its variable is one an operator may hand a server on purpose (`HF_TOKEN` for a Hugging Face
    server, with a list). A read of models.json that may pass is retried;
  - each reference is a name the job will hold: a `run.secrets` name, or a `PI_FORWARD_ENV` name the worker holds a
    non-empty value for, as the container env is built (`mcp-secret-unmapped`);
  - each server keeps the way in it had through the tools the trigger's `run.excludeTools` leaves, routed as pi
    routes it: a `direct` tool needs nothing; a `codemode` or `deferred` tool is reached by whichever discovery tool is
    active (codemode calls both kinds, tool_search loads both; pi activates each for a server that has its kind, and
    codemode only while `autoEnableCodemode` holds); a server's resources go through `read_mcp_resource`, which pi
    registers once with the widest exposure among the servers offering resources and which reads any of them; a
    server's exposures follow pi's first-match order, so a pattern after `*` never applies (`mcp-excluded`,
    `mcpRouteProblem`). Whether a server lists resources is unknown before it connects, so each one that is not
    hidden is assumed to: a server with none, whose tools the exclusions remove, passes and connects to no use. The
    overlay's own hiding is never the trigger's to be refused for;
  - with the egress policy on, each streamable HTTP server is reachable through the proxy, read as squid reads the
    allowlist (`egressRefusalFor`; an `http://` url on port 443 is refused, as it would speak plain HTTP to a TLS
    port), and each package runner's registry hosts are allowlisted (`mcp-egress-unreachable`,
    `mcp-package-runner`). An allowlist read that may pass is retried; any other failure to read it refuses.
  A job whose authored trigger names servers but which arrived without `mcp` is refused as `trigger-skew`
  (`AUTHORED_NARROWING_FIELDS`), the backstop for a receiver older than the worker.
  The name `forge` is not the file's (`DES-FORGE-MCP`): its entry is the worker's, so the file is needed only for the
  other names (a missing one passes a job naming only `forge`; one that cannot be read still refuses it), a job that
  is not a github or gitlab one naming it is `mcp-server-unknown`, its one reference skips the two secret rules, and
  the egress rule asks about its API host.
  The public comment is one fixed sentence per reason and the server's name: the reason's detail names hosts and
  variables, which go to the worker's log, since the comment posts on a thread anyone can read. The capability gate
  `mcp` refuses every such job on an image that does not declare it, which until the runner reads `/job/mcp.json` is
  every image.
  An MCP server off port 443 reaches the proxy as a declared model endpoint, and an endpoint is matched to a url by
  one function (`endpointsAt`) for a model's baseUrl, this check and doctor alike. Doctor's endpoint probe then
  passes an endpoint that an enabled overlay MCP server dials and no overlay model does on any answer through the
  tunnel, since such a server has no `/v1/models` to answer 200 on, and on the socket an `https:` server closes,
  since the probe's request is plain HTTP; one a model also dials is judged as a model server.
  Rejected: skipping that probe (nothing else proves the tunnel to the declared port opens), and a probe in the MCP
  protocol (doctor would then speak to a server with no credential, which the route does not need).
- **Rejected**: checking at load (the loader is fs-free, and the overlay is re-staged by `import-pi` without a worker
  restart); reading the overlay again in `prepare` (two reads of a file the operator may be editing could pass one
  list and write another); letting a reference to the minted forge token through (a server would act with the job's
  own forge identity, which an operator should choose explicitly rather than reach by naming a variable; naming
  `forge` is that explicit choice, of a server this repository pins, `DES-FORGE-MCP`); inheriting
  `run.mcp` into a chained child (the servers are reached with credentials granted to the parent's trigger, and the
  child's task is agent-authored, `run.secrets`' reason).
- **Residuals**: the allowlist is read from the worker's folder, which is the folder the proxy mounts; a name that
  resolves to the proxy's own machine passes here and is refused by the proxy; a package runner's registry is judged
  by the runner's name, so one pointed elsewhere by its own arguments or environment fails when it starts, before the
  prompt; a custom provider whose models.json key is a `!command` names no variable the reserved check can see.

## DES-MCP-TARGETED-LIFECYCLE

- **Decision**: The runner hands pi's MCP extension a guarded API (`image/runner/src/mcp.mjs`, `guardedApi`) and fires
  its session events itself. pi's MCP connects only in its `session_start` handler, and the SDK emits `session_start`
  only from `bindExtensions`, which the runner never calls; `AgentSession.dispose()` emits no `session_shutdown`. So
  the guarded API CAPTURES those two handlers, and `run-job.mjs` calls
  `lifecycle.start(session.extensionRunner.createContext())` after the shadow check and before the command check and
  the prompt, and `lifecycle.stop()` before `dispose()` and in the catch path, bounded at 5 s (pi-mcp's own exit hook
  kills a stdio server's process group if that runs out). The same API answers `getMcpServers` with nothing (a server
  another extension registers is never connected), drops `mcp_servers_change` and the `/mcp` command, and passes
  `before_agent_start`, `tool_call` and `turn_start` through. A subscription outside that table throws, which refuses
  the extension at load; the handlers it captured are kept only once pi's factory returned whole, so the job then
  refuses at `lifecycle.start` rather than connecting servers for an extension pi discarded. `lifecycle.start` waits
  for every enabled server (15 s, or a server's own longer `timeout`, at most 120 s), observed on the transports the
  runner builds as pi's connect runs: ready once `notifications/initialized` is sent, `tools/list` has answered when
  the server declares tools, and no request of that connect is unanswered, one turn of the event loop later, by when
  pi has registered the tools. Since pi 1.2.0 the connect asks no resource list (the resource tools list them on
  demand), and the transport's `send` takes the client's `{ signal }`, which the observed transport passes through so a
  request pi gave up on is not dispatched after it. Answers are matched to requests as responses, so a server's own request reusing an id
  is not one. A refusal (an error answer to `initialize` or `tools/list`, a failed send of either or of `initialized`,
  a close before ready, a non-transient HTTP status, a redirect, a transport that cannot be built) is
  `mcp-unavailable` (exit 2); a server still pending is `mcp-unreachable` (exit 1, retried). Pending includes a
  transient failure of an HTTP server (pi's `isTransientError`) and the close pi makes after it, since pi retries an
  HTTP server then and nothing else. pi's verdict on an answer is read off the transport too: a transport pi has begun
  to close (its `closed` flag, set at once) is never ready, and a request pi cancelled (`notifications/cancelled`, its
  own timeout of a list it tolerates) is no longer waited for. A server's own `timeout` shorter than its start is pi's
  to enforce, and ends as a refusal. The job's MCP factory also holds every `tool_call`: a reserved name another
  extension registers after the shadow check (from a timer, say) is refused its calls. That catches a collision, not a
  hostile extension: one loaded first can rewrite the event the guard reads, as any in-process extension can already
  rewrite a tool's result. `lifecycle.stop` ends by releasing each stdio server's pipes, which a process the server
  started in a session of its own would otherwise hold open past the runner's exit line.
- **Rejected**: calling `bindExtensions` (it fires `session_start` for EVERY extension, the repository's and the
  overlay's included, which the runner has never done, and it binds UI and command actions a job has no use for);
  counting a server ready on its `initialize` answer (pi still checks the protocol version and lists the tools, and a
  server that fails either would have let the job run without it); letting the first prompt connect the servers in
  the background as the CLI does (a server that never answers would let the job run its flow without it and report
  success); trusting pi to close the servers (dispose does not).
- **Residuals**: a server that answers the handshake and then fails each call is the agent's to report; a server's
  tools, resources and instructions are untrusted text the model reads, like an issue's; a `tools/list_changed` the
  server sends before its first tool list makes a failed refresh read as a failed connect; a hand-run container's
  `/job/mcp.json` may reference the provider's key (the worker refuses that, `mcp-secret-reserved`; the runner refuses
  only its own `PI_*` and meter variables).

## DES-MCP-TRANSPORTS-OWNED

- **Decision**: The runner builds every MCP transport itself (`createTransport`) from `/job/mcp.json`, and passes pi
  `loadConfig` (that file, nothing else), an inert OAuth store, a log in the job's temp folder, and an `openUrl` and
  `updateConfig` that throw. References are resolved by the runner, once, from the container's environment: pi's
  resolver is never reached, so a value that starts with `!` is text and a value holding `${OTHER}` is not resolved
  again. HTTP: pi-mcp's `StreamableHttpTransport` with the resolved url and headers, no auth provider (a 401 refuses,
  never signs in), and a fetch that admits only the server's own origin and refuses a redirect rather than following
  it, and bounds every body but an event stream at 16 MiB (pi-mcp reads a JSON answer and an error body whole, and
  bounds only a stream's events); that fetch calls `globalThis.fetch`, which the restored env-proxy dispatcher sends
  through the egress proxy. A control character in a document value or a resolved header is refused before spawn or
  fetch would refuse it with a TypeError pi reads as the network. stdio: pi-mcp's `StdioTransport` with `inheritEnv:
  false`, the cwd `/workspace`, and an environment of the server's own resolved `env` over a fixed base (PATH, HOME,
  locale, zone, temp, the proxy variables, and the child meter's `NODE_OPTIONS`, `PI_DISPATCH_CHILD_LEDGER` and
  `PI_DISPATCH_RUNNER_PID`, which a server may not replace). The transports are subclasses, so pi still sees a
  `StdioTransport` (its stderr tail, its close on exit), and the runner's pi-mcp is held to the copy pi uses and to
  pi's version (`pi-pin-check`).
- **Rejected**: pi's default transports (a stdio server would get the runner's whole environment, the provider's key
  included; config values would run `!commands`; an HTTP server's redirect would be followed to any host; a 401
  would start a browser sign-in and write `mcp-auth.json`); an allowlist of variable names for the stdio base built
  from the job's env (any name not fixed here is one a server did not ask for).
- **Residuals**: a stdio server runs code with the secrets its entry names, inside the job's container and its
  egress; a JSON batch body over 16 MiB is refused though each message in it is smaller.

## DES-MCP-CODEMODE-MODELS

- **Decision**: A job's codemode scripts may call `models.classify()` and `models.generateImages()`, as in the pi
  CLI, unless the overlay's `mcp.json` says `"codemodeModels": false`. They were off until this was proven: a script
  runs in a QuickJS worker, but each `models.*` call crosses to the main thread and reaches the session's
  ModelRegistry, which forwards to `ModelRuntime.prototype.classify` and `generateImages`, the two result methods the
  process-wide meter wraps. So each call is counted in the job's totals and its per-model ledger, held to the job's
  model list, and judged by the cost guard like any call: a classifier is bounded on its input (a classifier with an
  output price, and every image call, cannot be bounded, and is refused under a cap); concurrent calls are judged
  against the bounds already in flight; the model is resolved again from the catalog, so a script's own model object
  (a base url, headers) cannot redirect a call. `image/runner/test/codemode-models.integration.test.mjs` proves each,
  through pi's real codemode tool in a real session against a stub classifier and image server.
- **Rejected**: leaving them off for good (a job then lacks a documented pi capability for no reason the meter
  cannot answer); a per-trigger switch (the spend they make is the same kind any model call makes, which the
  trigger already bounds with `run.maxCostUsd` and `run.models`).
- **Residuals**: under a cost cap every image call is refused, priced or not, since its output is not boundable at
  the pin, and a refused call stops the job as any refused model call does (the meter's first refusal is its stop),
  so a capped or listed job cannot try a model and carry on; an image model pi's catalog prices at zero settles at
  zero on a job with no cap, since pi prices it from the catalog alone.

## DES-FORGE-MCP

- **Decision**: A github or gitlab trigger may name the reserved server `forge` in `run.mcp`, and its job gets its
  forge's own MCP server as a stdio server, run as the forge token the job already holds. The worker writes the entry
  (`forgeMcpServer` in `worker/src/mcp-config.mjs`); neither the trigger nor the overlay defines it, and the overlay
  may not define a server by that name. Everything else about it is an ordinary server: it is named per trigger, it
  goes into `/job/mcp.json` in `run.mcp` order with the same `dispatch_*` hide, `run.excludeTools` judges it like any
  other, and the runner reads and starts it with no code of its own.
  - **Two servers, both pinned in the job image.** github: `github-mcp-server` 2.0.2, GitHub's own, from its release
    tarball (`github-mcp-server_Linux_x86_64.tar.gz`, `github-mcp-server_Linux_arm64.tar.gz`) checked against a
    sha256 per architecture, run as `github-mcp-server stdio` with `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN=${GH_TOKEN}`,
    `GITHUB_TOOLSETS=default` and `GITHUB_LOCKDOWN_MODE=1`. gitlab: `@zereight/mcp-gitlab` 2.1.67, installed with
    `npm ci --ignore-scripts` from a lockfile committed in `image/forge-mcp/gitlab` (not a workspace, so a pi bump
    never re-resolves it), started with `GITLAB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN=${GITLAB_TOKEN}`, `GITLAB_API_URL` the
    worker's configured GitLab URL with `/api/v4` added once (a literal: the deployment's, not a secret), and
    `GITLAB_DISABLE_VERSION_CHECK=true`. A `GITLAB_URL` that is not plain `http` or `https`, or that carries a user
    name, a password, a query, a fragment, or a comma (mcp-gitlab reads one as a list of instances; surrounding
    whitespace is dropped, as the worker's own clients drop it), refuses `forge` at the pickup as `mcp-server-unknown`, the reason in the log. The entry names neither
    server but its wrapper, `/usr/local/bin/forge-mcp-github` or `/usr/local/bin/forge-mcp-gitlab` (below). The
    variable names were read in each pinned release's source (github-mcp-server's `cmd/github-mcp-server/main.go`,
    viper with the `GITHUB_` prefix; mcp-gitlab's `build/config.js` and `build/index.js`), and both servers were run
    offline with a fake token and answered an MCP `initialize`. The image declares them with the `forgeMcp`
    capability, and a job naming `forge` on an image without it is refused before spend
    (`job-image-forge-mcp-unsupported`): an image that had `mcp` and lacked the servers would otherwise reserve the
    budget and then refuse at start as `mcp-command-missing`.
  - **Some tools withheld, as a convenience not handed out, not as a boundary.** `CONST-MERGE-NEVER-AUTOMATIC` keeps
    the harness from merging, and counts an approval as a merge by another name, so the harness does not hand the
    agent a forge's dedicated merge or approval tool either. Each wrapper (`image/forge-mcp/forge-mcp-github.sh`,
    `forge-mcp-gitlab.sh`) forces its list after anything the entry's env holds, ignores its caller's arguments, and
    runs the server under `image/forge-mcp/withhold.mjs`, a stdio gate:
    - every server message that carries a tool list (`result.tools`, whatever request it answers, so an id the
      server reuses cannot carry an unfiltered list) loses the withheld names;
    - a `tools/call` of a withheld name, or of any name not in the list the client was last shown, is refused before
      it reaches the server;
    - a client line is forwarded as the gate parsed and re-serialized it (no duplicate key or second object on a line
      read two ways), and a batch or a line that does not parse is not forwarded;
    - a pipe that closes under a write is not an error of the gate's: the server's exit decides the gate's.

    github withholds `merge_pull_request`, `pull_request_review_write` (its review may be an APPROVE), and
    `assign_copilot_to_issue` and `request_copilot_review`, which start Copilot's own agent or review and spend
    outside the job's meter (`CONST-BUDGET-BEFORE-TOKENS`, in spirit); its own `GITHUB_EXCLUDE_TOOLS` and
    `--exclude-tools` remove them too (measured: gone from the list, a call answered `unknown tool`). gitlab withholds
    `merge_merge_request` (with its `auto_merge` and `merge_when_pipeline_succeeds`), `approve_merge_request`,
    `unapprove_merge_request` and `approve_deployment`, the tools of its 263 named for merging or approving, and
    `discover_tools`, which would turn on toolsets past the default list the image's proof saw (118 of its 263 tools
    by default, measured), and `execute_graphql` by name, though no toolset lists it, so a later toolset setting
    cannot list it. Its own `GITLAB_TOOL_POLICY_HIDDEN` and `GITLAB_DENIED_TOOLS_REGEX` only filter the list:
    measured, a direct call of a hidden tool still runs, and so does one of `execute_graphql`, which no toolset lists
    and whose mutations can merge; only its permission mode is checked at the call, and `readonly` would take every
    write the job needs. So the gate's "listed or refused" rule is what holds on GitLab, and the hidden list is a
    second layer. `verify-image.sh` runs both wrappers offline and fails on a withheld name in the list, on a `merge`
    or `approv` name outside a fixed list of the other names that mention a merge request, and on a call of a
    withheld or unlisted name that is not refused as unknown.

    It is not a boundary, and nothing here claims one. GitLab runs quick actions (`/merge`, `/approve` and the rest)
    written in a note or a description, and the listed tools post both (`create_merge_request_note`,
    `create_note`, a thread, `update_merge_request`'s description); the job's `gh` or `glab`, or the server started
    from the job's shell without its wrapper, act with the token's full role. A text filter on what the tools post
    was rejected below. The boundary is the one `CONST-MERGE-NEVER-AUTOMATIC` has always relied on for the CLI: the
    token's role and the branch's protection (on GitLab a Developer token, "Allowed to merge" left at Maintainers,
    and approval rules that do not count the token's user; `docs/gitlab.md`).
  - **Token reuse, not a new credential.** The server's one reference is the token the worker mints for this job
    and writes under that name (`CONST-TOKEN-SCOPED-PER-JOB`), so the entry is exempt from `mcp-secret-reserved`
    and `mcp-secret-unmapped`, the two rules that keep that token from every other server. It holds no more than
    the job's `gh` or `glab` holds with that token; a GitHub installation token lives one hour, and the server stops
    with the job. It gets only the token under the server's own name: the base environment of a stdio server
    (`DES-MCP-TRANSPORTS-OWNED`) carries neither `GH_TOKEN` nor `GITHUB_TOKEN` nor a provider key. An empty token is
    refused by the runner (`mcp-secret-missing`) before the server starts, which matters on GitHub: the release
    binary falls back to its own OAuth client and a browser login with a local listener when its token is empty.
  - **Lockdown and toolsets (GitHub).** `default` is context, repos, issues, pull requests and users: `actions`
    (workflow runs and the tool that triggers them) stays off. Lockdown mode withholds, on a public repository,
    content authored by someone without push access; upstream calls it a best-effort filter and not an
    authorization boundary, and so does this entry: the token reads the same content through `gh`.
  - **No browser, no listener (GitLab).** mcp-gitlab opens an HTTP listener only on `SSE` or `STREAMABLE_HTTP`
    `true` and an OAuth flow only on `GITLAB_USE_OAUTH` `true`; a stdio server starts with `inheritEnv: false` and
    only its own `env` over the runner's base names, so none of those can reach it, and the entry does not set them.
  - **Egress.** With the policy on, the pickup asks the proxy's question of the server's API host, as it does of a
    streamable HTTP server's url: `https://api.github.com/` for github, the GitLab `/api/v4` url for gitlab
    (`mcp-egress-unreachable` otherwise). github-mcp-server also reads file contents from `raw.githubusercontent.com`;
    that is not required, since a job reads its own checkout, and the docs say to allowlist it to use that tool.
  - **The overlay is optional for `forge` alone.** A job naming only `forge` needs no `mcp.json` and no overlay at
    all (the top-level switches then take their defaults); a file that is there governs it like any server, so one
    that cannot be read whole refuses it too.
  - **Refused on the other kinds, at load.** A cron trigger holds no forge token of its own (a `run.github` token is
    a local job's option, not a forge job's identity); forgejo and Azure DevOps have no forge MCP server this
    repository has verified. A job of another kind that arrives naming `forge` (queue data from elsewhere) is
    refused at the pickup as `mcp-server-unknown`, never handed another forge's entry.
- **Rejected**: GitLab's own MCP endpoint (`/api/v4/mcp`): it takes an OAuth token with the `mcp` scope, which a
  project, group or personal access token cannot carry, and an OAuth flow is exactly what a job cannot finish
  (`DES-MCP-OPERATOR-ONLY` refuses `oauth` for the same reason). GitHub's hosted server
  (`api.githubcopilot.com/mcp`): its tool set is GitHub's to change under a pinned deployment, and the binary is
  pinned by a digest. A filter on the text the tools post (a quick action in a note): it would be a boundary that
  the job's own `glab` skips, and a grammar of quick actions to keep current; the role and the protection are the
  boundary instead. Withholding the merge tools by the worker's `toolExposure` (`hidden`): that hides them only as
  pi routes a call, nothing refuses one at the server, and the names would have to be written in `worker/src`, which
  the merge grep forbids by design; the image is where the pin is, so the list sits beside the version it was read
  against. mcp-gitlab's `GITLAB_PERMISSION_MODE=readonly`: the one setting it checks at the call, and it removes
  every write a job exists to make. An operator-written overlay entry for the forge server: it would have to
  reference the minted token, which the overlay rules refuse for every other server for good reason, and its pin
  would be the operator's to keep. A separate trigger field (`run.forgeMcp`): one more field to sweep for near
  misses, when `run.mcp` already names, orders, excludes and gates servers. Fetching either server at job start
  (`npx`, `go run`): every job would run whatever the registry serves that day.
- **Residuals**: the withheld tools are a convenience not handed out: a quick action in a note or a description, the
  job's CLI, or the unwrapped server run from the job's shell act with the token's role. With a Maintainer GitLab
  token, the server's settings tools (`unprotect_branch`, `protect_branch`, `update_project`,
  `update_default_branch`, `create_commit_status`) can weaken the very protection the boundary rests on, as `glab`
  can: they are not withheld, and `docs/gitlab.md` asks for a Developer token. The servers' other writes are the
  token's (`SECURITY.md`, the agent's own token). A later pin may add a merge or approval tool, which
  `verify-image.sh`'s name check catches only by name. What the tools return is untrusted prompt content
  (`CONST-ISSUE-TEXT-IS-DATA`); lockdown is best effort; a self-hosted GitLab on a port other than 443 needs a
  declared endpoint to pass egress. Forgejo and Azure DevOps are `OQ-040`.

## DES-PLAYWRIGHT-CLI-NOT-CHROME-DEVTOOLS

- **Decision**: `@playwright/cli` with Chromium bundled in the job image, with
  `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` set at **both** build and run.
- **Why**: `@playwright/cli` is headless by default and built for agents, so it works in a container
  with no display server. The `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` detail is not incidental — it resolves a direct
  collision between two of our own constraints. Installing Chromium as root at build time puts it in
  `/root/.cache/ms-playwright`; the non-root runtime user that `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB`
  requires has a different `$HOME` and **cannot see it**. Setting the variable at both stages makes
  install and lookup agree. Note pi-playwright itself has no browser-resolution logic — it delegates
  entirely to standard Playwright resolution — so this is ours to get right.
  **`@playwright/cli` does not install browsers.** Verified from the published tarball: it is a 115-line
  wrapper with `bin: {"playwright-cli": …}` and no browser-fetch code; its own `install` subcommand
  installs *agent skill files*, not binaries. Browsers come from the standard installer —
  `npx playwright install --with-deps chromium`. Note it depends on `playwright@1.62.0-alpha-1783623505000`
  — **an alpha, pinned exactly by the package itself**; treat that as another upstream pin to watch.
  **Chromium must run `--no-sandbox`** — see `INT-CONTAINER-RUNTIME-CONTRACT`. The alternative is
  re-granting `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or widening seccomp, which trades the container boundary for Chromium's
  internal one against adversarial input. The container is the sandbox.
- **Evidence (upstream)**: `guwidoe/pi-playwright @ 7d3eeeda` — `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` appears
  nowhere in the repo; `scripts/pw.js` is a passthrough to `@playwright/cli` ·
  `npm @playwright/cli@0.1.17` — `bin: {"playwright-cli": "playwright-cli.js"}`, deps pin
  `playwright@1.62.0-alpha-1783623505000`; no installer code in the tarball
- **Reference** (no authority): Playwright docs — default Linux browser path `~/.cache/ms-playwright`;
  Chromium sandbox needs custom seccomp (`clone`/`setns`/`unshare`) or `SYS_ADMIN` when non-root;
  Chromium download ~281 MB, with `--only-shell` documented as a smaller headless-only variant (a real
  trade with feature gaps, not a free win — evaluate against `REQ-FRONTEND-VISUAL-VERIFY` before taking).
- **Rejected**: *pi-chrome-dev-tools* — drives the **system Chrome with a persistent profile**. There is
  no system Chrome in the container, and a persistent profile contradicts
  `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB` directly. It is a desktop tool.
- **Traces to**: `REQ-FRONTEND-VISUAL-VERIFY`, `INT-CONTAINER-RUNTIME-CONTRACT`

## DES-SCOPED-PAUSE-VIA-MOVE-TO-DELAYED

- **Decision**: A per-folder/repo scheduled pause (`REQ-SCOPED-PAUSE-WINDOWS`) is enforced by **deferring**
  the job, not dropping it: in the processor, before any spend, `pauseUntilMs(windows, job.data, now)` returns
  the window-end ms for a scope-matching active window, and the worker calls `job.moveToDelayed(end, token)`
  then throws `DelayedError` (BullMQ's own recognise-as-delayed signal). Windows live in a validated
  `pause-windows.json`, boot-loaded fail-loud and live-reloaded through a directory watch, whose stop
  handle is registered with the worker's shutdown (`DES-WATCHERS-CLOSE-WITH-THE-WORKER`) — the exact
  `triggers.json` machinery (shared validator, atomic write, keep-last-good-on-bad-edit). The predicate
  `pauseUntilMs` and its timezone helpers are pure and injected-`now` testable; timezones use the built-in
  `Intl` (a one-pass offset correction, DST-correct outside the ~1h transition seam).
- **Why**:
  - **Defer, not drop.** A `{ outcome: "policy" }` return (the existing refusal shape) would *drop* the job —
    fine for over-budget, wrong for "pause then run after": a github issue job has no re-trigger, so dropping
    loses it. `moveToDelayed` keeps the job's identity/dedup (the delivery-GUID jobId), survives restart
    (Redis-persisted delayed set), and **auto-resumes** with no explicit unpause when BullMQ re-picks it.
  - **Not the global pause.** BullMQ's `queue.pause()` is whole-queue, untimed, and has no per-job worker
    hook to scope by folder/repo. The scoped gate is a separate check inside the pickup path; the two compose.
  - **Before `reserveBudget`.** The gate sits first in the processor wrapper — before the kill timer, the
    settings read, and the budget reservation — so a deferred job arms no timer, reserves no slot, and spends
    nothing. Same placement discipline as the branch-protection and token-cap gates; consistent with
    `CONST-BUDGET-BEFORE-TOKENS` (a deferred job is not a job start).
  - **Library-first + no new dependency.** BullMQ owns the delay; `Intl` owns the timezone math. Keyed on
    `job.data.repo` (any forge) / `job.data.folder` (local) by `job.data.kind`, `"*"` matching all, and since
    issue #498 a forge-qualified `<kind>:<repo>` window matching that forge's job only (`qualifiedScopeOf`).
- **Traces to**: `REQ-SCOPED-PAUSE-WINDOWS`, `INT-PAUSE-WINDOWS-FILE-CONTRACT`, `CONST-BUDGET-BEFORE-TOKENS`,
  `DES-CRON-VIA-BULLMQ-SCHEDULER` (the live-reload template), `DES-ADMIN-VIA-PI-EXTENSION` (the confirm-gated CRUD),
  `DES-WATCHERS-CLOSE-WITH-THE-WORKER`

---

## DES-SCOPED-LIMITS-AND-FOLDER-MUTEX

- **Decision** (issue #242): Per-scope run caps and per-scope concurrency live in a watched operator
  file, `scoped-limits.json` (`INT-SCOPED-LIMITS-FILE-CONTRACT`), on the pause-windows pattern: shared
  parser, boot-load fail-loud, directory watcher keeping last-good and closed with the worker
  (`DES-WATCHERS-CLOSE-WITH-THE-WORKER`), one mutable ref read once per
  pickup. The money windows reserve through `reserveBudget`'s existing `keyPrefix` seam under
  `budget:s:<16-hex sha256 of the matched row's scope>` (for a bare or folder row, the canonical scope it always
  was; issue #498): SCOPED FIRST, so a noisy scope's refusals never
  consume a global slot, with the compensating release when the GLOBAL window refuses after a scoped
  reserve committed (either order has a victim: scoped-second lets a scope's storm burn global slots,
  scoped-first-without-the-release lets a spent global cap drain every arriving scope's week and month
  with zero runs; the release eliminates the second victim while refused-still-counts stays intact for
  the scope's OWN refusals). Concurrency is a DEFERRAL at the pickup gate (fixed re-check,
  `SCOPE_BUSY_RECHECK_MS`), never a refusal. The one-job-per-folder mutex for local jobs is CODE —
  structural ceiling 1, `min()`-composed with any configured value, no file, no tool, no off-switch —
  because two agents in one bind-mounted working tree is the race `run.replicas` is refused for, and a
  cron trigger reaches it with no operator mistake at all (`DES-CRON-VIA-BULLMQ-SCHEDULER`, corrected).
- **Dollar windows and model rows** (issues #501 part 5 and #502 part 6, file version 2): a row may also carry
  `dayUsd`/`weekUsd`/`monthUsd`, and a `model:<provider>/<model>` row caps one model across every scope. They
  are dollar ledgers in `DES-DOLLAR-RESERVE-AND-SETTLE` (item 9), not job-count ones: they reserve with the
  deployment's dollar windows after both job-count reserves, and a refusal gives every dollar back (the
  job-count ledger's refused-still-counts does not apply to dollars). `budgetCapsFor` is unchanged and a model
  row is never a job's scope, so the job-count windows, the concurrency gate and the mutex never see it.
  **Why a version bump and not a new optional field**: the version 1 parser drops unknown fields, so a worker
  that predates this would silently drop a money limit while reading the file as valid; a newer version is
  what an old worker already refuses. **Why the writer stamps the lowest version**: an operator who never sets
  a dollar row keeps a file every worker in a mixed fleet reads. **Why a model row lives here** and not in the
  overlay or the triggers file: it is a runtime money control over a shared counter, the same class as a repo's
  window, and it must be editable live without a reviewed trigger change.
- **Forge-qualified scopes, row-keyed counters** (issue #498): a scope was the bare repo, so a GitHub `acme/web` and
  a Forgejo `acme/web` shared one limit, one lease, one pause and one cost row. A row may now say `<kind>:owner/name`
  (`qualifiedScopeOf`, `parseScopeString`, both beside `scopeOf` in `pause-windows.mjs`), and a job matches its
  qualified row first, then its bare row. **Every key comes from the MATCHED ROW** (`budgetCapsFor`,
  `dollarCapsFor`, `rowScopeFor` for the pickup slot and lease), never from the job. That is the whole migration:
  a bare row hashes the same string it always did, so its counters, its lease keys and the admin's reads carry
  over with no key moved, and a qualified row counts on its own. The boot sweeper already hashed row scopes, and
  until now only agreed with the gate because matching was exact; the gate and the sweeper are now one rule.
  `scopeOf` is unchanged, because the pause matcher and every existing bare window depend on its value.
  **Rejected**:
  - *Key counters by the job's qualified scope.* Every bare row's counter would reset at upgrade, and a bare row
    meant as one shared cap would silently split into one cap per forge.
  - *A precedence ladder where a qualified row beats a bare one.* One row applies to a job; with both present the
    file reads as two caps while only one counts. Refusing the mixed file, naming both indexes, is the simpler
    rule, and it is loud. It applies to dollar rows exactly as to count rows.
  - *The instance host in the scope* (`forgejo:git.example.org/acme/web`). One worker serves one instance per
    forge kind, so the host adds nothing there, and it would put a hostname into operator files and comments.
    The residual, two fleet hosts on different instances of one kind sharing one Valkey, is recorded in
    `INT-SCOPED-LIMITS-FILE-CONTRACT`.
  - *Rewriting existing keys to the new form.* Keys are hashes the admin recomputes from rows; a rewrite script is
    a new way to lose counts. A row an operator rewrites starts a new count, and the edit confirm says so.
  - *Refusing bare rows.* That would stop existing workers from booting. Doctor warns about a bare row or a bare
    pause window instead, when the triggers name more than one forge kind.
  - *A qualified row in a version 1 file.* Every released build reads `github:acme/web` as a plain repo string no job
    has, so it would drop the cap, the concurrency limit and the lease without a word: the failure version 2 exists
    to stop. A qualified row therefore needs version 2, and the admin stamps it, so an older build refuses the file.
    Pause windows have no version to bump; every host must run this build before a qualified window is written.
  - *Carrying a running job's slot across a scope edit.* A job keeps the slot and lease it took at pickup, so a row
    renamed while jobs run (bare to qualified, say) counts from zero under its new key beside them: with
    `concurrent: N`, up to 2N jobs can run until the old ones finish.
    Counting both spellings at the gate is more machinery than a transient edit window deserves; the edit confirm
    and the docs say so instead.
- **Project rows and ordered ledgers** (issue #499 part B): a `project:<id>` row caps every member of a project as
  one. Its keys come from its ROW scope like every other row's (`scopeKeyPrefix("project:<id>")`,
  `scopeDollarKeyPrefix("project:<id>")`, `slot:s:<hash16("project:<id>")>`), so the admin's reads, the boot sweeper
  and the fingerprint need no new rule. A job's job-count ledgers are ONE ordered list from ONE builder
  (`scopedLedgers`: repo or folder row, then project row; the processor appends the global ledger), reserved in order
  by `reserveLedgers` and given back in reverse by `releaseLedgers` over the processor's single `held` list. Every
  refund path walks that list: a later ledger's refusal, a dollar refusal, a config-refused job and a never-started
  container. Narrowest first for the scoped ledger's original reason: a refusal never consumes a slot in a wider
  ledger, so a noisy repo cannot drain its project's day and a full project cannot drain the deployment's. A project
  refusal is `project-cap`. The project's `concurrent` is a slot and fleet lease at the pickup gate, taken after the
  repo slot in that order for every job (no two jobs each hold one and wait on the other) and given back with it by
  one drain at every exit of the gate. A local member takes the project's fleet lease although its folder slot is
  in-process only, because a project id names one thing on every host where a folder path does not.
  **Rejected**:
  - *A `budget:p:` or `budget:usd:p:` keyspace.* Two key rules for one kind of row; the reserved `budget:usd:p:` is
    withdrawn rather than used.
  - *Hand-written releases per ledger* (the shape before: a `scopedReserved` flag and four scoped and three global
    release sites). Adding the project ledger by the same pattern would have meant ten sites, and the class #499
    names is the one where a new ledger is reserved and one refund path forgets it. One list, one helper.
  - *The project ledger before the repo's.* A full repo would then consume project slots on every refusal.
  - *Project caps in projects.json.* Caps have one home, this file, with its version rule and its admin surface.
  - *Dropping a dangling row silently.* A row naming a missing project caps nothing while the file reads as a cap; it
    refuses the boot, and a reload of either file is judged as a pair: against the other file as it is on disk (both
    taken together when they agree, so a rename in both files applies in either save order), else against the other's
    live copy, else last good is kept. A one-time retry of the refused side was rejected in review: a rename refuses
    both sides in turn and leaves each waiting on the other.
  - *Project rows in a version 1 file.* The released 2.1.0 reads `project:shop` as a plain repo row no job has, so a
    version 1 file would carry a cap one build enforces and another silently drops. A project row needs version 2 in
    every field, the qualified row's rule.
- **Job sizes on project rows** (issue #596, phase 1, file version 3): a `project:<id>` row may carry `memory`,
  `cpus`, `hostShare` and `minJobs`. The size lives in THIS file, on project rows only, for three reasons. It is read
  at pickup beside the other gates, so the size, the caps and the leases come from one snapshot (`resolveJobSize`,
  called next to `projectOf` in the pickup gate, and handed to the container as an argument); a size is what one
  project's jobs need, so the project is its natural key; and a per-trigger size would be a per-trigger relaxation of
  a safety bound, the shape this entry already rejects for limits (*Per-trigger `run.*` fields*, below). Repo and
  folder sizes are deferred: a repo belongs to one project at most, and two rules for one job would need a precedence
  ladder. Sizes are integers (`memMiB`, `cpuCenti`) and written in one spelling each, so the record, the panel and
  the argv agree, and the argv's memory is the spelling `memoryBytes` reads (pinned over the whole range), which the
  phase 0 OOM rule compares with. `hostShare` is a whole PERCENTAGE of a host's job budget (rejected: a fraction,
  whose float spelling invites `0.3333`; an absolute amount, which would not follow a fleet of unequal hosts).
  `hostShare` and `minJobs` were parsed, validated and stored in phase 1 and are ENFORCED since phase 2 by each
  host's budget (`DES-HOST-BUDGET`: the share at admission, the minimum through tier 1 holds); phase 1's views said
  "not enforced yet", and say them as plain limits now. The load-time checks are the host-independent ones (`minJobs`
  needs a size and may not exceed the row's `concurrent`); whether a share leaves room for `minJobs` times the size,
  and whether all minimums fit together, depends on a host's budget, so doctor WARNS where the budget is known rather
  than the file refusing at load: one file serves hosts of different sizes. Version 3 because a released build drops unknown fields: a
  size in a version 2 file would size jobs on one build and silently not on another. For the same reason a version
  3 row refuses a key it does not define (a misspelled `Memory` beside a valid field would otherwise drop out and
  the project would run at the default size); versions 1 and 2 keep the drop-unknown policy, so no file an older
  build reads changes meaning. The version refusal is a BOOT refusal only: a running older worker keeps its last good
  file on reload, so neither the size nor any later edit to the file (job counts, `concurrent`, dollar caps) applies on
  it until it is upgraded and restarted. The rule is "upgrade and restart every worker before writing a size", and
  each worker publishes `limitsVersion` so doctor can name one that predates it, judged on the version the file
  DECLARES (an older build refuses by that number, size or not) (rejected: a
  version number compared against a release, which this branch's own unreleased builds would fail).
  **Phase 2 items, found by the phase 1 gate and now handled by phase 2** (the CPU half of a size):
  - the `--cpus` ceiling (the runtime's CPU count minus one core at four or more) is a PER-CONTAINER quota, and
    quotas do not sum: two busy jobs on a 4-core cpuset with `--cpus=3` used 4.06 cores (measured). So it bounds
    any single job and keeps no core free across jobs. The aggregate reserve is the one parent cgroup every job
    container runs under, `pidispatch.slice`, whose quota is the host's CPU budget (`DES-HOST-BUDGET`, the aggregate
    CPU reserve; lab-measured on all five venues) (rejected for phase 1: shrinking each job's `--cpus` to fit, which
    is the hard cap the issue decided against);
  - `--cpu-shares` up to 262144 is `cpu.weight` 10000 on a current runtime, against 100 for the egress proxy,
    Valkey and the host's services, which carry no share, so large jobs could starve them under contention. Closed by
    the same parent, not by a weight scale: inside it a job's weight competes only with sibling jobs, and the parent
    competes as one group of weight 100 (measured); only a job run without the parent has its share capped at 1024
    (rejected for phase 1 and still rejected: clamping every job's share near 100, which would flatten the order
    between job sizes that the share exists for).
- **Why a file and not the overlay**: the deferral gate runs ABOVE the per-job settings read, so
  gate-read config must come from a watched mutable ref; and `KNOWN_KEYS` is a flat scalar list whose
  one map-shaped resident (`secretProfiles`) is deliberately model-unreachable — the opposite of the
  editability these limits require.
- **Why the count is process memory**: recorded on `DES-CONCURRENCY-3`'s second axis — one worker per
  daemon, reaper-before-drain, and the `OQ-008` two-sources-of-truth refusal of a Redis-held claim.
- **Deferral economics**: 5s re-check ⇒ at most ~360 wakes across a worst-case 30-minute hold, each
  ~1ms of synchronous predicate; a same-folder chained child (enqueued before its parent's release)
  pays exactly one re-check. No per-scope FIFO is promised — deferral is a gate, not a queue, and a
  sustained same-scope arrival rate can starve an individual waiter. Each wake's re-delay is one more
  transient-redis exposure; `attempts: 2` absorbs a single blip.
- **The admin surface** (issue #242's third slice): the pause-windows stack copied — confirm-gated
  `dispatch_limit_*` tools plus the panel's `m` key. The `m` hint lives in the section DIVIDER, not the
  footer: the footer's own width arithmetic (its review-gate comment) has no headroom for another hint,
  and `s`/`o`/Tab already use the divider route. The panel's status line shows the queue's `delayed`
  count only when nonzero and NEUTRAL — the delayed set is dominated by cron next-occurrences (one
  permanent entry per scheduler), so an amber-on-any would be always-on noise. Concurrency displays as
  configuration only, on the no-invented-numbers doctrine.
- **Rejected**:
  - *BullMQ Pro group concurrency/rate limits* — a paid dependency for exactly this feature, and it
    moves scope enforcement into the queue layer where a group-held job's budget semantics are
    undefined against `CONST-BUDGET-BEFORE-TOKENS`.
  - *The dead `limiter` option* — BullMQ's limiter is global, not per-key (recorded further up this
    file), and a rate is not a concurrency.
  - *`PI_CONCURRENCY=1`* — serializes the world to fix one folder, and an overlay edit can silently
    raise it again; the corrected cron claim must not depend on a setting.
  - *Per-trigger `run.*` fields* — many triggers feed one repo, so the scope is the wrong shape; and
    limits are runtime controls, not reviewed trigger content.
    `run.maxCostUsd` (issue #501) is a per-trigger field and is NOT this rejected limit coming back, for
    three reasons. It bounds ONE JOB, not a scope: a per-job dollar cap has the shape of `run.maxTurns`, a
    property of the run a trigger starts, so "many triggers feed one repo" does not apply to it; a repo's or
    folder's dollar budget is a scope limit and belongs in `scoped-limits.json` with the other windows. It
    can only NARROW: the job runs under the smaller of it and the deployment's cap, and a value above the env
    cap refuses the worker's load where the worker reads the file (the receiver still serves an edited
    webhook trigger, whose jobs get the smaller cap), so reviewed trigger content can tighten a runtime control and never loosen
    it. And it is reviewed content by design: no tool can set it, so it changes only with an edit to the file
    an operator already reviews.
  - *An overlay map key* — see "why a file" above.
  - *Redis in-flight counters* — see "why process memory" above, and see
    `DES-FLEET-LEASES-FOR-SHARED-BOUNDS` for the two cases issue #57 carved out of it. That refusal is
    narrowed rather than reversed: it holds for the LOCAL folder mutex, where routing makes the
    in-process count complete anyway, and it is answered for the two bounds that describe a
    deployment rather than a process.
- **Traces to**: `REQ-SCOPED-LIMITS`, `INT-SCOPED-LIMITS-FILE-CONTRACT`, `DES-CONCURRENCY-3`,
  `DES-SCOPED-PAUSE-VIA-MOVE-TO-DELAYED` (the seam), `CONST-BUDGET-BEFORE-TOKENS`, `CONST-RETRY-INFRA-ONLY`,
  `DES-WATCHERS-CLOSE-WITH-THE-WORKER`, `INT-CONTAINER-RUNTIME-CONTRACT` (the job's size)
