    exit key (an image declaring `exitAuth`), a transcript tail and a relay (a worker with Valkey), a transcript file,
    and an inbox directory it could make. Each missing part is a named skip (`steerSkipped`), and the job runs as it
    would without the field. Only an armed attempt gets `PI_STEER=1` and the mount, so an unarmed argv is
    byte-identical to one built before this entry. **AMENDED 2026-10-18 (issue #680), planned, built in #686**: on a
    COPYING venue (the first is `openshell`, `DES-OPENSHELL-VENUE`) the inbox part is the stdin frame channel below
    instead of the mount, and its parts are an exit key, an image declaring the planned `steerStdin` capability, the
    transcript stream over the exec's stdout (the copying venue's tail, #686) and a relay. A bind venue is armed exactly
    as above and never through stdin. Nothing of this ships today. **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (issue #686 part 1)**: that
    transcript stream is the exec's STDERR, not its stdout (the operator's decision, `DES-OPENSHELL-VENUE`'s "The live
    transcript over stderr"), and it is built: signed records the worker verifies and pushes into the same publisher,
    whose consumers the steer ack will be one of. The stdin frame channel and `steerStdin` are UNCHANGED, still to be
    built (#686's second part). **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (issue #686 part 2): built and served on `openshell`.** A steer
    job there on an image declaring `steerStdin` (and `exitAuth`, with the stderr transcript armed and a relay) is
    armed through stdin frames; the steer ack is a consumer of the stderr transcript exactly as of a tailed file; an
    attempt missing only that transcript is `no-transcript`, one whose image lacks `steerStdin` `venue-copies` as
    before. No skip reason was added.
  - **On a copying venue: framed, MAC'd stdin, and weaker than the mount, in so many words** (decided 2026-10-18,
    issue #680; built in #686, AMENDED 2026-10-19: shipped on `openshell`; three things the build settled that the
    decision did not, each measured: the frames reach the runner on fd 3, not its stdin, and its fd 0 is `/dev/null`;
    the runner reads them synchronously at its own moments; and an attempt with no staged transcript lets the relay
    write at the spawn. The bullets below say why, and `INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT` and
    `INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL` give the bytes). A venue that uploads `/job` once cannot show the runner a file written later, so the
    worker has no read-only path into the box but the main `exec`'s stdin, which issue #545 already uses for the exit
    key. A steer-armed attempt whose image declares `steerStdin` keeps that stdin OPEN after the key; every other
    attempt, on every venue, writes the key and closes the pipe as today (`INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`).
    - **Frames.** The pipe carries length-prefixed JSON frames, at most 4 MiB in total over the attempt (OpenShell's
      exec stdin buffer; a message that would pass the cap is refused by the worker and reported undelivered, never
      truncated). The exact bytes are `INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT`'s.
    - **Frame 1 is the exit key, drained before any tool exists.** The runner reads exactly one frame, the key, before
      pi loads, so #545's property is kept word for word: no tool has run while the key is in the pipe, and the
      agent never sees it. Only then does the runner start reading later frames.
    - **Every later frame is a steer message MAC'd under the attempt's exit key**, domain-separated from the ack and
      the exit line, over the job's `PI_JOB_ID` (the container name, as the ack's MAC uses), the frame's sequence
      number and the exact bytes of the message's file form (its id, mode, source and framed content), so a captured
      frame cannot be replayed relabelled from a steer to a follow-up; the byte-level formula is
      `INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT`'s. The content is the same `frameSteerMessage` text the mount's file carries, so the
      trust and framing are unchanged. A frame whose MAC does not verify is dropped, counted and logged once per attempt by code; a
      verified frame whose id the runner has already seen, or whose sequence number is not above the last accepted,
      is dropped too. **A key-shaped frame (`"t":"key"`) after frame 1 is a `shape` break** that ends the stream for
      the attempt, never a re-key: the runner accepts exactly one key, frame 1's.
    - **The threat, stated as the design assumes it.** The agent runs as the runner's uid. The runner's own
      `/proc/<runner>/fd/0` is refused to it by the exec-only node the runner and the in-image supervisor run under
      (`image/runner/src/exit-line.mjs`), but every other
      holder of the same pipe is not (the container's init today: `exit-line.mjs` records `/proc/1/fd/0` reaching the
      same pipe and `/proc/1/fd/1` opening on every venue), and how OpenShell's exec hands the pipe in is its code,
      not ours. So the design assumes the agent can open the pipe
      for READ and WRITE on Linux, and rests on nothing that says otherwise. **A frame it plants carries no valid MAC
      and is dropped**: it never holds the key, which left the pipe before it existed. **A frame it reads is
      consumed**, which WITHDRAWS that message: the runner never sees it, so no ack arrives, and the worker reports it
      undelivered exactly as it reports a message no ack confirmed today (`settleInbox`). A frame it reads and writes
      back is the genuine frame again, accepted once by its id and sequence number, so the agent can delay or drop a
      message, never forge, duplicate or reorder one. **A write that breaks the framing** (a bogus length prefix)
      desynchronises the stream; the runner then stops reading steer frames for the attempt, logs it, and every later
      message settles undelivered, which is the same withdraw at a larger scale and never a plant.
    - **Weaker than the read-only mount, and that is why bind venues keep the mount.** Under the mount the agent can
      neither plant, withdraw nor delay (the relay owns the directory, the kernel refuses the write); under stdin it
      can withdraw or delay. Delivery comes back as before, in the transcript under the ack's MAC, so a withdrawal can never be
      dressed as a delivery; what is lost is only the guarantee that a sent message reaches the agent at all.
    - **No TTY, and no other process channel.** The exec is started without a terminal, and tool children get
      `/dev/null` as stdin, so a `bash` call cannot read a frame by inheriting fd 0; `verify-image.sh` proves both in
      #686. The container still gains no network path, credential or listening socket.
    - **As built: the frames ride fd 3, and fd 0 is `/dev/null` (AMENDED 2026-10-19, issue #686 part 2).** The decided
      text had the in-image supervisor forward the later bytes "to the runner's stdin". Built that way, every child
      that inherits the runner's stdin would hold the frame stream, and the runner cannot move it: Node has no `dup2`,
      and reopening `/proc/self/fd/0` fails on the socketpair Node's `"pipe"` stdio is (ENXIO, measured in the image;
      the first build's probe read `inherit=socket:[...]` and failed). So the supervisor hands frame 1 on the runner's
      stdin and closes it there (the #545 handoff, unchanged in shape) and forwards the rest to the runner's fd 3,
      which a Node child's own children do not inherit (measured in the image's node, with inherited and ignored
      stdin alike), and the runner puts `/dev/null` on fd 0 by closing it and opening `/dev/null` before any extension
      loads. REJECTED: trusting pi's bash tool alone (it spawns on `/dev/null` at the pin, but an extension's or a
      staged package's child that inherits stdin is not pi's choice); reopening via /proc (impossible on a socket).
      Review round 1: a swap that leaves fd 0 unvouched for (`/dev/null` not opening after the close, or opening on
      another number) REFUSES the steered run before pi loads rather than failing open (L5); only a failed close, which
      leaves fd 0 the supervisor's socket at EOF, fails open, said. And fd 3 counts as the channel only when it is the
      supervisor's socket (L4): a bare node holds libuv's own descriptors there. `verify-image.sh` asserts both probe
      children hold no fd 3 (M2).
    - **As built: the pipe also ends at the exit line** (review round 1, M1). The relay closes stdin at its stop, after
      the exec closed, which is only safe while the CLI does not wait for EOF to exit; OpenShell 0.1.4 does not
      (measured on the real gateway), and this is the defence for one that would: the pipe is ended as soon as the
      exec's stdout carries the attempt's verified exit line (the runner has closed its inbox by then), or 5 s after an
      exit-shaped line that does not verify. REJECTED: ending it at the transcript's `end`, which the worker writes
      after the exec closed, the very wait this removes.
    - **As built: the runner reads fd 3 synchronously.** Under a cost cap of 0 the run ends about 10 ms after the inbox
      begins listening, every step between them synchronous, so an event-loop reader never fired and a message
      waiting since the spawn was never handed over (measured on Docker). The runner reads the non-blocking descriptor
      at its own moments (every scan, `agent_start`, `turn_end`, the poll, the close); a message is then read by the
      first `agent_start` at the latest, where pi polls steering once before the first model call. A real run reads
      one mid-run at the next `turn_end` or poll, as the mount's file is read.
    - **As built: an empty upload's baseline is known at the spawn.** The relay waits for the ack consumer's baseline
      so a restored transcript's deliveries are known before it writes. On this venue the baseline is the runner's
      signed baseline record, back about 600 ms in on Docker, after a cost-cap-0 run's single steering poll. An attempt
      with no staged transcript (not a resume, not a recovery) uploads the preparer's empty live file, which holds no
      prior line, so the relay is released at the spawn; a staged transcript waits for the record as before. This is a
      fact of the job's construction, not a host-side size read, which #709's review rejected as the baseline of a
      staged transcript.
- **Recovery and retries.** The inbox is keyed by the RUN id (`runIdOf`), so a #645 recovery and a BullMQ retry write
  the same inbox, each into a fresh directory of its own. Writing waits for the live tail's first pass over the
  staged transcript (`onBaseline`, which fails open on a refused or unreadable file). At that moment the relay
  re-baselines: a message the inbox calls `delivered` whose id is not among the transcript's prior lines goes back to
  `written` and is handed over again, because the transcript this attempt starts from never saw it; one whose id is
  there stays `delivered` and is never written into the new directory. A waiting message whose prior line VERIFIES
  under this attempt's key is marked `delivered` at the baseline, never re-written (review round 1, F5). The runner
  also seeds its seen set from the transcript's `pi-dispatch-inbox` entries before the prompt, but only from entries
  whose ack verifies under the CURRENT attempt's key. Neither can verify a line an EARLIER attempt wrote, since its key
  is gone, so across attempts the relay's re-baseline is the guard, and the residual below follows.
  - **A run id that is reused after its run ended** (review round 1, F1). A console retry of a failed job keeps its
    job id, so its run id, and met the previous run's CLOSED inbox: every push refused for an hour, and the re-baseline
    handing that run's delivered messages to a run never sent them. The relay now resets a closed inbox in one script
    before it registers the run (`resetClosedInbox`); an OPEN inbox (a recovery, an `InfraRetry` with attempts left) is
    kept, since those attempts continue one run. A reset that fails leaves the relay refusing to write into or
    re-baseline the closed inbox (`steer_inbox_closed`), so the job runs with its messages refused, never with the old
    run's handed to it.
- **Rejected**:
  - *stdin.* Taken by issue #545: the worker writes the exit key and closes the pipe at once, and the runner drains it
    to EOF before any tool exists, so the key is out of the pipe before the agent can run anything. A message channel
    there would keep the key's pipe open for the whole run, or need a framing protocol multiplexed with the key. And
    `DES-SANDBOX-IS-A-FRESH-CONTAINER` rejected a stdin channel to the agent for reasons this design answers only in
    the framed, read-only form recorded there. **Still rejected as an open pipe beside the key, and admitted since
    issue #680 in one framed, MAC'd form, on copying venues only** (above, built in #686): the "framing protocol
    multiplexed with the key" this bullet named is exactly what is admitted, with the key as frame 1 drained before
    any tool exists, so the key's pipe is open for the run but the key is not in it; every later frame verifies under
    that key or is dropped. It is admitted where the mount cannot exist and nowhere else, because it lets the agent
    withdraw a message, which the mount does not.
  - *A writable mount for messages or acks.* A writable `/inbox` lets the agent plant a message in its own inbox,
    withdraw one by deleting it, or write an ack file; a second writable directory for acks is the same thing in two
    halves. The transcript already holds what pi persisted, so the ack rides there, MACed. `verify-image.sh` proves
    `/inbox` read-only inside the image (a control write without `:ro`, a listing through `:ro`, then a refused
    plant and delete judged on the host).
  - *The container talking to Valkey.* A network path from the untrusted side to the queue's own database, a
    credential inside the job, and an end to the `--internal` network that holds only the job and the allowlist
    proxy (`CONST-EGRESS-POLICY-IN-THE-ARGV`). The worker is the only process that touches the inbox keys.
  - *`session.steer()`, `followUp()` or `sendUserMessage`.* They run the extensions' input handlers and expand prompt
    templates and `/skill:` commands, so a message that begins with `/name` would run a staged template.
    `sendCustomMessage` skips all of that: the text arrives exactly as the worker framed it (pinned by a test that
    drives the real session at the pin).
  - *`fs.watch`.* The directory is a bind mount whose writer is on the host, and inotify across a bind mount is not
    delivered on every venue (a VM-backed Docker Desktop shares files through a filesystem that drops the events). A
    `readdir` every second costs nothing, and the `turn_end` and `agent_before_settle` reads make delivery prompt
    where it matters.
  - *`prompt()` again after the run settles,* to answer a message that came too late. A custom message sent after
    settle with no new prompt is appended to the transcript and never answered, so its ack would claim a delivery
    the agent never acted on; and prompting again would keep a container alive, holding the minted token and the
    provider key, waiting for messages after its work ended, which is the extra container lifetime
    `DES-SANDBOX-IS-A-FRESH-CONTAINER` refuses. So the runner closes at `agent_before_settle` and a later message is
    `late` (`DES-STEER-LATE-MESSAGE-RESUME-OR-REPLY`).
  - *A copying venue.* A runtime that uploads mounts once at the start would never see a message written later. Such
    a venue is not armed (`steerSkipped: "venue-copies"`); every in-tree backend binds. **AMENDED 2026-10-18 (issue
    #680)**: still rejected as a mount, and such a venue is now armed through stdin frames (above) when the image
    declares the `steerStdin` capability (shipped in #686, AMENDED 2026-10-19), else it is skipped with
    `steerSkipped: "venue-copies"` as today. The planned `openshell` venue copies by default (`DES-OPENSHELL-VENUE`);
    its opt-in bind mode (#686) is a binding venue and takes the mount.
  - *A shadow guard on the custom type,* as the await and progress tools have. Nothing here can be answered by
    another extension: the message is pushed straight onto the agent's queue. `registerMessageRenderer` is read only
    by the interactive TUI, and an extension that sends a message of our type itself cannot forge the ack.
- **Residuals, named.** A `written` message's withdrawal is best effort: the runner may already have handed the
  message to pi before the relay unlinks its file, and a verified ack then turns it `delivered` anyway (a message the
  runner has read but still holds is checked again before the push, issue #670). An armed attempt whose tail could not be
  opened delivers messages no ack counts (`steer_acks_unread`), which settle as `late` though the agent may have read
  them, unless the runner's signed exit line names them (F3). A baseline that fails open can hand a message over
  twice. **A message delivered just before a crash can be delivered again by the recovery** (F5): its state is still
  `written`, its line is in the restored transcript, and that line was signed with the lost attempt's key, which no
  later attempt holds. Unverified earlier lines are deliberately not trusted, since the agent could plant them in a
  transcript a recovery restores and so mark delivered a message it was never sent; a framed duplicate is the cheaper
  error. pi drains its steering queue one message per turn, so a burst arrives over several turns.
- **Traces to**: `REQ-STEER-RUNNING-JOB`, `INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT`, `INT-CONTAINER-JOB-INPUTS`,
  `INT-CONTAINER-RUNTIME-CONTRACT`, `INT-LIVE-TRANSCRIPT-STREAM`, `INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`,
  `DES-SANDBOX-IS-A-FRESH-CONTAINER`, `DES-LIVE-TRANSCRIPT-STREAM`, `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB`,
  `CONST-ISSUE-TEXT-IS-DATA`, `CONST-EGRESS-POLICY-IN-THE-ARGV`, `DES-OPENSHELL-VENUE`, `CONST-VENUE-EGRESS-LAYER`.

## DES-STEER-TARGET-POINTER-IS-LIVENESS-NOT-INDEX

- **Status**: issue #646, part 1 (2026-10-17), written by the relay. Part 2 (2026-10-17): read by the receiver's
  comment routing (`receiver/src/steer.mjs` `trySteer`, through `liveRunsForTarget`, at most `STEER_FANOUT_LIMIT` 4
  runs), with the key derived by the relay's own `steerTargetOf`, imported from `@edgehero/pi-dispatch/inbox-relay`
  and never re-spelled: a key computed two ways is a key that one day differs, and then every comment silently
  starts a second job.
- **Decision**: whether a run takes messages, and which runs a forge target has live, are two short-lived Valkey keys
  written only by the relay of an armed attempt, never an index of jobs.
  - `run:steer:open:<runId>`: the host name, `PX` 30 s. **The one authority** on whether a run takes messages: the
    push script refuses `gone` without it, and the CLI refuses an active job without it.
  - `run:steer:target:<sha256(kind\0repo\0targetType\0number), first 32 hex>`: a ZSET, member the run id, score the
    instant it stops counting (`now + 30 s`), `PEXPIRE` 60 s. Each refresh drops members whose score has passed, so a
    target steered by many runs over its life does not grow, and a reader ignores a member the moment its score
    passes, whatever the key's own TTL says. Only a forge job has one (`steerTargetOf`); a local or cron job is
    reached through its open key alone, by the operator surfaces.
  - The relay sets both at the container's start (`registerLive`), refreshes them every 2 s in one `MULTI` that also
    refreshes the inbox keys' hour, and when it stops it HOLDS them rather than removing them (`holdLive`, issue #646
    part 2 review round 1): the open key and the target member are set for `STEER_HOLD_TTL_MS` (15 minutes, longer
    than the 10-minute semantic window), the target key's TTL only ever lengthened, and nothing is done when the inbox
    is already closed. So a message sent after the container exited and before the settle, or between two attempts
    (an `InfraRetry`'s backoff, a #645 recovery waiting to be picked up), still lands: the next attempt writes it, or
    the settle closes it `late`, where the late rule answers or resumes it. Removing the keys at the stop left a gap in
    which a comment found no run and fell through to an enqueue the run's still-held window swallowed. The final close
    (`closeInbox`) drops both, in its own script; a run that never settles loses them at the hold's TTL.
    `unregisterLive` is kept for a caller that must make a run unreachable at once, and the relay no longer calls it.
    **Residual, named**: `registerLive` sets the target key's TTL to 60 s at every refresh, so while another run on the
    same target is live it shortens the key a held member sits in; if that run then stops refreshing without a hold
    (its worker died), the key expires 60 s later and takes the held member with it before its 15 minutes. A comment
    then falls through to an enqueue, which the held run's window can swallow inside its ten minutes.
  - Several runs on one target (replicas, or parallel armed jobs) are several members; a message is meant to fan out
    to each live one (comment routing). A #645 recovery keeps its run id, so it re-registers the same member; a
    BullMQ retry keeps its job id.
- **How the receiver uses it: comment routing** (issue #646 part 2, `receiver/src/steer.mjs` `trySteer`, called by
  `steerOrEnqueue` in all four webhook arms of `receiver/src/receiver.mjs` and by the poller's `gate`, one body so no
  forge can weaken it alone). **Per target, not per trigger**: the relay registers an armed run under its target
  alone, so a phrase comment reaches any steer-armed run live on that issue or pull request, whichever trigger
  started it (a label-triggered run takes a comment from the comment trigger); the comment trigger's own `run.steer`
  is what lets its comments steer at all, the run's arm what lets it take one. The filters stay pure: a filter only says THAT a comment may steer, by setting
  `steerMode` at job level (`"steer"`, or `"followUp"` by the `later` grammar, `predicate.mjs` `steerModeOf`) on the
  comment route of a steer-armed comment trigger, after the author gate, with the phrase, never on a parked reply or a
  command rule. Whether a run is live is a Valkey question asked after the gate and before any enqueue, in this order,
  every free refusal first: the body is scrubbed and bounded by the worker's own rule and the entry validated
  (`steer_comment_skipped` with a fixed reason: `no-body`, `malformed`, `empty`, `too-large`; renamed in review round
  1, since `steer_skipped` is `runContainer`'s line for a run it could not arm); the target pointer is derived;
  the target's live runs are read (at most 4); and for each run the **fallback job is stored BEFORE the push**. Store
  then push, because the run's final close can land between the two calls: push, close, store would leave a `late`
  message whose fallback is not there yet when the settle step reads it, neither run nor answered. The cost is an
  orphan fallback under a run that then refused the push, read by nothing and gone with the inbox's hour; a failed
  store skips that run's push for the same reason. The fallback hash is capped at `STEER_MAX_FALLBACKS` (32, twice
  the message cap, because a store precedes a push the run may refuse) by its own script; a redelivered id
  overwrites its entry, and a 33rd new id is refused `full`, so that run is not pushed and, when no run took the
  comment, it falls through to an ordinary enqueue. A comment counts as steered on any `ok` or `dup` (a redelivered
  GUID the run already holds: enqueueing it now would double it), answered `202 {status:"steered", runs}` with no
  enqueue; everything else (no live run, every run `gone`, `closed` or `full`, a refusal, a Valkey fault, no client)
  falls through to exactly today's enqueue, `steerMode` removed: steering is an optimisation over a job, never a way
  to lose one.
  **A steered delivery leaves a marker** (review round 1). A steered comment is never enqueued, so the queue's
  delivery-GUID shield never sees its id, and a redelivery of the same GUID after its run ended (a forge redelivery,
  a poller cycle retried after a crash) would find no live run and start the paid job the steer replaced. So after a
  push succeeded (`ok` or `dup`), `trySteer` sets `steer:steered:<forgeDeliveryJobId>` (`SET ... EX` 31 days, the GUID
  job id's own retention, `NX`), and the fall-throughs that follow a successful live-run lookup (no live run, every
  run `gone`, `closed` or `full`, or a mix) first ask for it: present, the delivery is answered `202
  {status:"steered", runs:0}` (the poller: nothing enqueued, nothing counted), logged `steer_redelivered`, never
  enqueued. Set AFTER the push, never before: a marker for a comment whose enqueue then failed would swallow the
  forge's redelivery of it, a lost job. A marker read or write fault is logged `steer_marker_failed {op}`; a failed
  write leaves the comment steered and only its later redelivery unshielded. The lookup-failed path and a fanout in
  which every store or push errored log `steer_lookup_failed` and fall through without asking for the marker.
  **Two spellings, named.** The repo in the target key is the job's own spelling: for the poller that is the
  `POLL_REPOS` entry's, which is also the spelling the poller's own runs registered under (the relay derives from the
  queued job), so a poller deployment agrees with itself; only a deployment running both the webhook and the poller
  with a `POLL_REPOS` entry cased unlike GitHub's name keys the two apart, and its comments fall through to an
  ordinary job, never get lost. And the webhook and the poller see one comment under different delivery ids, so on
  a repository served by both the comment can be handled twice (steered twice, or steered once and enqueued once),
  the residual those two transports already had for enqueues.
  No timeout on these calls: the enqueue that follows uses the same Valkey with none, and a push that
  succeeded but answered after a timeout would become a steer AND a job. The client is the shared queue's own
  connection (`queue.client`), so a receiver opens no second connection; the poller passes its own.
  - *Rejected: routing inside the filter.* The filters are pure and offline-testable (`REQ-TRIGGER-AUTHOR-GATE`), and
    four copies of a Valkey call are four places one quietly loses a step.
  - *Rejected: steering only the newest run of a target.* Replicas are deliberate parallel runs of one start; a
    correction meant for the work reaches each of them (and the fanout is bounded at 4).
  - *Rejected: answering the forge when a comment is steered* (a reaction or a reply). Out of scope
    (`REQ-STEER-RUNNING-JOB`), and a write the receiver does not otherwise make.
- **Why this is not the index `DES-SESSION-KEY-IS-DERIVED-NOT-INDEXED` rejects.** That entry refuses a durable query
  surface mapping jobs to transcripts: a second retention authority beside the reaper, and the first cross-record
  content query. These keys are liveness, nothing more. They are gone within 30 s of a running relay going quiet,
  and within the 15-minute hold of a relay that stopped (or at the close, whichever is first); they
  name a run id, never a transcript, a session key, a branch or a path; nothing reads them for history, and no record
  carries them. They are the class of `cancel:req` and the host registry's beat, and they pass
  `INT-CANCEL-CHANNEL-CONTRACT`'s falsification test: delete the whole keyspace while the fleet runs and every job
  behaves as before, and the only casualty is a message sent in that moment, whose sender is told (`gone`). Which
  transcript a job resumes is still computed from the job, and nothing in the steer path reads or writes the session
  store.
- **Rejected**:
  - *A "message job" the worker decides on*: enqueue the message as a job of its own, and let the worker find the
    run. It would wait behind the very run it targets (the same target, the same concurrency), the semantic dedup
    window of the delivery that started that run would swallow it (`REQ-DEDUP-BY-DELIVERY-GUID`), and on a fleet the
    worker that picked it up would still need to know which host holds the target's run, which is this map anyway.
  - *Scanning the queues' active jobs for the target.* Per queue, per host, and a read of every active job's data to
    answer one question, for every comment; and an active job is not yet a run that can take a message (its container
    may not have started, its attempt may not be armed).
  - *Recording the target in the run record or the session store.* That is the index, arriving from the other side.
- **Traces to**: `REQ-STEER-RUNNING-JOB`, `INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT`, `INT-CANCEL-CHANNEL-CONTRACT`,
  `DES-SESSION-KEY-IS-DERIVED-NOT-INDEXED`, `REQ-DEDUP-BY-DELIVERY-GUID`, `OQ-008`.

## DES-STEER-HELD-WHILE-PARKED

- **Status**: issue #646, part 1 (2026-10-17). `image/runner/src/inbox.mjs` (`isParked`, read from the await tool's
  state).
- **Decision**: once the agent has called `await_human_input` (`REQ-AWAIT-INPUT`), the runner hands over nothing
  more. A message that arrives then, or was waiting, stays on disk, is logged by count (`steer_held_parked
  {pending}`, never text), and is settled as `late` when the run ends parked.
- **Why**: pi's loop polls its steering queue after a terminating tool, so a message queued there would un-park the
  run: it would go on working after it posted its question, with the label set and the key about to be marked
  `parked`, and the person's answer would then arrive at a run that no longer waits for it. The park is the run's own
  decision to end and wait (`DES-AWAIT-INPUT-ENDS-THE-JOB`); a message must not reverse it from outside.
- **What becomes of a held message.** An operator's held message is `late` and reported only, like any late
  operator message. A held forge message (issue #646 part 2) takes the late-message rule: a park is not an
  `operator-cancel`, so when the comment's trigger resumes (its stored fallback job has `resume`) the first held
  message becomes the resumed job and any further ones are pre-seeded into it; otherwise they get the one fixed reply
  (`DES-STEER-LATE-MESSAGE-RESUME-OR-REPLY`). The resumed job is an ordinary comment job: it is not routed as a parked
  answer (`parkedReply`), and it resumes the key the parked run left.
- **Residual, named**: a steer pi had already queued in that same turn (the one in flight when the tool ran) still
  un-parks the run, one at most, and its verified ack shows it as `delivered`. A follow-up cannot (issue #670): the
  runner hands one to pi only at the settle boundary, where a parked run gets nothing.
- **Rejected**: *pushing anyway and letting the agent decide.* It un-parks the run, as above. *Holding the message
  inside a live container until the answer comes.* That is waiting in a container, which `DES-AWAIT-INPUT-ENDS-THE-JOB`
  rejected first.
- **Traces to**: `REQ-STEER-RUNNING-JOB`, `REQ-AWAIT-INPUT`, `DES-AWAIT-INPUT-ENDS-THE-JOB`,
  `DES-STEER-LATE-MESSAGE-RESUME-OR-REPLY`.

## DES-STEER-LATE-MESSAGE-RESUME-OR-REPLY

- **Status**: issue #646, part 1 (2026-10-17): the close and the operator branch. Part 2 (2026-10-17): the forge
  branches and the window release, with comment routing. `worker/src/inbox-settle.mjs` (`settleInbox`,
  `isFinalOutcome`, `makeLateForge`, `STEER_LATE_REPLY`), called from `worker/src/index.mjs` (`settleSteer`), the
  host-lost sweep and the failed listener in `worker/src/start.mjs`, which wires one `makeLateForge` into all three;
  `worker/src/queue.mjs` (`enqueueLateForgeJob`, `releaseSemanticWindow`); `worker/src/steer-inbox.mjs`
  (`readFallbacks`, `preseedInbox`, `STEER_PRESEED_TTL_MS`).
- **Decision**: at a run's FINAL outcome, immediately before its record is written, its inbox is closed in one Lua
  script (`closeInbox`): `closed` is set, the open key and the target member go, every `queued` or `written` message
  becomes `late`, and the script returns every entry and state. After it every push is refused (`closed`), and
  everything pushed before it is in its reply, so no message is accepted and then silently never answered. The
  counts of `delivered`, `late` and `withdrawn` become the record's `steered`.
  - **Final** is every returned result except a #645 handoff (`recovery-enqueued`, whose recovery keeps the run id
    and must find the inbox open, and `recovery-superseded`, whose run settled elsewhere), and every thrown error that
    ends the job: anything that is not an `InfraRetry`, or an `InfraRetry` on the job's last attempt. An `InfraRetry`
    with attempts left is not final: the next attempt re-registers the run and writes the waiting messages again. A
    bolt test holds every record write in `index.mjs` to a settle on the line before it, and the host-lost sweep's
    record settles too. Since review round 1 (F2) so does the failed listener's terminal branch (`job.finishedOn`,
    `start.mjs`), for a terminal failure the processor never saw: a stall-kill of a crashed worker's job, a rethrow
    above its catch; a failure the processor did see was already settled, and closing again changes nothing. A bolt
    covers it.
  - **An operator's late message is reported only** in this release: the CLI says `late` (exit 1) when it sees it
    within its poll, the record counts it, and no job starts. An operator who reads `late` can start a run; a CLI
    message that silently queued a paid job would be a spend nobody confirmed.
  - **A steer-armed run releases its semantic window at its final outcome**, whatever its inbox held, before anything
    below. Once the run is over, a comment on its target is no longer a steer (the run left the target's live set at
    the close) and must start a job of its own, which the window the run's start delivery still holds would swallow
    for the rest of its ten minutes (`REQ-DEDUP-BY-DELIVERY-GUID`). It is the parked branch's release
    (`releaseSemanticWindow`, the job's own compare-and-delete, so it never frees a window a later job holds), and it
    logs under that branch's names (`parked_window_released`, `parked_window_release_failed`). `settleInbox` awaits
    the seam with the run's context (`{ job, runId, result, error }`) at the FIRST successful close only, with no late
    entries too, so the release and either branch finish before the record is written. `closeInbox` answers `first`
    (true only for the call that made the closing transition, review round 1): a terminal thrown failure is settled
    twice, by the processor and then by BullMQ's failed listener, and both get the same late entries back; the second
    only counts them, so nothing is answered or resumed twice.
  - **A forge author's late message** (`makeLateForge`). The forge-source late entries are taken in inbox order and
    split by `hop`. A message with `hop >= 1` was carried once already and is only ever answered: that is what ends a
    chain of runs. Of the rest (hop 0), the FIRST decides:
    - **(A) A resumed job.** When the outcome is not `operator-cancel` (the operator stopped this work; starting it
      again behind their back is what the cancel promised not to do), the receiver stored a fallback job for that
      message (`run:inbox:fallback:<runId>`, `INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT`), the fallback has `resume === true`, and it
      names this run's forge, repo, target type and target number (the type since review round 1: GitLab and Azure
      number issues and merge or pull requests separately, so issue 5 and merge request 5 are different objects), that
      job is enqueued (`enqueueLateForgeJob`): under its own
      delivery-GUID id, with the forge job's retry policy and retention, and with NO deduplication option, on the
      queue that ran the run (a `pi-dispatch@<host>` queue stays on its host, anything else goes to the shared queue;
      the host-lost sweep sends it to the shared queue, since that host is gone). Its own message is its trigger
      comment, so it runs as the job the comment would have started had no run been live. The other hop-0 messages are
      pre-seeded into the new job's inbox with `hop: 1` (`preseedInbox`, keyed by the new job's id, which is its run
      id), so its relay writes them as steers at its loop start through the same framing, acks and settle as any
      steer. Only when the fallback is itself steer-armed: an unarmed job has no relay and no settle, so a carried
      message would wait unread and never be answered; those messages are answered instead, and the job still starts
      for the first one. A pre-seed that fails keeps the job (its own message is in it) and answers the rest.
    - **(B) One fixed reply.** Otherwise (an `operator-cancel`, no fallback stored, a fallback without `resume`, a
      fallback for another forge, repo or target, an unreadable fallback hash, a failed enqueue): answered. Everything
      answered at one run end gets ONE comment on the run's target (`STEER_LATE_REPLY`: the run had already finished
      when the message arrived, so it did not see it; comment again with the trigger phrase to start a new run),
      however many messages it covers: no mention, no quote of the message, fixed words. A failed post is swallowed;
      the `steer_late_replied` line still says how many it covered.
    At most one extra job per run end. A failure along branch A falls back to branch B, logged by code: a message is
    either carried or answered, never neither. Why pre-seed the inbox rather than carry the messages in the new job's
    data: the relay already writes every `queued` message of its run's inbox at its start, and a retry, a recovery
    and the console all see them there; in job data they would need a second delivery path into the relay, and would
    be durable job data holding attacker-chosen text the record and the console must never show. A pre-seeded
    message waits a day (`STEER_PRESEED_TTL_MS`, not the inbox's hour), because the new job is queued and may wait
    behind a full host or a pause window; the relay's first refresh puts the hour back once it is live.
    Logs: `steer_late_resumed {jobId, runId, n, queue}` (n counts the messages the new job carries, its own first one
    included), `steer_late_replied {runId, n}`, and by code only `steer_late_fallback_unread`,
    `steer_late_fallback_mismatch`, `steer_late_resume_failed`, `steer_late_preseed_failed` and `steer_late_failed`;
    ids and counts, never text. An unwired `settleInbox` (a test, a caller without the worker's queues) keeps the
    part 1 no-op, `steer_late_forge_unanswered {count}`.
  - **Known gaps, named rather than glossed.**
    - *Replicas each reply.* A comment fanned out to several replicas of one run is late in each of their inboxes.
      Branch A starts at most one job between them (the GUID layer: the same delivery id is the same job, and the
      second pre-seed skips ids already there), but branch B runs per replica, so the target can get one fixed reply
      per replica.
    - *A recovery job cannot release the original's window.* A #645 recovery is its own BullMQ job without the
      original's dedup id, so when a recovered run ends the release finds nothing to release and the original
      delivery's window lasts out its ttl. The late branches still run (they key on the run id).
    - *A failed close keeps the window.* When `closeInbox` fails, `settleInbox` answers null without calling the seam,
      so the window is not released and nothing is answered; the messages keep their states until the inbox's hour
      runs out. `steer_settle_failed` names it. (A failed first close followed by a successful second one, the failed
      listener's, is that second call's `first`, and it answers.)
    - *A pre-seeded message that waits over 24 h expires unanswered.* When the resumed job has not started within a
      day, its inbox keys expire with the carried messages in them, and no reply is posted for them.
    - *Between the container's exit and the final outcome* (the gap part 2 first shipped with, closed in review round
      1): the relay now holds the open key and the target member for 15 minutes at its stop (`holdLive`,
      `DES-STEER-TARGET-POINTER-IS-LIVENESS-NOT-INDEX`), so a comment in that interval lands in the inbox and is closed
      `late` with the rest. What remains is that entry's named residual: a held member can drop out of the target
      early when another run on the same target refreshed the key's 60-second TTL and then died without holding.
  - **Never throws.** A Valkey fault is logged by code (`steer_settle_failed`), and the record is written without
    `steered`: a run's outcome never waits on, or is rewritten by, its inbox.
- **Rejected**:
  - *Leaving the inbox open until its TTL.* A push would be accepted for a run that is over, and its sender told
    nothing for an hour.
  - *Starting a job for an operator's late message.* Above: a spend nobody confirmed. The console and the CLI show
    `late`, and the operator decides.
  - *Delivering a late message into the target's next run without saying so.* The next run may be hours away, about
    something else, or never come.
  - *One reply per late message.* A run that ends holding five comments would post five identical comments; one
    covers them all.
  - *Carrying the late messages in the resumed job's data.* Above: a second delivery path, and durable job data
    holding attacker-chosen text.
  - *Carrying a carried message again.* A chain of runs, each started by the previous one's late messages, with
    nobody having asked for the later ones; `hop >= 1` is answered instead.
  - *Releasing the window from the receiver, or skipping it for a steered comment's fallback.* The receiver cannot
    tell a follow-up from a duplicate; the worker knows the run is over.
  - *Answering at every close* (part 2 as first written). A terminal failure settles twice, so its late comments were
    answered, or resumed, twice; the close says which call was first.
- **A sibling, not a branch: held replies** (issue #638, 2026-10-19, `DES-AWAIT-INPUT-ENDS-THE-JOB`). An awaitInput
  run's held replies are TAKEN inside its park sequence, before the parked comment, and enqueued WITH the semantic
  window (unlike a late steer's window-less job: the park already released the window and invited further answers,
  which must be coalesced against the one resumed job); the final-outcome settle at the same three sites as this one
  (index.mjs's `settleSteer` calls `settleHeldReplies` first, so the bolt that pins this settle to every record write
  pins that one too) is their backstop, with the same `isFinalOutcome` and the same closing script answering `first`.
  When a held reply was taken, this settle answers its late messages rather than resuming one (`heldResumed`), so the
  two never both start a job. They live in keys of their own (`run:await:*`, `run:held:*`,
  `INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT`), never in this inbox, for two reasons. An awaitInput run need not be steer-armed, and
  registering it under `run:steer:target:*` would put it in front of `trySteer`, which would push a phrase comment
  into an inbox no relay reads. And a held reply is an answer for AFTER the park, never a message for the running
  agent: written into the inbox, the relay would frame it as a steer (and a steer handed over after the terminating
  tool un-parks the run, `DES-STEER-HELD-WHILE-PARKED`). `worker/src/held-replies.mjs`, `worker/src/held-settle.mjs`,
  `receiver/src/held.mjs`.
- **Traces to**: `REQ-STEER-RUNNING-JOB`, `CONST-RETRY-INFRA-ONLY`, `REQ-RUN-RECOVERY`, `REQ-DEDUP-BY-DELIVERY-GUID`,
  `DES-STEER-HELD-WHILE-PARKED`, `INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT`, `INT-RUN-HISTORY-FILE-CONTRACT`.

## DES-SANDBOX-IS-A-FRESH-CONTAINER

- **Decision**: To let an operator inspect what a run built, **retain the run's inputs and start a new
  container**, rather than preserving the original one in any form. The job container stays single-use,
  `--rm`, TTY-less and port-less; `pi-dispatch sandbox <jobId>` launches a second, differently-named
  container from the same image with the same mounts and no credentials
  (`REQ-RESURRECTABLE-SANDBOX`, `INT-SANDBOX-CONTRACT`).
- **Why**: The thing an operator actually wants is *the app running against the files the agent wrote*.
  That needs the image and the workspace — both of which already exist and are already cheap to keep. It
  does not need the original process tree, and every design that tries to keep one trades away a property
  the whole security model rests on. Framing it as "make it reproducible" rather than "make it survive"
  is what keeps the change confined to how long a directory lives.
- **Rejected**:
  - *Keep the job container alive and `docker exec` into it.* A job container with an open operator
    channel is a different security object from the one every isolation flag was chosen for: it is alive
    while adversarial code has run in it, it still holds the minted forge token and the provider key in
    its environment, and `--rm` — the flag that makes leakage between mutually-untrusting issue authors
    structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely — has to go. The convenience is real and it is
    not worth reopening `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB` for.
  - *A stdin channel to the running agent.* Same objection plus a worse one: it makes the operator an
    input to a session whose prompt already carries untrusted issue text, so the two trust classes meet
    inside a running agent rather than at a boundary. **Still rejected as stdin, and admitted since issue #646
    in one framed, read-only form** (`DES-STEER-VIA-READONLY-INBOX-MOUNT`, `REQ-STEER-RUNNING-JOB`): a trigger that
    sets `run.steer` lets a message reach its running agent through files the worker writes into a per-attempt
    directory mounted read-only at `/inbox`. stdin itself stays out (issue #545 uses it for the exit key, written
    and closed before any tool exists). The objection above is answered on four counts, and each is a property of
    the mechanism rather than a promise. **The same trust and framing as the text that started the run**: a message
    is framed by the worker as data, not instructions, with its sender named only by closed-charset fields, and
    fenced with the fence the issue text gets, so the trust classes still meet at a boundary the worker draws,
    exactly where they meet for the invoking comment. **No operator authority**: an operator's message is framed
    with no more authority than a comment's, since standing operator authority lives in the reviewed triggers file
    (`run.instructions`), so a console token or a shell cannot rewrite a run's guardrails in flight. **One way, read
    only**: the job cannot write `/inbox` (proved by `verify-image.sh`), the delivery ack travels back in the
    transcript under a MAC keyed by the attempt's exit key, and the container gains no network path, credential or
    process channel. **No extra container lifetime**: nothing keeps a container alive to wait for a message; the
    runner closes its inbox when the run settles, a message after that is `late`, and the container ends when its
    run does. What this does not change is the rest of this bullet's neighbours: no `docker exec` into a job, no
    TTY, no published port, `--rm` kept. **Admitted since issue #680 in a second form, framed and MAC'd stdin, on
    copying venues only** (`DES-STEER-VIA-READONLY-INBOX-MOUNT`, decided there, built in #686 and shipped on `openshell`, AMENDED 2026-10-19):
    where a venue uploads `/job` once and no mount can carry a later message, a steer-armed attempt whose image
    declares `steerStdin` keeps the main exec's stdin open after the exit key, which is frame 1 and drained before
    any tool exists, and every later frame is a steer message MAC'd under that key. The same four counts, answered
    the same way except the third. **The same trust and framing**: a frame carries the worker's `frameSteerMessage`
    text, unchanged. **No operator authority**: unchanged, the framing is the same. **One way, and NOT read only**:
    the agent can open the pipe through `/proc` for reading and writing, so a frame it plants has no valid MAC and is
    dropped, but a frame it reads is consumed, which withdraws that message; the withdrawal shows as an ack that never
    arrives, reported undelivered as today, never as a delivery. That is weaker than the mount, stated as such, and it
    is why a venue that binds keeps the mount and never takes this form. The container still gains no network path,
    credential or listening socket, and tool children get `/dev/null` as stdin. **No extra container lifetime**:
    unchanged, the runner closes the channel when the run settles. And still no TTY: the exec is started without
    one.
  - *`docker commit` the container at exit.* This preserves strictly more — installed packages, process
    residue — and costs gigabytes per run to do it. It serves a 5% case that image+workspace already
    serves, and the extra it preserves is mostly the part that should have been in the image. The honest
    version of the contract ("same image, same workspace, fresh processes") is the one that stays cheap.
  - *Publish a port on job containers, gated by config.* An always-available network surface on the
    untrusted side, live for every run, to serve the runs an operator is watching. The publish flag
    exists only on an operator-started sandbox and only while it is up, bound to `127.0.0.1`.
  - *Exempt `pi-sandbox-*` from the boot reaper by editing its filter.* The reaper's `name=pi-job-`
    filter is a substring match, so a **separate namespace** already achieves this with no change to the
    reaper at all. Editing the filter would put the guarantee in the reaper's code; keeping the names
    disjoint puts it in the names, where a test can pin it. **Still rejected after issue #337**, and that
    issue is what tested it: a session network left by a dead shell needed a sweep, and it got one inside
    the SANDBOX reaper, keyed on the shape `sandbox.mjs` itself builds. The boot reaper's filter is
    untouched, so "a worker restart cannot kill a shell you are sitting in" stays a property of the names.
  - *Widen `makeLogReaper` to sweep retained directories too.* Its `.log`/`.json` filter and `logsDir`
    scope are a documented contract, and these directories have a different retention policy, a
    different PII class, and one requirement neither sibling has — asking docker what is live before
    deleting. `session-store.mjs`'s `reapSessions` already set this precedent for the same reasons.
    **The half that still holds is that last one, and issue #337 leaned on it**: the sandbox reaper now
    sweeps two kinds of object on two predicates, directories on the clock and session networks on the
    directory, and both need the docker reads only this reaper makes. The other half, "one reaper per
    retention policy", is unchanged: nothing moved into `makeLogReaper`, and the new work is a sweeper
    INJECTED into the sandbox reaper so `sandbox-store.mjs` stays docker-free in its own tests.
- **Traces to**: `REQ-RESURRECTABLE-SANDBOX`, `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB`,
  `CONST-TOKEN-SCOPED-PER-JOB`, `INT-SANDBOX-CONTRACT`, `DES-RUN-HISTORY-FLAT-FILES-NO-DB`,
  `DES-STEER-VIA-READONLY-INBOX-MOUNT`, `DES-OPENSHELL-VENUE`

## DES-EGRESS-DENY-ON-A-DEDICATED-NETWORK

- **Decision**: Ship the egress control as **one `--internal` Docker network per job, named in the worker's
  own `docker run` argv**, plus **one long-lived allowlist proxy** attached to each of those networks for the
  life of that run, filtering by hostname and never terminating TLS: a `CONNECT` to port 443 or a plain request
  to port 80, both to a listed host, and nothing else (issue #508). The provider is an ordinary
  entry on the allowlist. A **pre-spend check** on the proxy refuses a job the policy cannot serve. Off
  unless `PI_EGRESS=0`, and on every job with no per-trigger opt-out (`REQ-EGRESS-ALLOWLIST`,
  `INT-EGRESS-POLICY-CONTRACT`).
- **Why**: The rules were already written down and already run (`docs/sandbox.md`, issue #199, which touched
  zero code files). What was missing was not the mechanism but **the worker knowing about it**. Every
  property this project relies on -- reporting a refusal an operator can act on, checking a control in
  `doctor`, refusing before money is spent -- needs the policy to be an object the worker names. That is
  what makes this an argv change rather than a documentation change, and it is why the network and not the
  proxy is the load-bearing half.
- **Plain HTTP on port 80, not HTTPS only** (issue #508, the owner's decision). The rules had no port rule for a
  request that is not a `CONNECT`, so any tool that forwards plain HTTP (npm undici's `EnvHttpProxyAgent`
  without `proxyTunnel`, a package manager) reached every port of a listed host. The job image's git is not one:
  it ignores `HTTP_PROXY` for an `http://` remote, so a forge must be `https://` on 443 with the policy on.
  They now carry stock squid's `Safe_ports`, narrowed to port 80, as `http_access deny !Safe_ports !CONNECT`
  right before `http_access allow allowed`. Refusing plain HTTP entirely was the alternative, and it is rejected
  for now because some package mirrors and redirects still use port 80; pi itself does not need it, since pi
  and the runner tunnel every origin. What port 80 carries crosses the network in clear text, and
  `docs/egress.md` says so. Also rejected: a port rule after the allow (first match wins, so it would never
  apply), and a `dst` rule ahead of `allowed` (it would resolve every requested name, a DNS channel out). `doctor`
  reads the rule back with a third canary probe, a raw forward request to `api.anthropic.com:443`.
- **What cleans up, and why never `-f`** (issues #357, #350). The job path removes its own network in a
  `finally`; what that cannot cover is a worker that DIED, and the boot reaper's sweep for those was a bare
  `network rm` inside a `try {} catch {}` whose comment said an in-use network "belongs to something else".
  On the one path the sweep exists for it does not: the container is reaped, and the only thing still holding
  the network is this worker's own long-lived proxy, which nothing detached when the process died. So the
  failure had nowhere to go and the network survived every later boot, silently. The reaper now inspects
  first, detaches WHAT IT SAW, removes without `-f`, and names anything that stays. `doctor`'s canary had the
  same shape from the other end: its 30 s bound kills the docker CLI, not the container the CLI started, so a
  wedged proxy left a probe on the canary network and the teardown's `network rm` failed unread.
  - **The namespace is the NAME, not the filter.** `docker`'s `--filter name=` is a SUBSTRING match, so
    `network ls --filter name=pi-job-` also returns an operator's own `my-pi-job-notes` and anything with
    the prefix in the middle. Measured on docker 27.4.0 by creating exactly that name and watching it come
    back. So the filter is the cheap server-side narrowing and an ANCHORED test on the name is the namespace
    decision, in both halves of the sweep. This matters MORE than it did before the sweep detached: the old
    one would only have failed to `rm` a foreign network that was in use, while this one detaches first, so
    without the anchor it would strip an operator's containers off their own network.

    **What that anchored test IS changed at issue #360, and it is a decision reversed, not refined.** This
    bullet used to say the sweep decides on the shape the producer builds
    (`networkNameFor(jobContainerName(id))`), derived from both constants, "and the container half takes the
    same narrowing". The container half never took it: it was a bare `startsWith(JOB_NAME_PREFIX)` the whole
    time, and no charset rule could have narrowed it, because the ids reaching `jobContainerName` are
    BullMQ's `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` and `runner_default` is a legal one. So the two halves gave DIFFERENT answers
    to "what is ours": an operator's `pi-job-runner_default` lost its container at every boot and kept its
    network. Both halves now ask one exported predicate, `isJobNamespace`, and it is the prefix.

    **The cost is real and is accepted rather than argued away.** A compose project named `pi-job-tools`
    builds a network `pi-job-tools_default`; under the old shape it was not a candidate, and now it is.
    Its members are detached before it is removed, and the one carve-out that exists does NOT save them: the
    sweep leaves a network alone only while a container UNDER THE PREFIX is attached, so a stack whose
    services carry explicit `container_name:` values keeps running with its network gone. The weighing:
    a rule that destroys half of a stack while sparing the other half by an accident of suffix is not a
    protection, it is a coin flip, and that is the whole of the argument. It is deliberately NOT the argument
    two earlier drafts of this entry made, and both of them were wrong in the same direction: that the
    network half is the cheap one. Measured on docker 27.4.0 and compose v2.31.0, it is not. `docker network
    connect` cannot undo it at all, because this sweep removes the network rather than only detaching from
    it. `docker compose up -d` does restore the network with its labels, aliases and service-name DNS, and it
    RECREATES the service containers to do so, discarding everything written inside them -- the same loss the
    container half causes outright. A hand-made network loses its subnet, gateway, driver options and labels;
    a compose `external:` one is worse still, since `up -d` then refuses outright and leaves the containers
    attached to nothing. So the two halves cost about the same, and this change is taken on coherence rather
    than on cheapness. `SECURITY.md`'s *What is NOT defended* states the whole of it for operators.

    **ONE PREDICATE IS NOT ONE QUESTION, and the two questions are now BOTH answered (issue #379, item 1).**
    The halves ask the same thing OF A NAME and deliberately different things OF THE DAEMON. The container
    loop lists with `docker ps`, running-only. The network loop asks twice: `network inspect`'s `.Containers`
    for what the daemon itself guards, and then `ps -a --filter network=` for members in ANY state. Without
    the second, a `created` or `exited` `pi-job-` container survived the container half and lost its network
    to the network half -- and could then never start, because it holds a network id the daemon no longer
    has (`docker start` answers `network <id> not found`, measured on docker 27.4.0 for both states; the
    carve-out could not save it, since `.Containers` lists only running endpoints).

    **The states are an ALLOWLIST** (`ENDPOINT_LISTED_STATES`, following `sandbox.mjs`): `running` and
    `paused` are what `.Containers` lists and what makes `network rm` refuse on its own, so for those the
    existing detach-or-leave logic is the right conversation. Everything else -- `created`, `exited`, `dead`,
    a Podman state nothing here has measured -- keeps the network and is named in
    `network_not_reaped {reason: "container-attached-not-running", containers}`. `restarting` is excluded on
    purpose: whether a flapping container appears in `.Containers` depends on the instant of the ask.

    **The container half is NOT widened to `ps -a`, and that asymmetry is the decision.** This half only
    DECLINES to remove a network, which costs a leftover network and a line saying so. The container half
    `rm -f`s what it finds, so listing stopped containers would destroy an operator's own and a crashed job's
    forensic one. A stopped container also spends nothing, and the reaper exists for the ones that do.

    **The egress proxy is the one member this rule steps over, and the sweep would not work otherwise.** This
    sweep exists for the shape where a worker died mid-job and the only thing still holding the network is
    that worker's own long-lived proxy. If the proxy is STOPPED at reap time -- an operator who turned the
    policy off, a host that rebooted -- protecting it would leave every leftover job network standing
    forever, logged once per boot, with nothing in the project that would ever remove them. A stopped
    container can be detached (`network disconnect -f`, exit 0, measured), and the network it loses is a dead
    job's, which is not one the proxy needs in order to start.

    **Residuals, stated rather than closed.** A leftover `created` or `exited` `pi-job-<id>` keeps its
    network and is named on every boot, which is the intended cost: that container can still be started by
    hand and would be unstartable without it. On Podman that hazard does not arise at all, MEASURED (issue #452,
    4.9.3 and 5.8.1): its `network rm` without `-f` refuses while a member in ANY state remains, a lone `created`
    or `exited` one included, so a sweep there cannot strand a container by removing its network; the refusal
    costs a leftover network and a line instead, and the reaper now reads that member with `ps -a` on Podman since
    4.9 renders no `.Containers`. Rejected: a `stillClear` callback, which would add a reconnect path
    to a sweep with no live owner, and force-detaching stopped members, which silently rewrites an operator
    container's configuration.

    **The alternative, and why it is not taken.** A docker label (`--label dev.pi-dispatch.job=<id>` plus
    `--filter label=`) is unambiguous and would survive an operator choosing the same prefix. It cannot be
    on what a worker that crashed BEFORE the change already created, and recovering those is the entire
    reason this sweep exists, so the migration is the real content of that decision and it has not been
    made. The sandbox's own `SANDBOX_NETWORK_SHAPE` deliberately keeps a full shape with a capture group,
    because that sweep parses the session id back out of the name; a predicate cannot answer that question,
    which is why the two look inconsistent and are not.
  - **Detach what is attached, never a proxy named from configuration.** It needs no `env` seam in the
    reaper, and it is right where a configured name is wrong: a network left before a `PI_EGRESS_PROXY`
    change holds the OLD proxy, and with the policy off it holds nothing. Inspecting is also the only way to
    see the one case that must be left alone.
  - **Three primitives in `egress.mjs`, not a generic sweeper.** The "not there" rule classifies ANOTHER
    tool's prose across two runtimes and was earned over three review rounds in `live-probes.mjs`, so it is
    one copy beside the proxy name and the network suffix, on this file's own stated ground that a rename
    landing in the producer and not in the reaper is the failure mode. What is NOT shared is the policy: each
    site's protected endpoint is a different security argument, and a helper whose parameters are the
    decision hides the decision.
  - **The fourth namespace: a SESSION network, swept on the retained directory's clock** (issue #337).
    `openSandbox` creates `pi-sandbox-<id>-net` before `docker run` and removes it in its own `finally`; a
    shell whose terminal died leaves it, and nothing removed it, because #277 had withdrawn removal AT OPEN
    TIME, where it raced a second open. A background sweep does not race that: an open in progress always
    has its retained directory, so the sandbox retention reaper takes only an id that is absent from BOTH the
    directory listing the pass began with and a fresh one read immediately before the sweep, is not running,
    and has no `pi-sandbox-` container attached. Two listings rather than one, because each end of the pass
    leaks a different way. Keying on what SURVIVES the pass would remove the network of a run being opened
    between `createJobNetwork` and `launch`, since the same pass expires directories and an open that passed
    `resolveSandbox` a moment earlier is mid-launch. Keying on the pre-pass listing ALONE leaks the other
    end: `retainJobDir` creates a retained directory at job end, in this same process, so a job can finish
    and its run be opened while the pass is still running, and that id is in neither the old listing nor the
    running set. A re-read that throws skips the sweep rather than sweeping on half the evidence, and the
    price of the first half is that a network outlives its directory by one whole pass. The LAST call before the removal is a
    `docker ps -a` for that id, and its placement is the point rather than a detail: read at the top of the
    pass it is OLDER than the candidate listing, because an open creates its network before its container,
    and a review pass drove exactly that on real docker (486 ms of exposure, the network removed, the
    operator's `docker run` dead with a 125). Candidates first, then the evidence that protects them,
    freshest last. Only `exited` and `dead` free a network; every other state is hands off and is SAID, since
    a container stuck mid-launch is invisible to every other listing and to `--list`. It exists because of a
    measurement that CORRECTS one this project shipped under #357: `.Containers` lists running endpoints only, and the earlier comment generalised that to "listed and
    holds the network agree". Measured on 27.4.0: a container created on a network but never started is
    absent from `docker ps`, absent from `network inspect`, and the `network rm` SUCCEEDS, after which
    `docker start` fails with "network not found" and the container can never run. So the daemon is a
    backstop for a RUNNING endpoint and for nothing else, and `docker run` holds a sandbox in that state for
    230 ms on a local image and for the whole pull when it is not local. The endpoint guard gates the DETACH
    rather than the removal, which is the sharper way to say what is left for it: for a running endpoint the
    daemon already refuses the removal, so the harm remaining is stripping the proxy off a shell someone is
    sitting in. The refusal at open time is unchanged, and the cost is named rather than hidden: a leftover
    on a run that is still re-openable survives until its window closes, which is #337's acceptance line
    narrowed deliberately, since the stricter reading is what reopens #277.
  - *Rejected*: `network rm -f` at any of the four sites (it pulls a network out from under a live endpoint,
    restating the #344 entry); detaching the CONFIGURED proxy by name rather than what is attached; building
    `removeNetworkOrSay` on `removeJobNetworkWith` (it would force-detach the proxy before anything inspected
    the endpoint list, which is exactly the harm the guard exists to prevent) or the reverse (it would add an
    inspect to the job's own teardown, which a test pins as exactly two calls); a generic
    `sweepNetworks(prefix, protect)`; `--cidfile` for the canary probes (it earns its complexity in
    `live-probes.mjs` because those containers are `-d` and one name is deliberately reused, so a name is
    ambiguous THERE; here each name is unique per process and per direction, and the 125 branch shows the
    NAME is the discriminator wanted, which a cidfile cannot express); and putting the canary's dead-pid
    sweep in `--live` (the module that makes an object sweeps it, and `--live` is opt-in by typing a flag,
    so operators who never ask for a container read-back would accumulate networks forever). For the session
    sweep specifically: a `network inspect --format '{{.Created}}'` grace period (it needs a timestamp that
    parses on BOTH runtimes, and Podman renders Go's `time.Time`, which `Date.parse` is not guaranteed to
    accept, so a rule whose safe direction depends on an unparsed string fails in the wrong direction on the
    runtime nobody measured); remembering a candidate across two consecutive sweeps (state the periodic sweep
    deliberately does not carry, and at the 24 h default it buys a day of latency for no extra safety over
    the directory); keying on the directories that SURVIVE the pass rather than the ones it started with; and
    widening the boot reaper's own filter to `pi-sandbox-`, which `DES-SANDBOX-IS-A-FRESH-CONTAINER` rejected
    and which the injected sweeper honours rather than reverses.
- **One canary, on the runtime of the venue it reads** (issue #431). `doctor`'s canary (`runEgressCanary`) is one
  function over a venue's bounded runner and its CLI's name, and three callers share it: docker's plain `doctor`,
  the `podman` venue's `doctor --live` under the worker account's own rootless Podman, and
  `.github/scripts/podman-conformance.mjs`. Its dead-pid sweep takes the same runner, so each runtime's leftovers are
  listed and removed in that runtime's own namespace under the unchanged name filter. The point is WHICH proxy is
  read: a podman job's network is joined to a proxy under the same rootless Podman, so docker's canary said nothing
  about it, and the conformance script's own copy, a plain `fetch`, proved the network and the allowlist but not the
  runner's route (#427's gap, a second time). On podman the probe containers are built by the podman job builder as
  the job user (`egressCanaryProbeArgs`), with no mount; docker's argv is left exactly as it was and pinned against a
  capture taken before the move. Rejected: a podman argv like docker's short one (the account's containers.conf
  defaults what an argv does not pin, #428, so such a probe could carry doctor's environment or the host's proxy
  variables and pass for a reason no job has); `PODMAN_PINNED_FLAGS` and the user added to that short argv (still a
  second argv for a job-shaped container, which is the drift the builder exists to prevent); running the podman
  canary on every plain `doctor` as docker's does (two cold keep-id starts, and `--live` is where this venue already
  starts job-shaped containers, so the plain run points there instead); and a canary copy kept in the conformance
  script. The earlier Rejected entry "the canary's dead-pid sweep in `--live`" still holds for docker and is not
  reversed for podman: there the sweep sits with the only thing that makes the object, which is that entry's own
  rule, and an operator who never types `--live` never has a podman canary network to accumulate.
- **Rejected**:
  - *The `DOCKER-USER` host recipe as the shipped form.* It works. What it cannot be is **known**: the
    worker cannot report it in the run record, `doctor` cannot check it, a Docker upgrade that rewrites the
    chain removes it with no signal, and a second worker on the host inherits it without asking. An
    operator who believes they have a control they cannot verify is in a **worse** position than one who
    knows they have none, because the belief displaces the credential bound that is actually holding it.
    Shipping it as code is worse still: a host process that deliberately refuses to mount `docker.sock`
    because "a socket mount is root-equivalent access to the host" would instead take root directly, to
    write firewall rules, on Linux only, for a worker whose own `service.mjs` also renders launchd plists
    and nssm services. It survives as an appendix in `docs/egress.md`, for an operator who wants a layer
    *underneath* docker's rules rather than instead of them.
  - *One shared network with `com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false`.* This was the design until it was
    measured. ICC governs **every** container pair on that bridge and the proxy is a container, so the
    option blocks job-to-proxy along with job-to-job: the control defeats itself. Verified in both
    directions against a control network where the same connection succeeds. Without the option, a shared
    network is a shared L2 segment for `DES-CONCURRENCY-3` mutually-untrusting issue authors -- and worth
    stating precisely, because the tempting overclaim is available: two job containers on docker's default
    bridge can already reach each other **by IP** today, so a shared network would not create that
    adjacency, only make it resolvable **by name**. Per-job networks remove it outright.
  - *A network-layer rule permitting the provider by address*, which is what the recipe does and what
    `OQ-004` recorded as forced. Refuted by measurement rather than preference (see the requirement): the
    provider follows the proxy once `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY` actually reaches the runner, and the flag was
    missing from the recipe's `PI_FORWARD_ENV` line, not unavailable. (Once pi is loaded it also needs the
    runner to put the proxy back, issue #427; the design is unchanged by that.) An address rule permits whatever
    answers on that address and goes stale silently when the provider re-resolves; it also cannot be
    expressed inside a docker internal network at all, so adopting it would have dragged the whole design
    back to host firewall rules.
  - *A TLS-terminating, secrets-injecting proxy.* `OQ-011`'s mechanism, and not merely larger: a
    **different security object**, in which the provider key stops living in the container and starts living
    in a host process that reads provider plaintext, needing its own constitution entry and its own story
    for the proxy's own compromise. Named here so this design is never mistaken for a down payment on it,
    and so the conflation `OQ-004` warned about (its corroboration bullet, "the two must not be conflated",
    `open-questions.md:168-171` at issue #680; the `:89-92` this bullet cited had gone stale) does not happen at the
    one moment it was warning about. **SUPERSEDED for a venue that declares its own egress layer (issue #680)**:
    `CONST-VENUE-EGRESS-LAYER` is the constitution entry this bullet asked for, with the compromise story, and
    `DES-OPENSHELL-VENUE` is its first venue, where the layer is the venue's own supervisor and not a proxy this
    worker runs. It is NOT superseded for `local` and `podman`: the Decision above is UNCHANGED for them, squid stays
    hostname-only and never terminates TLS, and the conflation is still refused, because the layer is the
    secrets-holding object and the allowlist proxy stays the allowlist.
  - *The worker starting the proxy at boot.* Today the worker starts only ephemeral `--rm` containers it
    reaps by a name filter. A long-lived, network-attached, restart-policied component is a different
    lifecycle object, and making the worker responsible for a security control's **uptime** creates the one
    failure this whole feature exists to prevent: a control that is believed up while it is down. It is a
    compose profile, and `up` offers it behind the same consent gate every other host mutation gets.
  - *A `run.network` trigger field.* A per-trigger egress relaxation is a per-trigger security downgrade,
    and it would need a model-callable exclusion maintained in perpetuity. The deployment configures egress;
    a trigger never does.
  - *An allowlist read from the serviced repo's `.pi/`.* Merge-gated content, and `DES-AI-TRIGGER-FLOW-GATE`
    takes only a **boolean** from that file for precisely this reason: an egress allowlist from a repo is
    the repo naming where the agent may send the operator's credentials.
  - *A denylist.* It fails open on everything nobody thought of, which is the failure mode this exists to
    remove.
  - *Handing the operator a `squid.conf` to edit*, which is what the recipe does. A misordered `http_access`
    silently allows everything, so the ordering ships and the operator's file is a list of hostnames with no
    ordering in it at all.
  - *Caching the preflight's answer across jobs.* `image-preflight.mjs` caches nothing on purpose, and a
    stale "the proxy is fine" is wrong in the direction that costs a budget slot.
  - *A per-job reachability probe.* It would prove what the presence check cannot, and it costs a throwaway
    container start on the money path before every job, converts a determinate gate into a flaky one, and
    means every job on every deployment makes an unauthenticated request to a third party before it starts.
    That belongs in `doctor`, once, when a human asks for it.
- **Read back** (issue #344): `doctor --live` builds two job-shaped networks with the job path's own
  `createJobNetworkWith`, puts a peer on each and checks that the first cannot reach the second by name or address
  while it can reach the proxy, and that the second answers its own addresses before and after the attempt
  (`INT-LIVE-PROBE-CONTRACT`), so the adjacency this entry removes is read back on the
  operator's own daemon, Podman's netavark included, rather than assumed from the Docker measurement.
- **Residual, measured rather than reasoned (issue #345)**: `--internal` bounds where the network routes, not who
  the host is. The network's gateway IS this host, so a service listening on `0.0.0.0` here answers a job that
  dials the gateway address, while one bound to `127.0.0.1` does not. Measured on Docker 27.5.1 and rootful Podman
  5.8.2 with the job path's own `createJobNetworkWith` and the builder's argv: `0.0.0.0:9999` answered from inside
  a job, `127.0.0.1:9997` and an unused port both gave `ECONNREFUSED`. The loopback binding is what bounds it, which
  is why `deploy/docker-compose.yml` publishes Valkey on `127.0.0.1` and why `docs/egress.md` now says so where it
  used to say "no route anywhere except an allowlist proxy". The `DOCKER-USER` appendix is the layer that would
  close it, and shipping that recipe as code is already Rejected above. The loopback binding bounds it only while
  nothing maps the host's loopback into a container's network, and on the native `podman` venue an account's
  containers.conf can (issue #428, measured): that venue refuses such a conf outright
  (`DES-PODMAN-NATIVE-ROOTLESS-BACKEND`), and `deploy/egress-proxy.conf` denies a listed name resolving to a fixed
  loopback, link-local or slirp4netns `10.0.2.2` destination before any allow, as defence in depth. That deny is an
  address rule, and it is not the one Rejected above: it only ever refuses, so it cannot go stale into permitting
  anything. It names `allowed` before `to_host_local`, so an unlisted name is never resolved by the proxy at all
  (a bare `dst` rule resolved every name asked for, a DNS channel out, measured).
- **The teardown's detach has a runtime side effect on Podman 4.9 (issue #458, measured).** The per-job
  `network disconnect` of the proxy, unchanged here, tears down a rootless Podman 4.9 account's shared network
  helper under the running proxy whenever no other bridge container runs, so every later egress job got 503. The
  network-per-job design stands: the fix is a runtime workaround on that venue, the rootless network keeper
  (`DES-PODMAN-STACK-AS-QUADLET-UNITS`), not a change to what is created, attached or removed. Never detaching, a
  reused pool of networks and restarting the proxy after each teardown were weighed there and rejected.
- **A local model server is reached THROUGH the proxy, never around it (issue #503).** A declared model endpoint
  (`INT-MODEL-ENDPOINTS-FILE-CONTRACT`) is one more CONNECT allow in the proxy's rules, rendered into an included
  file, for exactly one host and one port. The job keeps its `--internal` network with the proxy as its only peer,
