- **A job's size on this venue** (issue #596, phase 1): the podman builder shares `argsFromSpec`, so a podman job
  carries the same size flags as a `local` one, in the same place (`--memory`, an equal `--memory-swap`, `--cpus`,
  `--cpu-shares`, `--shm-size`). Measured on this venue: `--memory-swap` equal to `--memory` reads `memory.swap.max` 0
  rootless on Podman 4.9.3 and 5.8.1 (where the default gives swap equal to memory, and Fedora's zram makes that real
  swap), and `--cpu-shares` reaches `cpu.weight` rootless with the cpu controller delegated, the controller `--cpus`
  already needed (an account without it fails every job at create, which doctor's delegated-controllers line names).
  crun 1.14 maps shares linearly (1024 to 39) and crun 1.27 so that 1024 is 100, both keeping the order. The `--cpus`
  ceiling comes from this venue's own `podman info` (`host.cpus`), read with the job user, minus one when it has four
  or more; a rootless account's own `cpu.max` or `memory.max` (its systemd user service, `max` on both lab hosts) is
  not read in phase 1, and the phase 2 host budget takes the smaller of the two.
- **Traces to**: `DES-PODMAN-STACK-AS-QUADLET-UNITS`, `DES-CONTAINER-BACKEND-REGISTRY`, `DES-PODMAN-THROUGH-ITS-DOCKER-API`,
  `DES-JOB-USER-INFERRED-READ-BACK-ON-REQUEST`, `INT-CONTAINER-RUNTIME-CONTRACT`, `INT-LIVE-PROBE-CONTRACT`,
  `INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`, `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB`, `CONST-EGRESS-POLICY-IN-THE-ARGV`, `OQ-036`,
  `OQ-037`

## DES-PODMAN-STACK-AS-QUADLET-UNITS

- **Decision**: On the native rootless `podman` venue the long-lived containers the worker needs, Valkey and
  (while `PI_EGRESS` is armed) the allowlist proxy on its route-out network and the rootless network keeper on a
  network of its own (issue #458, below), are **Quadlet units in the worker account's own user manager**, shipped as
  six files in `deploy/` (`pi-dispatch-valkey.network`, `pi-dispatch-valkey.container`,
  `pi-dispatch-egress-out.network`, `pi-dispatch-egress-proxy.container`, `pi-dispatch-netns-keeper.network`,
  `pi-dispatch-netns-keeper.container`) and
  installed by ONE planner, `worker/src/podman-stack.mjs`, which both `pi-dispatch service install` (user scope) and
  `pi-dispatch up` call: `up.mjs`'s own doctrine that two ways of starting one thing is two places for it to drift.
  Install is: write the files into `~/.config/containers/systemd/`, `systemctl --user daemon-reload`,
  `systemctl --user start` the container units, **never `enable`**. The worker unit gains `Wants=` and `After=`
  on exactly the units installed. `up` shows the planner's action list and, on consent (or `--yes`), hands the SAME
  objects to the applier, so what runs is literally what was shown.
  - **Which parts.** Valkey only where `local` is not blessed: with `local` in `PI_BACKENDS` docker is on the host
    and its Valkey (compose, or `up`'s docker step) stays the queue, and a second one would only fail to bind. `up`
    also leaves Valkey alone while anything listens on `127.0.0.1:6379`, as its docker step does; `service install`
    keeps (and orders the worker after) a Valkey unit an earlier run installed even though that unit is now the
    listener. **Whose listener** (issue #464, the comment on it): on a host with several accounts a fresh account's
    install took ANOTHER account's Valkey on 6379 as its own, and its worker drained that account's queue. So both
    commands decide through one function, `decideValkey`, on the verdict of `judgeValkeyListeners`, which doctor uses
    too, and which the WORKER runs at every start (`resolveWorkerValkey`, gate round 2): the judgement lives where the
    connection is made, since a `VALKEY_URL` edited after `service install` refused it, a `0.0.0.0` URL, and another
    account publishing `[::1]` after the install each reached another account's queue through an unjudged worker
    (measured on Fedora 44). The worker refuses with exit 2, and every Valkey client it makes connects to the judged
    literal address (`pinnedValkeyUrl`; a `rediss:` name kept as the TLS servername), so no later DNS answer or
    address order can redirect it. Of the addresses that answer, the first this account holds is chosen; another
    account's listener on another address of the same name is reported, never dialled. Rejected: refusing the whole
    name there, which would let any account stop another's worker by publishing a port on `::1`, and pinning what
    `service install` judged, which a restart would have to read back from somewhere and would still be wrong after
    an edit. Unspecified addresses (`0.0.0.0/8`, `::`, `::ffff:0.0.0.0`) are this host's loopback of their family,
    which is what a connect to them reaches. `PI_VALKEY_SHARED` is read from `.env` only, by all four; subordinate uid
    ranges come from `getsubids(1)` where installed (SSSD ranges included), else `/etc/subuid`, and the refusal says
    which. Every Valkey client of the project connects the same way (`valkey-endpoint.mjs`): `connection.mjs` builds
    each ioredis and BullMQ client with a connector that asks `judgedEndpoint` for the address on every connect (the
    name resolved once per process, the pinned address re-judged each time), `makeQueue` and the worker refuse a
    connection built otherwise, and a test fails on any file that imports ioredis or bullmq or constructs a client
    outside those three places. The receiver and the admin panel already import `connection.mjs` from this package,
    so they share the one function rather than a copy. Gate round 3 made the rule one for every client, depending on
    neither the directory it runs from nor a guess at the venue (it had depended on both: `pi-dispatch run` and the
    receiver started from `$HOME` found no `.env`, judged nothing and reached another account's Valkey, and the admin
    panel adopted another account's `[::1]`): on Linux a listener held by a uid that is neither this account's, nor a
    subordinate uid of it, nor root is refused by every client on every venue, `PI_VALKEY_SHARED=1` in the `.env`
    excepted; root's (and an answer no socket row explains, which only the kernel's NAT gives, as docker without its
    proxy) is refused only where the deployment's venue is `podman` without `local`, since there no root-owned
    Valkey is this deployment's, while on `local` docker-proxy's is. `PI_VALKEY_SHARED` is never read from the
    environment, even with no `.env` found: it is a fact of the deployment the worker reads from its `.env` only, and
    an environment opt-in would let `run`, the panel or the receiver started elsewhere send jobs into a queue the
    worker refuses. The `.env` is read as bytes through the hardened reader; a hazard in it is carried as an error,
    and a listener other than this account's own is then refused, naming it. A lookup that fails or times out is a
    judgement to retry (the worker and the receiver wait for it, then exit 1), never another host. A judgement that
    throws inside the connector hands ioredis a socket destroyed with that error on the next tick, never a rejected
    `connect()`: measured on ioredis 5.11.1, a rejected connector promise sets the client to `end` for good, so one
    Valkey restart failed every later job; a failed socket goes through its close and retry path, judged again.
    The receiver and its poller judge before building their queue and before listening, and exit 2 on a refusal. Rejected: a judgement at each call site (the CLI, the receiver,
    the panel), which is how the first two rounds left `pi-dispatch run` unjudged. The port is `VALKEY_URL`'s, read from `.env` as the service reads it (6379 unset; `up` takes this shell's only
    where the file sets none and stops when they disagree). The host is resolved as the worker's client resolves it,
    every address (Node tries each in turn, so `localhost` is `::1` and `127.0.0.1`, `::1` first on Fedora 44); every
    one that is this host's (loopback, or an address on its interfaces) is probed, and a name resolving to none of
    them is another host, which adds no Valkey and says so. Each address that answers is judged by the uid of the
    LISTEN socket that answers it in `/proc/net/tcp` and `tcp6`: for IPv4 a socket on the address or `0.0.0.0`, or on
    tcp6 `::` or the address IPv4-mapped; for IPv6 a socket on the address or `::`. Measured on Fedora 44 (pasta) and
    Ubuntu 24.04 (4.9.3, rootlessport): a rootless container's published port is a socket of the ACCOUNT's uid there,
    and one run with `--network host` a socket of one of its SUBORDINATE uids (1467000998 for uid 1467), both files
    readable by every account, where `ss -p` names the process only for the caller's own sockets. Only the account's
    uid and its `/etc/subuid` range count as its own. Root (docker-proxy, a rootful container of any account with
    sudo), a system account, another account and a listener no row explains are refused, naming the owner and both
    ways out: `VALKEY_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:<port>`, at which port the Quadlet Valkey is then published
    (`PublishPort=127.0.0.1:<port>:6379`, the template byte-identical at 6379), or `PI_VALKEY_SHARED=1` in `.env`, the
    one named opt-in for a Valkey shared on purpose, after which each command says whose it is. The refusal is
    blocking: `service install` writes nothing, `--force` or not (`--force` replaces changed files, and taking
    another account's queue must not ride along with that); `up` adds and adopts nothing and exits non-zero; doctor
    prints a ✗ for a `VALKEY_URL` whose listener fails it, so a worker pointed at someone else's Valkey later is
    caught too, and a `VALKEY_URL` line in `.env` doctor cannot read the way the service's loader will is a ✗ in place
    of an owner verdict about the default it would otherwise judge. An `[::1]` URL with nothing answering is an error,
    not an install: the Quadlet Valkey publishes on `127.0.0.1` only. An installed Quadlet Valkey is kept only while
    what answers is this account's; a shared Valkey taken with the opt-in is the queue instead, since a Quadlet
    republished on its port would not bind. Rejected: asking `podman ps` alone, which sees only this account's containers and so cannot tell
    another account's Valkey from a distribution package; probing and judging `127.0.0.1` only, which the first
    version did (a `localhost` URL then reached another account's `[::1]` Valkey, measured end to end on Fedora 44);
    and a `UID_MIN`..`UID_MAX` range to tell "another person" from "a system service", which the first version also
    did: an LDAP or SSSD account sits above `UID_MAX`, Lima's default user at 501 below `UID_MIN`, and a system
    service's Valkey is another tenant's queue all the same, so it is the opt-in's to allow, never a silent rule's.
  - **The Valkey's password** (issue #468). The owner rule above stops an accident; every account on the host shares
    loopback, and a Valkey with no password let any of them read, enqueue or delete another's jobs. So the Quadlet
    Valkey starts with the deployment's `VALKEY_PASSWORD` (from `.env`; `service install` and `up` generate one into
    it when it has none, never for a shared or operator-owned Valkey). The planner writes it to
    `~/.config/pi-dispatch/valkey.env` (0600, the one key), planned like the proxy's rules copy: shown by its path,
    written before the unit, a change (or a mode wider than 0600) restarts the Valkey, `service render` names it and
    never prints it, and uninstall removes it with its unit. The unit reads it with
    `EnvironmentFile=%h/.config/pi-dispatch/valkey.env` (Quadlet passes `%h` through to both lines it generates, and
    systemd expands it; measured on 5.8.1 and 4.9.3), and its `Exec=` is a `sh -c` that hands the value to
    `valkey-server` as configuration on stdin (`valkey-server -`, read from a 0600 temp file that is opened and then
    deleted before the image's entrypoint runs, the value written by the shell's `echo` builtin so it is on no argv),
    unsets it, and execs the image's own entrypoint, whose chown and drop to the `valkey` user run as before. Every `$`
    in the unit is `$$`: Quadlet also loads the file into the unit's own environment, and systemd would expand a bare
    `$VALKEY_PASSWORD` in `ExecStart` into the value, putting it on the podman command line. The health check sends
    the password through `REDISCLI_AUTH` and requires `PONG` (a bare `valkey-cli ping` exits 0 on `NOAUTH`,
    measured). The same script, one constant (`valkey-auth.mjs`), is the compose file's command and `up`'s `docker run`
    (`-e VALKEY_PASSWORD`, the value in the CLI's own environment), and a test holds the three equal. Rejected:
    `--requirepass` on the command (measured: the image's PID 1 is `tini`, which keeps its argv for the life of the
    container, and another account read the password in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` on both VMs; Valkey rewriting its own
    process title does not reach PID 1); the image's `VALKEY_EXTRA_FLAGS` (it appends to that same argv); a mounted
    `valkey.conf` (the image drops to uid 999 before reading it, so a 0600 file of the account is unreadable, and a
    world-readable one defeats the point); a Podman `Secret=` (a second store to keep in step with `.env`, a
    `podman secret create` with the value on stdin in the plan, and compose has no rootless equivalent); `CONFIG SET
    requirepass` after start (a window with no password, and lost on every restart); a password inside `VALKEY_URL`
    (printed by doctor, stored in the admin's pointer, quoted in refusals). The upgrade of a Valkey that ran without
    one is `service install --force`: the new unit and password file restart the Valkey (a SIGTERM stop, so its AOF
    is written out and the volume keeps the queue), and the plan then `try-restart`s the worker and receiver units
    the manager reports active, after it, since they read the password only at start; the install warns, as it does
    for the proxy, that a running job is interrupted. `up` keeps its rule of starting only what does not run, so it
    does not restart a running Valkey for a password; doctor names `service install --force`. The password never
    reaches a log (PR #475's review): ioredis hangs a failed command, a failed AUTH's password included, on the error
    it emits, and a BullMQ Queue or Worker without an `error` listener printed that whole object with `console.error`
    after a rotation (measured against Redis with `CONFIG SET requirepass` and `CLIENT KILL`). `connection.mjs` keeps
    only the command's name on every error any client of the process emits, and every Queue and Worker the project
    builds carries a listener that writes the message alone. Round 2 of that review found the hook on `emit` alone
    missed two paths, both measured: ioredis' `silentEmit` skips `emit()` on a client with no listener, and the same
    error object rejects every command waiting on the connection (`flushQueue`, `abortError`, a reply error). So the
    scrub also wraps `silentEmit` and every `Command`'s `reject` (as `initPromise` makes it), the worker's shared client
    gets a listener, and the entry points print an unhandled rejection as its message alone.
  - **All or nothing for files** (issue #464). A `service install` that failed part way (a root-owned `~/.config`)
    left the stack files it had written and said nothing of them. Every file is now written before any command runs,
    the worker unit inside the applier's `beforeRuns` hook, each write journalled with what was there before it; a
    failed write puts every one back (a new file removed, a replaced one given its old bytes; a write refused before it
    touched the file is not counted), and the refusal names any it could not put back. A COMMAND that fails after the
    writes (a unit that does not start) leaves the stack's files, which its units already run from, names them, and
    puts only the worker unit back, followed by a `daemon-reload`, as the unit was never enabled. `up` journals its
    Quadlet writes the same way: a failed write puts back every file of that run and names what it could not, and a
    failed command names the files that remain. `up` never replaces a file (one that differs is refused first), so
    what it puts back is always a removal. A partial put-back (the worker unit alone) never says that no file of the
    run remains, and names `service uninstall` for the rest; `service uninstall` removes files whose units the manager
    never loaded (a failed `daemon-reload`, whose `stop` then exits 5), asking the manager unit by unit and refusing
    only while one of them runs. The proxy only while armed and only under the default name: a `PI_EGRESS_PROXY` naming another
    container is the operator's own proxy, and a Quadlet of that name would `podman run --replace` it away, so
    neither command installs one and both say why. `up`'s docker egress step follows the same rule since this
    issue: it used to inspect and offer to start the shipped name whatever `PI_EGRESS_PROXY` said. The keeper
    whenever armed, WHATEVER `PI_EGRESS_PROXY` names (issue #458), since the worker detaches an operator's own proxy
    from every job network just the same, and on every Podman version; `up` leaves a running keeper alone, reading
    `{{.State.Running}}`'s output as it does for the proxy, and offers it even where the missing allowlist stops the
    proxy, since it mounts nothing.
  - **The rootless network keeper** (issue #458, measured on Ubuntu 24.04's Podman 4.9.3). `podman network
    disconnect` of the proxy from a job's network, which every egress job's teardown runs, tears down the account's
    shared rootless network namespace and its slirp4netns under the RUNNING proxy whenever no other running
    container is on a bridge network: v4.9.3's `libpod/networking_linux.go` counts the disconnecting container as the
    caller and cleans up at one (4.9.4 and 4.9.5 are identical; gone with Podman 5.0's rootless network rewrite,
    containers/podman#20772 and containers/common#1761, which counts attachments). The next bridge container starts a
    new namespace, the proxy's eth0 goes with the old one, and every later egress job got 503 from the proxy (job 1
    200, jobs 2 to 5 503, through the worker's own `createJobNetwork`/`removeJobNetwork`); `aardvark-dns` stays in the
    dead namespace with a stale record for the proxy (`os error 99`, upstream #20396). A running Valkey unit is a
    bridge container and masked it, so the default stack looked fine while `local`, an external Valkey, a Valkey
    restart window and the conformance job were exposed. The keeper is one idle container that is always a running
    bridge member: `sleep` under catatonit (`RunInit=true`, which Quadlet 4.9.3 has and renders as `--init`, measured) in the proxy's own image and digest (nothing new to pull or pin), on an
    `Internal=true`, `DisableDNS=true` network of its own, `ReadOnly`, `DropCapability=all`, `NoNewPrivileges`, uid and
    gid 65534, no port, no mount, `--image-volume=ignore`; inside it the proxy and 1.1.1.1 were unreachable. With it,
    4.9.3 gave five sequential egress jobs 200 each and the doctor-shaped two-network teardown stayed clean; on 5.8.1
    it changed nothing. `Restart=always` (not the proxy's `on-failure`, since any exit of `sleep infinity` is one to
    undo) brought it back from `podman stop`, `podman stop -a` and `podman rm -f` behind systemd's back, with
    `RestartSec=1s` and `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` (measured on 4.9.3: back on its bridge 1.2 to 1.3 s after a kill; 10
    quick kills and 15 s of a keeper that could not start never ended `failed`; the generator passes the [Unit] key
    through; systemd's defaults, 100 ms and 5 starts in 10 s, would let a keeper that cannot start lock itself out
    `failed` in under a second; 250 ms was measured too, back in 0.45 s, and not taken, because the order rule below
    already treats a keeper that came back under a long-running proxy as damage whatever the gap, and a keeper that
    cannot start would retry four times a second), and `SuccessExitStatus=143` keeps a clean stop `inactive` rather
    than `failed` (measured: without it every stop left the unit failed). Its names are outside every prefix a sweep
    removes, by a test that reads the prefixes off the source. Its network is made again before every start
    (`ExecStartPre`, the `.network` unit's own `podman network create --ignore --disable-dns --internal`, a test holds
    the two equal), because that unit runs once and stays active: measured on 4.9.3, a `podman network prune` with the
    keeper stopped (running, prunes leave it) used to leave every later start failing, and a `podman network rm -f`
    under it killed it for good; with `ExecStartPre` the start after a prune recreated the network, and after a
    `network rm -f` the keeper was back holding in 1.2 s. `reset-failed` stays the first step of every documented repair.
  - **The keeper counts only running on its own bridge network** (issue #463's gate, measured on 4.9.3). A container
    of its name on `--network none`, `slirp4netns`, `pasta` or `host` runs and holds nothing open, and doctor called
    it ✓, `up` "already running", and `doctor --live` then ran the canary whose teardown broke the proxy. One reader
    now serves all three and the worker (`judgeNetnsKeeper` over one `podman inspect` of `{{.State.Status}}`,
    `{{.HostConfig.NetworkMode}}` and the attached networks): it holds only when running, in `bridge` mode, and on
    `pi-dispatch-netns-keeper`; anything else is named. Doctor and the worker add two rules (PR #463 round 2), with an
    injected clock and the proxy's `{{.State.StartedAt.UnixMilli}}` (measured to print epoch ms on 4.9.3): it must have
    run for 3 s (a keeper killed every 0.5 s read as running on its bridge in 57 of 224 back-to-back reads), and it must
    not have started more than 15 s after the proxy. That second one is the only evidence there is of the restart
    window's damage (below): a keeper that came back under a running proxy may have let a teardown cut the proxy's route
    out, which the proxy's own state never shows, so the remedy said is a PROXY restart. The grace is for both starting
    together, and no wider (PR #463 round 3, measured on 4.9.3: 4 to 52 ms apart in three `service install`s, 17 to 50
    ms in three boot-like manager restarts, 63 ms in an `up --yes`; it was a minute, and a review measured a keeper death
    and a teardown inside that minute go unseen). A keeper that does not hold under a proxy up longer than the grace is
    told both steps at once, start it and then restart the proxy. Doctor also reads the keeper's network as it is
    (`{{.Internal}} {{.DNSEnabled}}`, ✗ unless internal with DNS off, on every version), since its units' `--ignore` keeps
    a same-named network whatever its options. The installer says to restart the proxy, by its real name, whenever it
    starts or restarts the keeper beside a proxy it leaves running (an operator's own `PI_EGRESS_PROXY`, or ours already
    up). `managerEnvRefusal` unquotes systemd's `$'...'` form (measured: `$'/home/a b/.config'`) and compares realpaths. `up` asks only the shape, since it only decides whether to leave a keeper be.
  - **The worker checks it pre-spend** (issue #463's gate). On the `podman` venue with egress armed and Podman 4.x or
    an unreported version, the egress preflight reads the keeper after the proxy on every job (the version from the
    bundle's cached `podman info`, the keeper never cached), and one that does not hold is `{ unavailable, keeper }`:
    an INFRA retry before anything is spent, carrying the keeper's sentence and the repair commands, where it used to
    start, spend, and get 503 mid-job. On 5.x nothing is read. Its reason is its own fixed token,
    `netns-keeper-not-holding` (PR #463 round 2), so the run record and the failure hook name it, and a job that runs
    out of retries gets a terminal comment keyed by that token that names the keeper and `pi-dispatch doctor` (never
    the error's words); the whole sentence is logged per attempt (`egress_keeper_not_holding`, and
    `job_failed_netns_keeper` beside the 120-character `job_failed`), and once at boot
    (`netns_keeper_not_holding_at_boot`), since a deployment upgraded without re-running the installer would otherwise
    learn it only from retried jobs. Measured live on 4.9.3 through the worker's own preflight: admitted with the
    keeper up, retried while it was down and for its first 3 s back, admitted again after, retried with "restart the
    egress proxy" once a keeper restart landed more than the grace after the proxy's start (measured with the minute it
    then was) (egress then really was
    broken: a teardown in the gap), and admitted after the proxy restart (egress back).
  - **A keeper that is merely young is waited out, not failed** (issue #476, measured on 4.9.3). When the stack starts
    together (a fresh `service install`, a boot with linger) the worker reads the keeper under a second after it
    started (0.5 to 0.8 s, and 7 ms after the proxy), so the 3 s age rule failed EVERY such start: the boot logged
    `netns_keeper_not_holding_at_boot` with a remedy that restarts the keeper after the proxy (the order the rule then
    flags), and a job queued before the start spent its first attempt on `netns-keeper-not-holding` and ran on its
    second. The age rule was there to catch a crash loop, and a keeper running on its own bridge holds the helper open
    while it runs, so its age alone is a reason to wait, not to fail. `judgeNetnsKeeper` marks a keeper `young`
    (`{ startedMs, ageMs, waitMs }`) when its age is its WHOLE fault: running, bridge mode, on its own network, start
    read, and not started more than the grace after the proxy (waiting cannot make a late start earlier, so an
    out-of-order keeper is not young). `waitMs` is until it is 3 s old plus a 1 s margin, so at most 4 s. It still
    does not hold: doctor keeps its judgement, and `up` and the detach gate never ask about age. Three callers now
    wait instead. The BOOT waits `waitMs` once (capped at 4 s, said as `netns_keeper_young_at_boot`) and judges
    again, and warns only if the keeper still does not hold. A JOB is held, the podman.service hold's move (issue #448): `moveToDelayed` to now plus `waitMs`
    and `DelayedError`, so no attempt is spent and nothing is recorded, with the keeper start it waited on, the hold's
    start and its last check stored on the job. Every pickup is judged by all the rules again, so no job runs any
    earlier than before and #458's protection is untouched: the hold changes only what a young keeper costs. The
    SANDBOX OPENER waits once and judges again, rather than refusing (the choice between waiting and refusing was
    made for waiting, since a refusal there sent an operator to restart a keeper that held).
    **The crash loop the age rule caught is still caught, and named.** A keeper that keeps dying (`Restart=always`,
    `RestartSec=1s`) is young at every start, so an unbounded hold would hold a job for ever. At a check within 30 s
    of the last, a keeper with a NEW start, or none on its bridge, after the job waited on one, is the loop; so is a
    hold that has lasted `NETNS_KEEPER_YOUNG_HOLD_MAX_MS` (30 s, which a keeper that stays up never needs: one wait of
    at most 4 s). Either is INFRA `netns-keeper-crash-loop`: retried (an attempt, as any keeper that does not hold
    costs), recorded, the sentence naming both starts and `journalctl --user -u pi-dispatch-netns-keeper.service`,
    logged whole beside `job_failed`, and a terminal comment of its own. A check more than 30 s after the last (a
    retry after its 60 s backoff, a paused queue) is a fresh hold, since the time between is no evidence of a loop.
    But the loop, once seen, is kept on the job (`netnsKeeperLoopSeen`, the starts seen), outside that window: the
    retry a minute later met a keeper restarted out of order against the proxy and failed as
    `netns-keeper-not-holding`, whose record and comment replaced the loop's (PR #479's gate, measured), so a later
    attempt that fails on the keeper for any reason is named the loop. And a cancelled job is never run again: before
    the processor hands any error back to the queue (this hold, the podman.service hold, or an ordinary retry), one
    shared check, asked on every error only after the cancel poll is stopped and its tick in flight awaited for
    at most 1 s (the
    same stop runs at the container's exit and as the run returns, so no ack ever contradicts a record),
    reads a cancel acknowledged since pickup or (for a retryable error) requested and not yet polled, and ends
    the job as `operator-cancel`; a non-retryable failure leaves an unread request unanswered, so the record and
    the requester agree it failed (`INT-CANCEL-CHANNEL-CONTRACT`).
    Rejected: reading a restart counter to tell a loop from a first start. Podman's `RestartCount` stays 0 for the
    shipped keeper (measured on 4.9.3: each systemd restart is a new `--rm` container), and systemd's `NRestarts`
    exists only for a keeper under the user manager and costs a second read on every young judgement; the start the
    job waited on, compared with the next read, is venue-agnostic and already in hand. Measured on 4.9.3 with this
    change: a fresh `service install` waited 3.4 s at boot and warned nothing; a job queued before a boot-order start
    ran on attempt 1; a job queued on a keeper 0.2 s old was held 3.8 s and ran on attempt 1; with the keeper killed
    at every 2 s of age (19 restarts, `NRestarts=19`, `RestartCount=0`) the job was named `netns-keeper-crash-loop`
    3.9 s after it was queued and never ran (its retry a minute later met no keeper and was named
    `netns-keeper-not-holding`, the defect the marker above closes; pinned by a two-attempt test, not re-measured).
  - **A plan that moves the keeper moves the proxy** (PR #463 round 2). Starting the keeper beside a proxy whose unit
    file stays the same (an upgrade), or restarting it, restarts the proxy after it, with the existing restart warning,
    so the order rule never asks for a proxy restart the installer could have done; a first install starts both
    together. `up` restarts a Quadlet keeper that is there, ours and unchanged but not holding (a paused one, where
    `start` was a no-op and `up` said "installed and started"), and when the proxy it leaves running stays up, says to
    restart it.
  - `doctor` reads it with egress armed: not holding is ✗ on Podman 4.x or an unreported version, ✓ on 5.x. There,
    `doctor --live` also tears nothing down under the proxy, since its own teardowns are the same trigger: no egress
    canary (a second ✗ line says so and names the start command), no stale canary sweep, no jobToJobIsolation peer
    networks, and a stale live-probe network with anything still attached is left and said rather than detached;
    `egress` and `jobToJobIsolation` read "not read back" naming the keeper. On 5.x, or with the keeper running,
    `--live` runs as before.
  - **Where the answer comes from.** Both commands read `PI_BACKENDS`, `PI_EGRESS` and `PI_EGRESS_PROXY` from the
    deployment's `.env` with one reader (`readStackKeys`), the way systemd's `EnvironmentFile=` reads it.
    `service install` reads the file alone, never the shell running it (nothing loads `.env` into a process, so a
    shell export says nothing about what the service runs). `up` lets its shell win where it sets a key, the
    precedence its doctor layering already uses and the one the wizard needs when it runs `up` with
    `PI_BACKENDS=podman` before init has written `.env`, fills the rest from the file, and since round 2 REFUSES a
    key both set differently (below). Since issue #471 doctor applies that one precedence to EVERY service key it
    judges, not only these three (`worker/src/service-env.mjs`, shared with the panel): this shell's value, else the
    file's plain line, a disagreement a ✗, an unreadable line named and unused. Doctor cannot tell a service (which
    never sees its shell) from a worker started by hand (which sees nothing else), and does not guess from the units
    it can read: when the two sources agree there is nothing to tell, and when they differ it fails and names both.
    Before review round 1 `up` read only its shell, so the documented
    "put it in `.env`, run `up`" gave the docker pass. A line touching one of the keys that the loaders read
    differently refuses both commands before anything runs: `PI_BACKENDS =podman` is set by systemd and yields no
    record, `export PI_BACKENDS=podman` the opposite, a value with `$` or quotes the shells expand, and a record of
    none of these would otherwise read as "no podman" and install a docker-shaped worker. An unparseable list or
    `PI_EGRESS` refuses too. On macOS and Windows the answer decides only a note, so it is read with that platform's
    loader and never refuses.
  - **A container the unit does not own is never replaced silently.** A Quadlet container unit runs
    `podman run --replace`, which removes any container of its name: a hand-started proxy (the by-hand route
    `docs/podman.md` still gives) with every job's per-job network on it. The shared installer asks each container
    of the plan for its `PODMAN_SYSTEMD_UNIT` label; one that does not name our unit is foreign, `service install`
    refuses unless `--force` (and then says it replaces it), and `up`, which has no `--force`, installs nothing and
    names both ways out. `up` reads a running proxy from `{{.State.Running}}`'s OUTPUT: an exited container prints
    `false` with exit 0 (measured), and the exit code alone called a stopped hand-started proxy present. Since issue
    #453 it reads `{{.State.Status}}` and counts only `running`: Podman reports a paused container `paused` and one
    between restarts `stopped` (measured on 4.9.3 and 5.8.1). Doctor's podman proxy line says ✗ for `stopped` and
    `restarting`, as docker's says for `restarting` (PR #456's final check), and names the raw status word: a
    `--restart=always` crash loop reads `stopped` continuously, about eight restarts a second, while `podman stop`,
    `--restart=no` and an exhausted `on-failure` read `exited` (measured on Podman 5.8.1, PR #466 gate round 1), so
    the ⚠ it printed ("retried once, then failed") read as a wait while every job failed. Its fix is worded as the
    likely cause rather than a fact, since `stopped` is not only a crash loop; the worker's preflight still retries
    through that state once, unchanged. The docker venue's proxy step reads the same Status, stdout alone, since the
    status word is what names a paused or restarting container (measured on Docker Engine 29.8.1: both read
    `.State.Running` true), and it also asks whether the shipped `pi-dispatch-egress-proxy` is CURRENT: the
    pinned squid digest, the image's own entrypoint and command (read from its registry config; neither compose nor
    `up` sets them), this folder's `deploy/egress-proxy.conf` and `egress-allowlist.conf` mounted, and no mount but
    those and the image's two anonymous volumes (`egress-proxy-state.mjs`). The mounts are compared only where every
    bind source resolves on this host: a runtime that reports its VM's own paths (Docker Desktop's shape, not measured
    here) would otherwise have every proxy read stale, so that half is UNKNOWN, said as a ⚠ and never the ground for a
    removal. A proxy whose image, entrypoint or command differs is still offered the replace while a mount is unknown
    (PR #456's final check: on Docker Desktop such a proxy was otherwise never replaced), resting on how the runtime
    reports those three fields, which is measured on Docker Engine and Podman and NOT on Docker Desktop; the offer is
    shown line for line and asked either way. UNKNOWN only for a source under a VM prefix (`/host_mnt/`,
    `/run/desktop/mnt/host/`) or on a macOS or Windows host (gate round 3's simple rule); on Linux a source that does
    not resolve is gone, and stale. The argv is
    normalised whatever the runtime's spelling: Podman 4.9.3's native inspect renders the entrypoint as a string
    (measured), Docker Engine and Podman 5.8.1, natively and through its Docker API, as a list (measured). Measured on
    Docker Engine 29.8.1 with compose 5.5.1 (rootful): a compose-made and an `up`-made proxy, from a real and a
    symlinked folder, all read current (the symlink's path is kept as given, and resolves to the folder). A current
    stopped one is
    offered `docker start` of that same container (a paused one `docker unpause`): that is what `docker compose
    --profile egress up -d` does to a stopped container whose configuration is unchanged, it keeps a compose-created
    container compose's, and it destroys nothing. A stale one, running or not, would bring back a policy this
    deployment did not ship, so it is offered `docker rm -f` and the shipped run, shown line for line (the network's
    create among them only when `pi-dispatch-egress-out` is missing, a read-only inspect deciding it before the
    question, since `--yes` runs exactly the lines shown and a conditional line is not a command; PR #456's final
    check), naming the job and sandbox networks attached to it, which the removal cuts off mid-run, and saying to stop
    the worker first; a container whose state `docker inspect` answers unreadably is left alone rather than run over;
    doctor's egress section says the same ✗ for a running stale one, judging the mounts only when run from a folder
    holding the two files. A container `PI_EGRESS_PROXY` names is the operator's: reported, never started or judged
    stale, and doctor's fix for it names `docker start`, not compose, which starts only the shipped name.
  - **A replaced file restarts its unit.** `--force` over a changed `.container` file restarts that unit, because
    `start` on an active unit does nothing, and warns first when it is the proxy. A changed `.network` file restarts
    nothing: its unit runs `podman network create --ignore`, which cannot change an existing network.
  - **The gate is stricter than the worker's boot, on purpose** (round 2, reversing round 1). The worker's
    boot-refusing causes stop `up` in the worker's words; a `podman info` that timed out or that nothing could read,
    a per-job retry at the worker, stops `up` too, because `up` is about to install units and run podman commands
    with no timeout of their own for a Podman it could not see: a wedged podman would hang the pass, and a remote
    one whose info merely timed out would get local units.
  - **A known disagreement is a refusal** (round 2). `up` takes a key its shell sets and `.env` does not, but when
    both set one differently it refuses, naming both values and their sources, since it would stand up one venue
    while the service runs the other. The wizard, when the deployment's `.env` already says something other than
    podman and the operator picks rootless Podman, stops before downloading anything and names the edit, never
    overwriting the key; when `.env` already lists podman it hands `up` no `PI_BACKENDS` of its own.
  - **The proxy's rules are an account-owned copy** (round 2, measured). The unit mounts
    `~/.config/pi-dispatch/egress-proxy.conf`, written by the installer as a planned write under the same
    changed-file and `--force` rules, because `z` cannot relabel a root-owned package file (`sudo npm i -g` on
    Fedora 44: `lsetxattr ... operation not permitted`, exit 126, the unit failed). A changed copy restarts the proxy.
  - **Queries read stdout alone, and fail closed.** podman prints warnings on stderr on ordinary accounts, which a
    merged capture compared into the running flag and the label (our own containers read as foreign). An inspect is
    "absent" only when stderr says no such container or object; any other failure, a locked store say, refuses,
    `--force` or not.
  - **The manager's own environment, or no writes** (issue #458, PR #463 round 3, measured on Podman 4.9.3). Every
    unit runs with the user manager's environment, and the Quadlet generator reads unit files from its
    XDG_CONFIG_HOME, while this installer writes to `~/.config/containers/systemd`. A manager whose environment names
    another account's XDG_CONFIG_HOME made the units "not found" (exit 5); another account's XDG_RUNTIME_DIR made every
    podman command in them fail ("XDG_RUNTIME_DIR directory ... is not owned by the current user"). Both reach a manager
    from /etc/environment, which Ubuntu's user managers read through environment.d (a GitHub runner image writes both).
    `service install` and `up` read `systemctl --user show-environment` first (`managerEnvRefusal`) and refuse, not
    forceable, naming the override that fixes it; measured live: refused with nothing written, then installed with the
    keeper holding once the account's own values were pinned.
  - **No user manager, no writes** (round 2, measured). Under `sudo -iu <account>` there is neither
    `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` nor a session bus and every `systemctl --user` fails; both commands refuse before writing a
    file, naming a real login, `machinectl shell`, or `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/user/<uid>` while linger runs the manager.
  - **Every refusal together.** `service install` gathers the worker unit existing, changed files and foreign
    containers into one list, so `--force` is consent to exactly what it printed; a missing allowlist, an unknown
    container state and a missing user manager are not forceable.
  - **Uninstall clears the failed state, stops the networks, and fails loudly.** squid ignores SIGTERM, so a proxy
    stop takes 10 s and ends 137 `failed` (measured); uninstall runs `systemctl --user reset-failed` on the units
    after removing them. It stops the network units as well as the containers (round 3, measured: left
    `active (exited)`, a reinstall after `podman network rm` failed with "network not found"), refuses without a user
    manager before touching anything, and a stop or disable that fails removes nothing and exits non-zero (it used to
    print success under `sudo -iu` with everything still running).
  - **System scope refuses** on a podman deployment, with the reason: the units belong to the account's user
    manager, which a system unit cannot `Wants=`/`After=`, and system scope's doctrine is that this tool writes
    nothing. A system unit with `User=` still runs rootless Podman (measured, `DES-PODMAN-NATIVE-ROOTLESS-BACKEND`),
    so the refusal names the by-hand route too.
  - **Linger is a warning, not a refusal**, matching the existing user-scope note: a worker that runs only while
    its operator is logged in is a real deployment. After every install the command reads
    `loginctl show-user <user> -p Linger` and says which of the two measured cases this host is.
  - **Every `.container` sets `Network=`**, Valkey on a bridge network of its own. Measured: a containers.conf
    `netns = "host"` puts a container started with no network option into the host namespace, where the port
    mapping means nothing. Valkey publishes `127.0.0.1:6379:6379` only.
- **Why Quadlet**: rootless Podman has no daemon, so a container started by hand is gone after a reboot, which is
  exactly the residual `DES-PODMAN-NATIVE-ROOTLESS-BACKEND` recorded. Measured on Fedora 44 with rootless Podman
  5.8.1: `NetworkName=` and `ContainerName=` give exactly those names (no `systemd-` prefix) and `Network=X.network`
  resolves through `NetworkName=`; `podman network connect <job network> <proxy>` works on the Quadlet-managed
  container and the unit stays active; `systemctl --user enable` is refused for a generated unit ("transient or
  generated") while the generator honours the file's own `[Install] WantedBy=default.target`; with linger on the
  units were active 25 s after a reboot with nobody logged in, and with linger off they did not start.
- **Rejected**:
  - **`podman run --restart=always` plus `podman-restart.service`**: a unit the operator must enable separately,
    which orders nothing, so the worker could not `After=` its queue.
  - **`podman generate systemd`**: deprecated upstream in favour of Quadlet, and it bakes one container's id and
    argv into a unit that a later render cannot reconcile.
  - **`Network=pasta` for Valkey**: it would also beat `netns = "host"`, but Ubuntu 24.04's Podman 4.9 defaults to
    slirp4netns and does not always ship passt; a named bridge is the one spelling both 4.9 and 5.x run.
  - **Following a renamed `PI_EGRESS_PROXY` in the Quadlet's `ContainerName=`**: `--replace` would remove whatever
    container of that name the operator already runs.
  - **`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/containers/systemd`**: the generator runs in the user manager's environment, which usually
    has no such variable, so a shell exporting one would put the files where the generator never looks.
  - **Refusing without linger**: it would lock out a desktop deployment that is fine running only while logged in.
  - **For the 4.9 teardown defect (issue #458)**: never disconnecting (the per-job networks pile up with the proxy on
    all of them, and each takes a /24, so `network create` fails after about 254 jobs); a pool of reused networks
    (job-to-job isolation across time would rest on the previous occupant being gone, and every reaper, the canary and
    the live probes are keyed on per-job names); restarting the proxy after each teardown (version detection, a 10 s
    squid stop under Quadlet, and a restart drops every other job's network, racing the worker's own concurrency);
    `podman network reload` (measured: the first reload fails with an IPAM error and only a second restores egress);
    installing the keeper on 4.x only (a version read at install time is one more thing to misread, and on 5.x the
    keeper is one idle container); a Quadlet `.pod` as the keeper (5.0+ only); relying on Valkey (optional, and it
    restarts on its own schedule); `Entrypoint=` for `sleep` (Quadlet 4.9.3 refuses the key, "unsupported key", measured)
    and a JSON array in `PodmanArgs` (`--entrypoint=["sleep","infinity"]` came through as
    `--entrypoint=[sleep,infinity]` and catatonit could not exec it, measured), so `--entrypoint=sleep` with
    `Exec=infinity`; `--memory` and `--pids-limit` on the keeper, left out rather than refuted: the investigation's
    keeper ran fine with `--pids-limit=8 --memory=16m` on a host with the controllers delegated, and they were dropped
    because `sleep` needs neither and a host without that delegation was not measured with them.
- **Residuals**:
  - **A proxy restart drops the per-job networks of jobs already running** (measured): the generated unit runs
    `podman run --replace --rm`, so a restart is a NEW container and the networks the worker connected to the old
    one are gone. A job started afterwards connects the new proxy and is fine; a job in flight has lost its only
    route out for the rest of that run. The worker does not re-attach (a re-attach loop is a second writer on the
    proxy's networks beside the per-job create and remove), so the advice is not to restart the proxy under running
    jobs.
  - Podman 4.9.3's generator accepts all six files (the deploy-lint `quadlet` job, which caught that 4.9 writes
    `--name=X` where 5.8 writes `--name X`); the keeper's pair ran on a 4.9.3 host (pd-ubuntu) and runs in the
    required conformance job from its shipped files, the other four ran on 5.8.1 only.
  - **The keeper's restart window** (measured on 4.9.3). A keeper killed behind systemd's back is back after
    `RestartSec` (1.2 to 1.3 s); a job teardown in that gap cut the proxy's route out exactly as with no keeper, and the
    keeper returning did NOT heal it (the proxy restart did). No new job starts into that damage: the worker's preflight
    retries while the keeper is down, for its first 3 s back, and afterwards whenever it started more than 15 s after
    the proxy, asking for the proxy's restart. What is left is the first 15 s after both started together (a keeper
    death AND a teardown both inside it), and the price of the order rule: a keeper restart that no teardown met still
    asks for one proxy restart.
  - **The keeper does not heal an account a teardown already broke**: the proxy needs a restart, and a leftover
    `aardvark-dns` in the dead namespace needs upstream's reset (with the stack stopped by `systemctl --user stop`,
    since `Restart=always` undoes a `podman stop -a`, kill it and clear `/run/user/$UID/containers/networks/aardvark-dns/`),
    which `docs/podman.md` gives, `reset-failed` first.
  - Measured on 2026-09-27 with the units as they ship (Fedora 44, Podman 5.8.1): Valkey on its bridge network
    published on `127.0.0.1:6379` and healthy, the proxy's exec-form health check reaching healthy, the
    `PODMAN_SYSTEMD_UNIT` label on each container, a job through the proxy, reboots with and without linger, and
    uninstall. `Restart=` and `TimeoutStartSec=` were carried, not exercised.
  - CLOSED by issue #447 (with its gate rounds 1 to 4): the general `.env` reader (`env-file.mjs`, doctor's)
    modelled systemd as never continuing a quote, wrong for a quote that OPENS a value (systemd's test-env-file.c,
    env_file_6). Its systemd reading now treats every line of such a value (`quotedRegions`) as part of it, so
    doctor shares the venue readers' rule. What the reader cannot model is refused instead: `envFileSystemdHazard`
    walks systemd's own parser states (PRE_KEY, KEY, PRE_VALUE, VALUE, the quoted states, their escapes, COMMENT)
    and names the first place systemd splits the file into lines differently from the reader:
    - a lone CR (a line break to systemd, outside a quoted value);
    - a quote reopened after a closing quote that does not close on its line (also on the line where an earlier
      multi-line value closes);
    - a value-opening quote under a non-identifier key that does not close on its line;
    - a trailing backslash outside quotes that the reader's line scan misses (behind a mid-value quote, after a `#`,
      or on a multi-line value's closing line; not in the issue, found by the measurement);
    - STRUCTURALLY, any line where systemd's quote state and the reader's own region model disagree
      (`unmodelled-quote`). Gate round 1 found the shape list alone was not enough: `quotedRegions` matched a
      value's first line with `.`, which stops at CR, U+2028 and U+2029, so such a value was no region and the
      lines it swallows read as assignments (`PI_EGRESS=1` read where systemd set `0`). The pattern is `[^\n]` now,
      as every line pattern in the reader and the writer is (`[ \t]` for blanks, never `\s` or `trim()`), and the
      comparison at every newline catches whatever a later pattern gets wrong.
    `envFileLoadHazard` adds what systemd refuses to LOAD, which fails the unit with every key unset: a NUL anywhere,
    and a key or value it stores that is not valid UTF-8 or holds a Unicode noncharacter (U+FDD0 to U+FDEF, and any
    code point ending in FFFE or FFFF, which a strict decoder accepts; gate round 2). It is judged on the value as
    systemd STORES it, quotes and escapes processed, so `X="\xC3""\xA9"` loads and `X="\xC3\\\xA9"` does not
    (both measured); a stray byte or noncharacter in a comment or on a line with no `=` loads. The walk runs over the
    file's BYTES, so `up`, `service install`, the wizard and doctor read bytes through `decodeEnvFile` (and, since
    #453 moved the venue read, `deploymentVenueEnv` and doctor's one shared read). An environment too large to exec
    is a load hazard too (`exec-too-large`, gate rounds 3 and 4): measured on systemd 259, a KEY=value of 131071
    bytes runs and of 131072 fails 203/EXEC "Argument list too long" (the kernel's bound counts the NUL), and 24
    values of 100 KiB fail where 19 run, so a KEY=value longer than 131071 bytes is refused, naming the key. The
    TOTAL is not a constant of systemd (the focus review, measured on systemd 259 under `systemd-run --user`, Fedora
    44): the kernel gives argv and envp together a quarter of the stack limit, 2097152 bytes under the default 8 MiB,
    and a `.env` of 2096288 counted bytes (21 assignments) started while 2096349 failed 203/EXEC, systemd's own 17
    variables, a pointer per string and the argv making up the rest. So a total over 2031616 bytes (2 MiB less a
    64 KiB margin for the argv, systemd's and the unit's variables and a changed LimitSTACK=, 8 bytes counted per
    variable) is refused as one that may fail, naming the total; the conservative 1 MiB it replaced refused a 1.1 MB
    file systemd starts. Only what reaches exec counts: the last value of each valid name
    (a 200 KB value reassigned small below runs, measured). A venue-key value over 4096 bytes is refused as the
    project's own cap, not systemd's (a venue key never
    needs that much). `readStackKeys` refuses a load hazard outright, and a line hazard when
    a venue key is spelled on a line that is not a comment, or on a comment after a lone CR on that same line (the
    only way such text becomes a key); a `#` line inside a value or continuation is no comment. Counting every
    comment spelling refused every docker deployment (`init` copies `.env.example`, which spells all three keys in
    comments), and counting them whenever the file had a lone CR anywhere did the same for a CR on another line.
    THE WRITER (`updateEnvFile`, planned by `planEnvEdit`) refuses a file that is not UTF-8 rather than rewrite bytes
    it did not mean to touch (a Latin-1 byte became U+FFFD on every `up`), never WRITES into a line any loader reads
    as value, and READS ITS RESULT BACK before writing: on Linux the key must be what systemd's own parser stores
    (`systemdReading`, so `KEY =x` below it counts), in a file systemd would split and load as this module does;
    elsewhere the line the loader takes must hold the value, a CRLF line's CR set aside where the loader strips it
    (systemd, the cmd wrapper; the final review: with two empty CRLF lines for the key the first was filled, the
    loader took the second, and the key was reported written). On macOS a line ending in a CR is refused for
    writing, naming the line and the fix (convert the file to LF line endings): the wrapper that sources the file
    keeps that CR, in a value or as a command of its own, so no key written there reads as written (the round-cap
    review; the final review had set the CR aside there too, which wrote `NEW` for a service that reads `NEW` plus a
    CR). Every such line counts, a comment line included: the focus review exempted a comment line's CR (harmless to
    the shells on its own) and the regression review found the writer then wrote `KEY=abc<CR>` into such a file in
    its CRLF ending, so the exemption was reverted, and the shell read-back keeps the CR as a backstop.
    "Unchanged" is said only when the loader reads it so: the line scan stops at the first set line and every loader
    takes the last, so a later line that empties the key (for systemd, an `export` only a shell reads, or for any
    loader a different last value on an overwrite) is refused by name, except where every POSIX loader reads the
    key blank, which is `up`'s own true EMPTY sentence (the focus review; on Windows this also names an `export`
    line, which the cmd wrapper reads as a variable called `export KEY`). A shell's value is read as the shell reads
    it: the first word of the command the line starts, continuations joined (`KEY=podman # c` and `KEY=podman \`
    above an empty line are `podman`), with "cannot confirm what line N reads" for one this command cannot read, and
    a fill whose value is only `$NAME` expansions is refused as unconfirmable, since it is empty whenever they are
    unset when the wrapper loads the file (the regression reviews). The file about to be WRITTEN is judged too: any
    hazard the platform's loader finds in it that the file read did not have refuses the edit, whatever the edit, so
    replacing the first line of a command that continues (leaving its tail a line the shells run) writes nothing (the
    third regression review). The platform loader's hazards are asked of the file as it
    stands before any line scan calls the key unchanged or already set (on macOS for every edit, on Linux wherever
    it would otherwise say so), so a hazard file is refused by name, never reported set (the round-cap review:
    `K=1 exit 0` above `WEBHOOK_SECRET=old` was "already set" while /bin/sh never reaches the key); otherwise
    nothing is written (gate round 2: appending after a file ending in a continuation or an open quote,
    and replacing a comment inside a quoted value, each left the key unset while the writer said it was written).
    It NEVER CLOBBERS (gate round 3): a line counts as already setting the key unless every loader reads it as
    value, and in fill-if-empty mode a key the platform's loader already reads as non-empty is refused rather than
    overwritten. Answering "is it set" with "any loader" appended a new WEBHOOK_SECRET under an operator's own one
    that only a shell read as quoted, and systemd took the new one. Gate round 4 closed its two platform halves: on a
    platform whose loader is a sourcing shell, a file with any shell hazard is not edited (`X=1 WEBHOOK_SECRET=abc`
    and a continuation into ` WEBHOOK_SECRET=abc` set the key where no line scan sees it, measured in sh, bash, dash
    and zsh), and on Linux a key only a shell reads (`export WEBHOOK_SECRET=abc`, which systemd drops) is refused by
    name, the line shown without its value, rather than reported "already set" about a service with no secret. An
    appended line uses the file's own line ending. On Windows (issue #470) the writer judges the file by the cmd
    wrapper's own reading (`cmdReading`, `for /f "usebackq eol=# tokens=1,* delims=="` then `set "%%A=%%B"`), and
    nobody here can run cmd.exe, so each rule is documented behaviour (`for /?`, `set /?`, `cmd /?`), the parser's
    community-documented phase model, or a cautious refusal where neither says, and the docblock marks which. A line
    that names the key other than as a plain `KEY=` line is refused by name: another case (`set` ignores case, so
    `webhook_secret=` removed a key the writer called unchanged), an indent or a BOM or a quote beside the name (for
    /f keeps leading blanks, since `delims==` replaces space and tab; what `set` does with them is undocumented), a
    blank before the `=` (kept in the name), a bare `KEY` (it removes the key), a leading `=` (for /f skips it and
    the line sets the key unseen). File-wide, a CR that is not a CRLF ending, a NUL, a Ctrl-Z, a `!`, a `^`
    or a character outside ASCII in a name (a caret is an escape cmd removes on a line delayed expansion
    touches, and how `set` folds case beyond ASCII is not documented), a name starting with `/` and a line
    whose `set` would pass cmd's 8191-character limit are refused. The value the
    wrapper takes for the key, before "unchanged" or "already set", and every value written, must hold none of a
    control character but TAB, a double quote, `%`, `!` (delayed expansion follows the registry, and a bare
    `setlocal` leaves it), `^`, a character outside ASCII (the console code page, not UTF-8) or a leading `=` (for /f
    drops it); the quote and `%` are carried by the phase model and refused anyway, cautiously. An empty value
    removes the key there, so it is never reported written, and the read-back compares the last plain line with the
    value written. Shell operators, parentheses, blanks and a trailing blank are carried, since FOR variables are
    substituted after the line is parsed. Linux and macOS verdicts are byte-identical (100000 seeded files). The
    setup wizard runs the writer's own plan dry
    (`envFileEditCheck`) before it runs `up`, so a file the
    write would refuse stops setup first, and keeps its own check that the result reads PI_BACKENDS=podman with the
    other venue keys unchanged, as a backstop the writer's read-back makes unreachable today (pinned through a
    seam). For the shell loader, any word after an unquoted blank (a command such as `K=1 z`, `K= unset
    WEBHOOK_SECRET` or `K=1 exit 0`, or a second `NAME=`; only more blanks, a `#` comment or the end of the command
    may follow a blank, the round-cap review), a NUL (the macOS /bin/sh stops reading the file there), any line ending
    in a CR, a comment line included (the wrapper keeps it; the fix named is converting the file to LF line endings)
    and `$'` quoting are hazards, judged on the whole COMMAND that continuations and quoted newlines join
    (gate round 2: `X=a\` + ` PI_EGRESS=0` set it in bash; the final review: `K="y` + `" WEBHOOK_SECRET=two`, and a
    continuation after the line a multi-line quote closes on, set it in /bin/sh on macOS, where the join had started
    only outside a quote and the macOS writer appended a new secret over it). A multi-line value that is one
    assignment, the documented PEM included, still reads, and a shell operator inside quotes is text, as sh reads it
    (`K="a;b"`). A backslash-newline is removed inside double quotes as well as outside them, as sh does before any
    expansion. Then, outside single quotes, the ONLY `$` forms allowed are `$NAME` and exactly `${NAME}` (NAME is
    `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`); every other `$` construct is a hazard: `$(`, `$((`, `$[`, `${` with anything but a
    bare name, a positional or special parameter, and a `$` before anything else or at the end. A backtick stays a
    hazard, and an escaped `\$` or `` \` `` is literal, as in sh. An allowlist because the list of forms that run it
    replaced was one short at every review (the delta review: a backslash-newline splitting `$(` inside double
    quotes, `$[WEBHOOK_SECRET=5]` arithmetic that the macOS /bin/sh evaluates, arithmetic inside `${K:...}` and
    `${a[...]}`, and a bad substitution such as `${}` that aborts the source under dash); `${HOME:-/tmp}` is refused
    with them. Doctor prints the line and the shape instead of a reading, and FAILS on a file
    systemd will not load. The rule follows states, not forms: after a closing quote any other character puts
    systemd in VALUE, where a quote is literal, so `K="a"b`, `K=a"b"c`, `K="a" # "b"` and a CR inside a quoted value
    read line by line in both. A comment line (`#` or `;` first) never continues in systemd 254+, and a `#` comment
    never continues in a shell, so its trailing backslash leaves the next line a line, modelled rather than refused;
    a `#` line reached by a continuation is value and does continue (all measured). Measured on systemd 259 (Fedora
    44) for 247 files, each loaded by a transient unit's `EnvironmentFile=`, and in bash for the gate rounds'; 214
    are the table in `worker/test/helpers/systemd-env-259.mjs`, the megabyte and length rows and the ones built on
    `.env.example` are pinned in the tests. The reader agrees with systemd (and bash) or refuses on every one. A port
    of systemd's parser, pinned to that table, is fuzzed against the reader in the suite (20000 seeded files; by hand
    500000 more, and the diff reviewer's byte-level port and exhaustive four-line fuzzer, find no disagreement). A
    backslash before CRLF continues nothing, to systemd (measured) or to a shell (it quotes only the CR), and since
    gate round 4 the reader agrees; treating it as a continuation had hidden a real key line below it from the
    writer on macOS, which then appended a new secret over the operator's. `X="\xC3""\xA9"`-style values that only the
    processed bytes make valid
    are read, not refused.
  - The reader's bare grammar (`UNQUOTED_PLAIN`, the unquoted half of what `readEnvAssignments` calls plain) takes an
    `=` inside a value since issue #477: `PI_BACKEND_FLOOR=isolation=enforced`, the form `docs/podman.md` shows, had
    been unread by doctor (every service key doctor resolves goes through this reader since #471), and doctor then
    judged no floor. Measured, each loader keeps an interior `=` as written: systemd 259 on pd-fedora
    (`systemd-run --wait -p EnvironmentFile=`, the unit's `env` read from the journal) for `isolation=enforced`,
    `egress=enforced,nonRoot=asserted`, `a=b=c`, `a==b`, `a=` and `a=:b`; `/bin/sh`, bash, dash and zsh for the same
    values (E2 oracle rows, run in every shell the host has, so CI's dash /bin/sh answers for itself); and the cmd
    wrapper's `tokens=1,*`, which takes the rest of the line after the first `=` run. A leading `=` and an `=` after a
    `:` stay refused (zsh expands both), and so does every other shape. The writer (`renderEnvValue`) now shares that
    set rather than keeping its own (PR #478's gate: it wrote a leading `=` and a `:=` bare), so what it writes bare is
    exactly what the reader reads as plain and everything else is single-quoted, and a value holding a control or
    invisible character (`QUOTED_CONTROL`, which the reader refuses even quoted) is refused by code point rather than
    written; over 600000 seeded writes, every value written on any platform reads back plain and exact. `unplainCause`,
    which words a refused line for `up`, `service install` and the clients, names the character refused, gives a
    leading `=` and a `:=` their own cause, and tells an operator to remove a control or invisible character, since
    quoting cannot help. A test holds every uncommented `.env.example` line
    and each documented floor form plain to all three loaders.
  - A path the proxy's `Volume=` cannot carry (a colon, whitespace, `%`, `$`, a quote, a backslash, a control byte)
    is refused rather than escaped, because none of the escapes was measured.
  - A key an `--env-setup` script exports is invisible to the install's decision (`DES-SERVICE-ENV-SETUP-SEAM`):
    `PI_BACKENDS` must be in `.env` for `service install` to see it.
