## DES-OPENSHELL-VENUE

- **Status**: decided 2026-10-18, issue #680; built in #683 (the backend), #684 (the policy layer: egress,
  credentials and MCP) and #686 (stdio steering and transcripts, and bind mode). **Nothing of it ships today**: there is
  no table entry, no adapter and no doctor line, and every word below is a plan this entry fixes so the three issues
  build one venue rather than three. The venue code they build on is generic since issue #681 (`listJobContainers` and
  `containerGone` are required bundle members, and no venue other than `local` and `podman` is treated as docker).
  **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (issue #683)**: the table entry, the adapter (`worker/src/backend-openshell.mjs`) and its
  conformance run now exist; the venue is still **not blessable**: `PI_BACKENDS` refuses `openshell` by name
  (`NOT_YET_BLESSABLE`) until #684 ships the egress rules and the per-job credential providers, because until then the
  job's environment, its provider key included, travels as the exec's `--env` and the sandbox's network policy is
  empty. The "Measured in #683" bullet below says what the build found that this plan did not know.
  **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (#684 part 2): BLESSED.** `NOT_YET_BLESSABLE` is empty and `PI_BACKENDS` admits `openshell`:
  the per-job network policy (part 1) and the per-job credential provider (part 2) are built, so the job's
  environment no longer carries a credential and its policy is no longer empty. What is still not served is refused or
  skipped by name ("Credentials and git push" and "Blessing" below).
  **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (#686 part 3): BIND MODE is built**, as its own venue `openshell-bind` ("Bind mode" below);
  copy mode stays the default and is otherwise unchanged.
- **Decision**: a third backend, `openshell`, runs a job in an NVIDIA OpenShell sandbox (v0.1.4, Apache-2.0,
  https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell) on a gateway this deployment owns.
  - **What OpenShell is, as far as this design rests on it.** A gateway control plane, and a compute driver that
    creates, per sandbox, an agent container with networking OFF and a supervisor container beside it, the two
    joined by an authenticated Unix socket. The agent's processes run under Landlock and seccomp; every connection
    is decided by an OPA policy, per binary; the supervisor terminates TLS under a per-sandbox CA; and a provider's
    credentials enter the agent only as placeholders the supervisor swaps for the real values at the endpoints the
    provider's profile names. The CLI covers the lifecycle: `sandbox create`, `upload`, `exec`, `download`, `delete`
    and `list -o json`, with `--cpu`, `--memory` and `--label` on create. `exec` returns the command's own exit code,
    and a signal as 128+n.
  - **Driven by the CLI with `-o json`, from the host**, on `DES-WORKER-ON-HOST`'s reasoning: the worker shells out
    to the real client, which owns its config and its endpoint resolution, instead of reimplementing either. Every
    read the adapter makes is a JSON document, never prose, so a failure is classified on values
    (`DES-TRANSIENT-VERSUS-DETERMINATE-IS-ONE-RULE`).
  - **The Docker and Podman compute drivers only, in v1**: the engines this deployment already runs and reads, on a
    host it owns (`CONST-VENUE-EGRESS-LAYER`'s third condition). Any other driver is refused by name.
  - **One sandbox per job, made and removed by the worker**: create (labelled with the job's container name, sized
    from the job's size through `--cpu` and `--memory`), upload, exec, download, delete. `ephemeral` therefore rests on
    the worker's create and delete and on the runtime honouring them, and the required `listJobContainers` and
    `containerGone` read `list -o json` by label.
  - **Copy mode by default.** The job's inputs are uploaded before the exec and its outputs downloaded after it, at
    paths under the image's WORKDIR, where OpenShell's filesystem policy places the sandbox's writable tree. This is
    the transfer downgrade `DES-CONTAINER-BACKEND-REGISTRY` already models (`transfersFromSpec` with `binds: false`,
    `copyDowngrades`): `/job` read-only is no longer a bind with `:ro` but a read-only path in OpenShell's Landlock
    policy, a kernel control the worker does not build, so `readOnlyJobInputs` is `asserted`; and the nesting trap that
    entry names (a forge job's `jobDir` containing `workspace/` and `session/`) is the adapter's to upload as one
    tree. **Bind mode is opt-in per host (#686)**, below under Rejected for why it is not the default.
    - **CORRECTED by measurement (issue #683)**: the read-only `/job` cannot come from OpenShell's own Landlock
      policy. Its uploads run as the workload's own uid UNDER the workload's own Landlock rules, so a path the policy
      marks `read_only` cannot be uploaded into (`tar: Cannot open: Permission denied`), and the filesystem policy is
      fixed at create ("include_workdir cannot be changed on a live sandbox"), so it cannot be tightened after the
      upload either (both measured on OpenShell 0.1.4, Docker driver, Linux 6.17). What makes `/job` read-only on this
      venue is the ORDER of events and one helper the image carries: the worker uploads first, then starts the runner
      through `/opt/pi-dispatch/pi-landlock` (`image/landlock/pi-landlock.c`), with the writable paths on the exec argv
      the worker builds. The helper stacks one Landlock domain that handles every write right and grants it only
      beneath those paths, and a domain is inherited by every child and can only narrow: measured, a write, a remove,
      a rename out, a symlink, a nested shell and a nested helper asking for `/` were all refused under `/job`, and the
      exit key on stdin passed through intact. `readOnlyJobInputs` stays `asserted`, now resting on an image claim the
      `sandboxLayout` capability gates and `verify-image.sh` proves on a Landlock host (the image job in CI), rather
      than on the vendor's policy; the helper refuses to start anything (exit 126) on a kernel below Landlock ABI 3.
      "Read-only" here means the bytes and the tree: Landlock (ABI 3 to 5) does not mediate chmod, chown, utimes or
      xattrs, so the agent can change an uploaded file's mode, which a `:ro` bind refuses, never its content. On ABI 6
      and later the domain is also scoped (signals and abstract unix sockets cannot leave it).
      The paths themselves are a closed layout name, `PI_JOB_LAYOUT=sandbox`, never a path in the environment:
      `/sandbox/{job,workspace,session,outbox,pi-global}` under the image's WORKDIR `/sandbox`
      (`image/runner/src/layout.mjs`, mirrored by `worker/src/job-layout.mjs`), the `mounts` layout keeping every path
      a binding venue always used. `INT-CONTAINER-JOB-INPUTS` has the table.
  - **Credentials through per-job providers**, under `CONST-VENUE-EGRESS-LAYER`: the worker creates a provider per
    job for its provider key and its minted forge token, the agent's environment holds placeholders, and the provider
    is deleted with the sandbox. The table entry declares `credentialCustody: layer` (the planned word, #683), and
    its property words are the list `DES-CONTAINER-BACKEND-REGISTRY`'s #680 amendment gives for a `layer` venue.
    `CONST-TOKEN-SCOPED-PER-JOB` is not relaxed by any of it: the token is as short and as narrow as on every venue.
  - **The policy is a document the worker generates per job** (#684), from the same allowlist, `model-endpoints` and
    forge hosts the squid venues read, handed to the sandbox and READ BACK before the exec. The job's MCP servers add
    no source: with the egress policy on, `makeMcpCheck` (`worker/src/mcp-preflight.mjs`) already refuses before spend
    a server whose host the allowlist and `model-endpoints` would not let the job reach (`mcp-egress-unreachable`,
    `mcp-package-runner`), so an MCP host is a subset of those sources and `CONST-VENUE-EGRESS-LAYER`'s second
    condition holds as written; #684 keeps that refusal on this venue. A read-back that differs, or a gateway-wide global policy that would replace it, refuses the job before spend
    (`CONST-BUDGET-BEFORE-TOKENS`), returned as a policy result and never retried (`CONST-RETRY-INFRA-ONLY`).
  - **No freeze, so `pausable` is `absent`.** OpenShell has no pause verb, so the venue checkpoints as every venue
    that cannot freeze does (`DES-RUN-CHECKPOINT-PAIRED`): live checkpoints off, an exit checkpoint only on an exit
    the processor may recover from (an infrastructure exit of an armed run), read from the tree the download brought
    back, and no recovery from a worker crash mid-run there. **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (#686 part 3)**: in bind mode the
    tree is the host's own, so a lost worker's workspace is salvaged as on `local` and `run.recover` is served there;
    live checkpoints stay off in both modes.
  - **No sandbox launcher.** `SANDBOX_LAUNCHERS` gets no `openshell` row, so `pi-dispatch sandbox` on such a job is
    refused by name (`INT-SANDBOX-CONTRACT`, `sandboxVenueRefusal`), never reopened on docker.
  - **No local-folder or cron-folder jobs in copy mode.** `localFolders` means a folder edited in place; a copy is
    edited elsewhere and written back afterwards, which races every edit the operator makes meanwhile and turns a
    failed download into a lost run. So the copy venue declares `localFolders` `absent`, and a job aimed at a local
    folder (a cron folder's included) routed there is refused before spend. What bind mode admits is #686's to decide.
    **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (#686 part 3)**: bind mode admits it (`localFolders: asserted` on `openshell-bind`); copy mode
    UNCHANGED.
  - **Steering and the live transcript over stdio** (#686). With no bind there is no `/inbox` mount and no
    `/session` file on the host to tail, so the steer channel is the framed, MAC'd stdin that
    `DES-STEER-VIA-READONLY-INBOX-MOUNT` decides (amended by issue #680, weaker than the mount and said so), and the
    transcript the tail and the ack consumer read comes back on the exec's stdout. The transcript was always the
    agent's to write (`/session` is agent-writable), so carrying it on stdout hands the agent nothing new; the acks
    and the exit line keep their MACs under the attempt's exit key. **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (issue #686 part 1), by the
    operator's decision of that day: the transcript comes back on the exec's STDERR, not its stdout**, as signed
    records ("The live transcript over stderr" below says why and what was rejected). The steer channel's half of
    this bullet is UNCHANGED, still to be built (#686's second part). **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (issue #686 part 2):
    steering is SERVED here**, over the framed, MAC'd stdin as decided: the relay opener start.mjs builds is handed to
    this bundle as to the binding venues, a steer job on an image declaring `steerStdin` gets `PI_EXIT_AUTH=stdin-frames`
    and its messages as frames behind the key, and its acks come back over the stderr transcript. Built against the
    decided text with three measured corrections (fd 3, a synchronous reader, the baseline of an empty upload;
    `DES-STEER-VIA-READONLY-INBOX-MOUNT`'s "As built" bullets). The stdin budget is OpenShell's measured 4 MiB less
    1 KiB (`INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT`). Recovery is still not served: `run.recover` stays refused before spend.
  - **The exit key passes through the vendor's exec relay.** On this venue the main exec's stdin, and so the exit key
    of EVERY attempt, steered or not, travels the CLI, then the gateway, then OpenShell's supervisor container before
    it reaches the in-image supervisor (`image/runner/supervise.mjs`). #545's property (no tool of the job sees the
    key) still holds inside the agent container, but on `openshell` it now also rests on that relay, a vendor trust
    step the worker cannot inspect; it is the same supervisor that already holds the job's credentials, and it is
    named in `OQ-047`.
  - **The exit code.** `exec` returning the runner's own code, and 128+n for a signal (the runner's own SIGTERM code
    is 143 already), is what `exitCodes` asks. The never-started set is the adapter's to declare, by the registry's
    rule: OpenShell's CLI failures are not docker's 125, 126 and 127, and #683 measures which exits mean the sandbox
    never ran. `abortable` is a `sandbox delete` on the timeout or a shutdown, told apart from a crash by the
    worker's own abort flag, as on every venue.
  - **Doctor and the refusals (#683, #684)**. Doctor checks the CLI's and the gateway's versions against a tested
    floor; the compute driver (Docker or Podman); that the gateway endpoint is loopback or a Unix socket on this host
    (OpenShell's local gateway listens on `https://127.0.0.1:17670` by default), which is how
    `CONST-VENUE-EGRESS-LAYER`'s third condition is checked rather than assumed; Landlock ABI 3 or later on the
    gateway's host (Linux 6.2); and that no gateway-wide global policy is active. The split: the **version floor** is
    checked by doctor and at boot; **Landlock, the global policy and the gateway's locality** are also free per-job
    refusals before spend (`outcome: "policy"`, before the token mint), because a doctor line read once is not a gate
    (`CONST-VENUE-EGRESS-LAYER`'s third and fourth conditions). Bind mode additionally needs the gateway's engine on
    the worker's own host (#686).
  AMENDED 2026-10-19 (#704 part 2): a job that would carry its project's secret bundle (`DES-PROJECT-SECRET-BUNDLES`)
  is refused on both OpenShell venues before spend, `openshell-bundle-unsupported` (`OPENSHELL_BUNDLE_UNSUPPORTED`, one
  sentence shared with `OPENSHELL_REFUSALS`), because the per-job provider would bind every bundle variable to every
  endpoint, or to nothing without a network rule, while the record said the job received it. #704 part 3 lifts it
  with per-endpoint bundle keys. `run.secrets` keep today's path unchanged. **AMENDED 2026-10-20 (#704): SUPERSEDED**
  by "Project secret bundles (#704 part 3)" below: both venues hold a bundle, and `openshell-bundle-unsupported` is
  retired (it shipped in no release).
- **Why**: the custody. On `local` and `podman` the provider key and the forge token sit in the job's environment,
  where the agent reads them, and in the host's argv (`OQ-028`); on this venue they never enter the agent's
  container, the provider is to be created with no value on any command line (#684, so `OQ-028` is not reproduced on
  the CLI's argv), egress is decided per binary rather than per hostname, and the box itself is confined by Landlock
  and seccomp on top of the container. The price is paid in this vocabulary's own words: the walls and the policy are the vendor's, so the words
  `DES-CONTAINER-BACKEND-REGISTRY`'s #680 amendment lists are `asserted` where `local` says `enforced`, and `PI_BACKEND_FLOOR` lets an operator
  refuse that trade at boot (`egress=enforced` refuses `openshell`). That is why it is a third venue beside the
  enforced two, never their replacement: `DES-EGRESS-DENY-ON-A-DEDICATED-NETWORK` is UNCHANGED for them.
- **Rejected**:
  - *The TypeScript SDK.* It is published to GitHub Packages, which needs a login token to install, so every
    `npm install` of the worker would need a credential, and the vendor would enter the worker's import graph. The
    CLI is one binary the operator installs and doctor reads.
  - *The MicroVM driver, in v1.* Not on Gondolin's objection (`CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB`): that driver runs
    the whole agent in the VM, not only pi's built-in tools. It is deferred because a VM in place of a container is
    an isolation decision of its own, which `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB` would have to make before any word
    in the table could be declared for it.
  - *Wrapping OpenShell as a policy layer around our own `docker run`.* The compute driver creates the agent
    container itself and joins it to the supervisor; there is no mode in which it adopts a container built from this
    worker's argv, so the "wrapped" form would be a supervisor beside a container it did not make, a configuration
    nobody states guarantees for. OpenShell owns the container, so it is a venue.
  - *Bind mode as the default.* A bind bypasses OpenShell's filesystem policy for every bound path, so the Landlock
    read-only `/job` the copy gets is gone, and it needs the gateway on the worker's own host to resolve the paths at
    all. It is admitted opt-in per host for what a copy cannot do (in-place folders, the mount steer channel), #686.
    **UNCHANGED, checked (#686 part 3)**: still not the default; what replaces the Landlock read-only `/job` there is
    a read-only bind plus the policy entry ("Bind mode" below).
- **Residuals, named** (`OQ-047`): a compromised supervisor holds every credential the job would have held, and
  provider and forge plaintext exist in a vendor process; OPA's per-binary rules pin binaries by path, which can
  drift silently with the image; OpenShell is v0.1.x and marks interfaces experimental, so a patch release can change
  what the CLI's JSON says, which the version floor and the JSON reads catch only as far as a shape check can;
  Landlock needs Linux 6.2; the exit key of every attempt passes through OpenShell's exec relay (CLI, gateway,
  supervisor container), a vendor trust step #545's property rests on here; and the stdin steer channel caps at
  4 MiB per attempt and lets the agent withdraw or delay a message.
- **Traces to**: `CONST-VENUE-EGRESS-LAYER`, `CONST-ISOLATION-CONTAINER-PER-JOB`, `CONST-EGRESS-POLICY-IN-THE-ARGV`,
  `CONST-TOKEN-SCOPED-PER-JOB`, `CONST-BUDGET-BEFORE-TOKENS`, `CONST-RETRY-INFRA-ONLY`,
  `DES-CONTAINER-BACKEND-REGISTRY`, `DES-WORKER-ON-HOST`, `DES-EGRESS-DENY-ON-A-DEDICATED-NETWORK`,
  `DES-STEER-VIA-READONLY-INBOX-MOUNT`, `DES-SANDBOX-IS-A-FRESH-CONTAINER`, `DES-RUN-CHECKPOINT-PAIRED`,
  `INT-SANDBOX-CONTRACT`, `INT-CONTAINER-RUNTIME-CONTRACT`, `INT-EGRESS-POLICY-CONTRACT`, `OQ-011`, `OQ-012`,
  `OQ-028`, `OQ-047`
- **Measured in #683** (OpenShell 0.1.4, Docker driver, ubuntu-24.04 with Linux 6.17 and Docker 28.0.4; the image job's
  kernel; Docker Desktop 27.4 refused every create, `BoundaryConfigWriteFailed`, so 28 is a real floor):
  - **A sandbox name is at most 19 characters** ("name exceeds maximum length (34 > 19)"), so a job's sandbox is named
    `pi-job-s` and 11 hex digits of a hash of its container name (`sandboxNameOf`), still in the job namespace every
    sweep matches; a name already of that shape is its own sandbox name, so a leftover the host budget seeded from a
    listing maps to itself.
  - **The image is passed by ID**, read from the gateway's own engine just before the create: with the default
    `if_not_present` pull policy a NAME the engine does not hold was fetched from Docker Hub, and no registry serves a
    local image's ID, so `--from <id>` is this venue's `--pull=never` and pins the run to the image the preflight read.
  - **The policy** is `include_workdir` with the image's trees read-only (a policy with a filesystem section grants
    nothing it does not list: `/opt` and `/sys/fs/cgroup` were unreadable under the default one, and the supervisor
    reads the cgroup at a kill), `/tmp`, `/dev/null`, `/home/pi` and `/proc` read-write (without `/proc` the supervisor's
    `oom_score_adj` raise is refused), `landlock.compatibility: hard_requirement`, the image's uid as `run_as_user`, and
    no network rule. It is written as a JSON file beside the job dir and read back with `policy get --full -o json`, which
    returns the body as given; a different body, or a source other than `sandbox`, never starts the job.
  - **Uploads** keep a directory's basename and merge into the destination, so the job directory (which holds the
    workspace and the session) is staged as `job/` without them, and every upload passes `--no-git-ignore`, because a
    bind shows the agent the whole tree. **Downloads** go into a fresh directory that then replaces the host's, so a
    file the agent deleted stays deleted. One that fails after the job ran never throws: the run's own result rides
    back, its verified tokens and usage with it, so the spend is recorded; a run that did not end on a determinate
    refusal is reported as exit 1 (retried, its reservation kept, the safe direction), exit 2 stays exit 2, and an
    aborted run downloads nothing. The policy file and both staging directories sit BESIDE the job dir and are swept
    with it at boot (`BESIDE_JOB_DIR`), since the upload copy holds the job's prompt.
  - **A stop during the stage**: the job's timeout or a shutdown can land while the create or an upload is still
    running, when the stop's own `sandbox delete` finds nothing yet. The stop marks the name, the stage checks the
    signal and that mark after every step, and run-container ends the run as stopped before any exec, the teardown
    deleting what the stage made. While an attempt is between its create and its delete, the gone-check answers
    `false` for its sandbox by either name, so the host budget's sweep never deletes it as an orphan.
  - **Not measured yet, #684's to measure with its own uploads and env** (named so a reader does not assume them):
    whether `sandbox upload` copies a symlink's target from the host tree it uploads, and whether the host side of
    `sandbox download` refuses an archive entry that escapes the destination; and how an `--env` value with spaces,
    quotes, `$` or a newline reaches the process (measured only for a space). Until #684 the venue runs no job.
    **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (#684 part 2)**: no credential is on the exec's `--env` any more, so the quoting question is
    the non-secret values' alone; a credential's value travels in the CLI's own environment to `provider create`.
    The upload and download questions are UNCHANGED, still not measured.
  - **Never-started is the failed step, not a code**: a create, read-back or upload that fails is
    `container-never-started` (refunded, retried, the sandbox deleted anyway). The CLI's own failures exit 1, which is
    the runner's own infrastructure code, so such an exec is retried as one with its reservation kept (the safe
    direction). `--timeout 0`, since the gateway's own timeout exits 124 and the worker owns the job's; a `sandbox delete`
    during the exec ends it with 143, which the abort flag tells from a crash.
  - **The per-job refusals before spend** (the processor's `venueRefused`, fixed comments): `openshell-gateway-not-local`
    (`openshell status -o json` names no loopback or unix server; `status` exits 0 even when the gateway is down, so its
    own field decides `connected`, and a gateway not connected is retried), `openshell-global-policy` (`policy get
    --global` answers; with none set it exits 1 with the one non-JSON sentence this adapter reads, "no global policy
    revision found", unwrapped first because the CLI breaks it across lines), and `openshell-landlock-missing` (on
    Linux, where the gateway on this host shares its kernel, `/sys/kernel/security/lsm` lacks `landlock`; elsewhere the
    read is impossible, logged `openshell_landlock_unknown`, and the create fails closed under `hard_requirement`).
  - **A folder job is refused twice**: at load when its trigger names the venue (`refusesLocalWorkspace` reads
    `localFolders: absent` beside `remote`), and before spend when the venue is only the deployment's default
    (`venue-local-folders-unsupported`), the loader's blind spot.
  - **Not served here yet**, each its issue's: the live transcript, progress, steering and recovery checkpoints (the
    session file is in the sandbox until the download, #686); a job's MCP servers, whose commands the mcp.json names
    under the `mounts` layout's paths (#684); the egress rules and the providers (#684). **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (#684)**:
    the MCP paths, the egress rules (part 1) and the providers (part 2) are served; `run.recover` is now REFUSED before
    spend rather than run unarmed (`openshell-recover-unsupported`); the live transcript, progress and steering stay
    skipped by name until #686. **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (#686 part 1)**: the live transcript, run progress and the status
    comment are SERVED (the runner's signed records on the exec's stderr, below); steering stays skipped by name
    (`steerSkipped: "venue-copies"`) and `run.recover` refused before spend, both still #686's. **AMENDED 2026-10-19
    (#686 part 2)**: steering is SERVED (stdin frames, above) on an image declaring `steerStdin`; an image without it
    still runs unsteered as `venue-copies`. `run.recover` stays refused before spend: recovery is the one item here
    not served. **AMENDED 2026-10-19 (#686 part 3)**: in copy mode UNCHANGED; bind mode serves it ("Bind mode" below).
  - **The whole run, live**: the conformance script (`.github/scripts/openshell-conformance.mjs`, which ships with part 3
    of #683 beside its CI lane) on that host passed every harness check, all
    eight read-backs (CapEff 0, NoNewPrivs 1, seccomp 2, pids.max 2048, memory.max the job's size, the sandbox gone
    after the run, nothing mounted under `/sandbox`, only `lo`, an outbound connection refused, an absent image refused
    before any sandbox, uid 1001), an append to `/sandbox/job` refused, and the real runner reached its own signed
    `cost-cap` line, keyed and offline, with its session brought back.

- **Egress (#684 part 1, AMENDED 2026-10-19)**: the policy is generated per job by `networkPolicyFor`
  (worker/src/openshell-policy.mjs) from the squid venues' own sources (the allowlist, the model endpoints, the job's
  forge), every endpoint `enforce`, and read back against the written body plus OpenShell's one measured baseline
  addition (`/var/log` read-only). Two things it does that squid could not: a request is read (`protocol: rest`), and
  `github.com` carries the git transport with a push allowed to the job's OWN repository only (GitHub only: the other
  forges serve their API from the git host, so narrowing it would refuse every merge request; they keep full access,
  as on squid). One thing it does not do, said so: the rule's binaries are no narrowing, since OpenShell matches
  ancestors and every job process descends from the runner's node, which is therefore always the first binary. A source it cannot translate without widening refuses before spend
  (`openshell-egress-untranslatable`). The table is `INT-EGRESS-POLICY-CONTRACT`'s.
- **Doctor and CI (#683, AMENDED 2026-10-19)**: the "Doctor and the refusals" plan above is built as follows. The
  version check is EXACT, not a floor: the CLI and the gateway must be `OPENSHELL_TESTED_VERSION` (0.1.4, one pin in
  `.github/openshell.json` that the CI lane installs by checksum and a test holds to the constant), because the
  interfaces this adapter drives are marked experimental and a patch release is untested until the conformance run
  passes on it. Doctor's lines run on `pi-dispatch doctor --openshell`, or once a deployment blesses the venue, so a
  host can be made ready before #684; they add the engine floor (Docker 28, Podman 5) and the job image's
  `sandboxLayout` to the plan's list. The boot half of the version floor is #684's, with the blessing. The CI lane is
  ADVISORY (`the openshell venue holds its declarations`), promoted to required in a later issue once it has passed
  across a round.
- **Credentials and git push (#684 part 2, AMENDED 2026-10-19)**: the "Credentials through per-job providers" plan
  above, as built and measured on OpenShell 0.1.4. Per job, `secretNamesOf` takes every env name the redactor does not
  list as non-secret (`NON_SECRET_ENV_KEYS`, the one list), and the adapter imports an ENDPOINTLESS profile for them
  (`providerProfileFor`, no endpoints and no binaries of its own, written 0600 at `<job dir>.openshell-profile.json`
  beside the job dir, never uploaded; `provider profile import -f`; AMENDED 2026-10-20 (#704): one file per provider,
  `<job dir>.openshell-profile-<provider>.json`, deleted as soon as its import answers, either way, the teardown's
  removal kept as the backstop), then creates a provider named like the sandbox
  with `--credential NAME` per secret and the owner label. `--credential NAME` reads `$NAME` from the CLI's own
  environment (measured), so the values ride the CLI child's environment (PATH, HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME and the values,
  nothing else of the worker's), never an argv and never a file: `OQ-028` is not reproduced on the CLI. The provider is
  attached at `sandbox create --provider`, and every endpoint of the network policy gets `credential_binding:
  {provider}`, so the agent sees `openshell:resolve:env:v<rev>_NAME` placeholders and the supervisor swaps the value
  in only in a request to a host the policy admits (measured for headers and for git Basic auth). The exec's `--env`
  carries no secret name. The read-back expects one more layer, `_provider_<name, dashes as underscores>` (measured,
  `expectedPolicies(policy, {provider})`). With no network rule no provider is made (`openshell_secrets_unbound`):
  the job reaches nothing, and its secrets go nowhere rather than back onto `--env`. Teardown deletes the provider
  after the sandbox (asked up to 10 times, 2 s apart, since it is refused while still attached and a sandbox's delete
  is asynchronous, measured), then its profile; the boot sweep's reaper (`makeOpenshellReaper`) deletes owner-labelled
  providers named like a job sandbox. **git push**: the clone's remote is tokenless, so a forge job's exec gets a
  credential helper through `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`_KEY_0`/`_VALUE_0` (`gitCredentialEnv`) that answers only `get` and
  prints the forge's username (`x-access-token` on GitHub, `oauth2` on GitLab, `pi-dispatch` elsewhere) and the token
  variable's placeholder as the password, which the supervisor rewrites in a request to any admitted host (each
  credential is bound to every endpoint: squid's reach, not narrower; review, 2026-10-19); with part 1's push rule
  a GitHub job pushes to its own repository only. **Rotation** does not reach a running process (a job is bounded at
  30 minutes, an App token lives about an hour): stated, not built. The supervisor sets `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` in the agent, so
  node trusts its per-sandbox CA, and strips the proxy variables (measured): the vendor's, relied on and not built.
- **Blessing (#684 part 2, AMENDED 2026-10-19)**: `NOT_YET_BLESSABLE` is empty. `PI_OPENSHELL_ENGINE` (`docker` or
  `podman`, default `docker`) and `PI_OPENSHELL_GATEWAY` (a registered gateway's name, or unset) are parsed into
  `config.openshell`, judged only while `PI_BACKENDS` names the venue. The boot builds the bundle (its allowlist the
  working directory's `egress-allowlist.conf`, ENOENT admitting nothing, one reader shared with the MCP check; its
  endpoints the model-endpoints snapshot), registers its reaper in the boot sweep, and reads the versions
  (`openshellBootVersions`): a CLI or a gateway not at `OPENSHELL_TESTED_VERSION` is a configError (exit 2); a CLI that
  does not answer is a plain error (exit 1, restarted); a gateway down at boot is only logged
  (`openshell_gateway_down_at_boot`), the per-job preflight being the gate. `PI_EGRESS=0` with this venue blessed
  refuses the boot (`backendRefusals`, keyed on `credentialCustody: layer`, the operator's decision: the layer has no
  "egress off"). `run.recover` is refused before spend (`openshell-recover-unsupported`, the first per-job check):
  the venue cannot checkpoint a running session. **AMENDED 2026-10-21 (#712)**: the stated cause was stale. #686 brought
  the transcript back over stdio, and copy mode still cannot recover: its workspace stays inside the sandbox until the
  exit's download and there is no pause verb, so a lost attempt leaves nothing on the host to salvage or restore (bind
  mode, whose workspace is on the host, serves it). The venue declares `serves.recovery: "no"`
  (`DES-CONTAINER-BACKEND-REGISTRY`), and a trigger naming it in `run.backend` beside `run.recover` is now refused when
  the triggers file loads or is written (`recoverVenueProblem`, `INT-TRIGGERS-FILE-CONTRACT`); this pre-spend check
  stays for a trigger that names no venue and lands here as `PI_BACKENDS[0]`. Doctor's "not yet
  blessable" line is gone, and a plain `doctor` runs the venue's lines when `PI_BACKENDS` names it. The CI lane stays
  advisory until it has passed across a round.
- **Review fixes (#684 part 2, AMENDED 2026-10-19)**: the exec's `--env` carries ONLY `NON_SECRET_ENV_KEYS` (an
  allowlist; a secret name no provider can carry is dropped and logged, `openshell_secret_unbindable`, never put on the
  argv as a value). A provider that reads its credential's value inside the job (`VALUE_READING_PROVIDERS`: Bedrock,
  Vertex, Codex, Copilot; Anthropic judged by the value, `sk-ant-oat`, as pi judges it) is refused before spend
  (`openshell-credential-reads-value`). The gateway's release is read per job too (`openshell-gateway-untested`). A
  same-named leftover provider and profile are deleted before a job's import (every attempt of one job shares the
  sandbox's name); the provider is recorded only after its create; the host budget's gone-check deletes a gone
  sandbox's provider; the CLI child that creates the provider runs in the worker's own environment plus the values.
  `run.recover` on a `kind: local` job is not refused (it runs unarmed, as everywhere). Doctor replays the boot's
  layer-venue egress refusal and reads the two settings from the service env. RESIDUALS, named: a provider that reads
  its key by value and is not listed fails with its own provider error, never silently; a profile whose provider was
  never created is found by the next attempt of its job, not by the reaper, which lists providers only. Measured in the CI lane (OpenShell 0.1.4, 2026-10-19): the agent's `$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `$GH_TOKEN` are
  placeholders, `/proc/<pid>/environ` opens and reads EMPTY inside the sandbox (its own and its parent's), and a stand-in
  on the gateway host received the real header value and git's Basic credentials, never a placeholder.
- **The live transcript over stderr (#686 part 1, AMENDED 2026-10-19)**: the session file is in the sandbox until the
  download, so no host tail can read it while the job runs, and with it go the live transcript, run progress and the
  status comment, which all read the same lines. **Decision**: the runner mirrors the file's complete lines over its
  own STDERR, each as one self-delimiting record signed with the attempt's exit key
  (`\x1epidt <seq> <type> <end> <mac> <base64>`: a baseline first, then lines with their file offsets, and a reset when
  the file is rewritten; the bytes and the MAC are `INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`'s "The transcript records"), and
  the worker demultiplexes the exec's stderr, verifies each record and pushes its line into the same
  publisher a bound file feeds (`DES-LIVE-TRANSCRIPT-STREAM`'s stdio source), so the console's live page,
  `pi-dispatch chat`, progress and the status comment read Valkey exactly as on every venue. Armed only where it is
  read (an opener and a job id), and only when the image declares the non-gating `transcriptStderr` capability and
  an exit key exists; otherwise `live_transcript_skipped` names `no-capability` or `no-exit-key`, and a copying venue
  that does not mirror would say `venue-copies`. The arming is the venue's own construction option (`transcript:
  "stdio"` on `makeRunContainer`, beside `layout`), not the call bag's `binds`, which the registry adds for a steer job
  alone. `status_comment_skipped` reads `no-transcript` there (it read `progress-off`, the wrong switch, while the
  bundle was not handed the opener). **Why signed, and what the MAC does NOT prove**: a tool can write to the
  container's stderr (the runner's `/proc/<pid>/fd/2`, as #545 measured for fd 1), so an unsigned record would let
  it forge the channel: lines, positions, resets. The MAC, under the key the agent never sees, authenticates the
  channel (the runner's mirror wrote this record, in this order, and a `seq` that only grows refuses one taken and
  written again); it does not authenticate the content, since the session file is the agent's to write and the
  mirror sends whatever pi-shaped line the agent appended to it. A line here has exactly the trust of a line the
  file tail reads on a binding venue. **Why self-delimiting**: OpenShell's `sandbox exec --no-tty` keeps the two
  streams apart but forwards each in reads of up to 4 KiB that are neither line-aligned nor ordered against the other
  (measured, 0.1.4), so the demux buffers across reads and holds only what may still be a record (the marker's head,
  at most 6 bytes, or a record while its bytes fit the record's grammar, at most 8 MiB of payload), and the marker
  starts a record wherever it appears, also after a foreign write that left no newline. A verified record's bytes
  never reach the job log; a byte that is in no record reaches it unchanged, except a foreign write's head that
  landed inside a record and fit its grammar (lost with the record); and a record broken by another writer ends at
  its first byte the grammar cannot hold, the bytes after that break reaching the log as ordinary text
  (`INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`'s "What reaches the job log" states it exactly). The runner notices a rewrite as
  the file tail does (a shrink, a new inode, or a first line whose bytes changed in place; a new inode before anything
  was read, its own quarantine's swap, is a reset to 0), reads at most what the file held when each read began (an
  agent appending without pause cannot hold it from its SIGTERM or its exit line), and a record whose write fails
  takes no `seq` and is sent again from the start of its line, so a line is never lost without a gap. A lost reset is
  recovered by the worker from the next line's `end` (not past the last one), and a lost baseline is no missing line.
  **Rejected: stdout**, which #680's text above named. It carries the runner's log and the signed exit line, which
  the worker reads from a bounded 64 KiB tail (`openJobLog`), so a burst of records there pushes the exit line's
  neighbourhood out of that tail, and the one stream whose last line decides the run would also carry a second
  protocol every reader of either must keep apart. stderr carries nothing the worker parses. The #680 sentence is
  amended by the operator's decision of 2026-10-19. **Rejected: tailing the sandbox's file through the CLI** (a
  `sandbox download` or an `exec cat` on a timer): a second exec per poll through the gateway, the supervisor and the
  relay, and a read of an agent-written file by a second process whose output carries no proof of the runner.
  RESIDUALS, named: a record above PIPE_BUF (4 KiB) is not atomic against a write from another process sharing the
  pipe and arrives broken (refused and counted, the line lost, shown as `skipped`; the positions stay exact, since
  every line carries its own offset); a foreign write's head that fits a broken record's grammar is lost with it, and
  the broken record's bytes after its break reach the job log as text; a lost baseline cannot be recovered (the
  run's lines are then all this run's, failing open: a resumed session's earlier turns count again); the transcript
  trails the file by
  the runner's 250 ms read plus the publisher's 500 ms flush; and the exit key that signs it passes through the vendor's
  exec relay, as the exit line's does (`OQ-047`). Measured in CI by the conformance script's real runner: its session
  lines arrive through the real publisher over stderr, none unverified, and no record reaches the output.
- **Bind mode (#686 part 3, AMENDED 2026-10-19)**: built as its own venue, `openshell-bind`, from the same factory
  (`makeOpenshellBackend({ mode: "bind" })`, not a second adapter: the image read by ID, the network policy and its
  read-back, the credential provider, the gateway checks, the stop, the teardown and the reaper must stay one copy).
  Measured on OpenShell 0.1.4, Docker driver, in the CI lab of 2026-10-19:
  - **The gateway must allow it.** A create carrying `--driver-config-json` fails on a default gateway ("caller driver
    config is disabled; a gateway administrator must enable allow_driver_config"); the gateway's gateway.toml needs
    `[openshell] version = 2`, `[openshell.drivers.docker]` with `allow_driver_config = true` and `enable_bind_mounts
    = true`, and `[openshell.drivers.docker.resource_admission] enabled = false` (the other two
    refusals, measured, name those two, each setting refused in turn until all three are on). `openshell gateway info -o json` does not reveal them.
  - **The binds** are the container spec's mounts (`bindMountsOf`), each host path at its `mounts`-layout path,
    `read_only` exactly where the spec mounts it read-only (`/job`, `/inbox`, `/opt/pi-global`), writable where it
    does (`/workspace`, `/session`, `/outbox`), keyed by the driver's name. Every target is admissible (none is
    `/sandbox`, which OpenShell reserves, or overlaps `/opt/openshell`, `/etc/openshell` or `/run/openshell`); the
    stage refuses one that is not, never handing the gateway a create it refuses in words this adapter does not read.
    No upload, no download. A sandbox carries the mode label `pi.dispatch.openshell-mode=bind`.
  - **The policy** is copy mode's with every bind target listed (`read_only` or `read_write`), `include_workdir`
    kept; the read-back is unchanged by the listing (measured), so `expectedPolicies` holds it as it holds copy mode's.
    The network rules, the provider and the placeholders are copy mode's exactly: `CONST-VENUE-EGRESS-LAYER` holds as
    written.
  - **`/job` read-only** is the read-only bind (measured: EROFS on a write) plus the `read_only` policy path
    (measured: denied). pi-landlock is NOT used: it would add nothing for `/job` beside the bind, which is the control
    `local`'s `:ro` is, and would tie the venue to the `sandboxLayout` capability for no guarantee. The exec runs
    `/entrypoint.sh` in `/workspace`.
  - **The runner reads the `mounts` layout**, so the venue is a binding one end to end: `binds: true` (the `/inbox`
    file steer channel, never stdin frames), `transcript: "file"` (the host's session file tailed, never the stderr
    mirror), the recovery staging as on `local`. `run.recover` is SERVED: a lost worker's host workspace is salvaged and
    an infrastructure exit snapshotted, as on `local`; neither needs a pause, and live checkpoints stay off (no pause
    verb, `pausable: absent`).
  - **The job user** (`decideOpenshellBindUser`, over `resolveImageUser`, issue #341's rule): a bind is written as the
    sandbox's uid (measured: files owned by the image's 1001), so the policy's `run_as_user`/`run_as_group` is the
    worker's own `<euid>:<egid>` unless that uid is 1001, which needs `anyUid`; a root worker (`worker-is-root`) and a
    primary group of 0 (`root-group`) are refused per job (`job-user-unmappable`), and darwin and win32 run the
    image's own user (local's `desktop-platform` row, unmeasured for OpenShell). Measured in the CI lab: a policy
    `run_as_user`/`run_as_group` of `2000` ran the workload as uid 2000 and gid 2000 (`id`, and node's `getuid()`), a
    write into a read-write bind of a host directory owned by 2000 landed as 2000, and the image's `/home/pi` is 0777, so
    `HOME` writes work for any uid. **The Podman driver is refused at boot** for bind mode
    (`openshellFrom`): unmeasured, and a rootless Podman maps the sandbox's uid away from the worker's.
  - **The gate, before spend** (`openshell-bind-mounts-disabled`, a fixed comment, the setting in the log as

- **Project secret bundles (#704 part 3, AMENDED 2026-10-20 (#704))**: both venues hold a project's secret bundle
  (`DES-PROJECT-SECRET-BUNDLES`), replacing part 2's refusal. Read at the pin (v0.1.4, `5a7728c`), the model is:
  - **One provider per endpoint, every key of a provider on every endpoint naming it.** A policy endpoint's
    `credential_binding` names one provider and nothing else (proto/sandbox.proto `NetworkCredentialBinding`); the
    gateway binds EVERY static key of that provider to the union of the endpoints naming it
    (crates/openshell-server/src/grpc/policy.rs `policy_static_credential_endpoint_bindings`, provider.rs
    `resolve_provider_environment_from_records_with_policy_bindings_and_credentials`); a key's placeholder is resolved
    only where it is bound (crates/openshell-core/src/provider_credentials.rs `resolver_and_body_classifier_for_endpoint`)
    and, sent anywhere else, answered 403 `credential_endpoint_mismatch` and never forwarded
    (crates/openshell-supervisor-network/src/l7/relay.rs `reject_credential_resolution`); two attached providers may not
    expose one env key (provider.rs `validate_provider_environment_key_ownership`); and two endpoints that can match one
    request may not name different providers (crates/openshell-policy/src/ambiguity.rs, the
    `credential_binding.provider` conflict). So a variable bound to ONE host needs a provider of its own.
  - **So, per job**: the job's own provider (named as the sandbox, #684's, its profile unchanged) holds every secret
    but the bundle's, `run.secrets`, the forge token, the model key and the forwarded secrets; each distinct bundle
    HOST gets a provider `<sandbox>-b<n>` (sorted by host, so every attempt names them alike) holding the variables the
    bundle's `endpoints` bind to it, attached with a second `--provider` and labelled with the owner label; the
    endpoints whose host is that host are bound to it, every other endpoint to the job's provider as before
    (`bundleProviderPlan`). The values travel as #684's do, `--credential NAME` from the CLI child's environment.
    **What that costs, stated**: at a bundle host only that host's bundle variables resolve, so a run.secrets value,
    a forwarded secret or the model key sent there is refused 403 by the supervisor; loud, before any spend at the
    provider, never a leak. So every host the job's own credentials are known to go to is refused as a bundle host
    (below). **CORRECTED in review round 1 (H2)**: this sentence first said a model's host was not judged because the
    catalog host could not be known; it can (`outputCapView` composes it), and a bundle endpoint on `api.anthropic.com`
    took the model key's binding and failed the run after spend.
  - **`auth` documents, the binding narrows.** The `endpoints` entry's `auth` becomes the profile credential's
    `auth_style` and `header_name` (`bearer` -> `bearer` + `authorization`, `basic` -> `basic`, `header:<Name>` ->
    `header` + the name lowercased; `bundleAuthFields`). At the pin these change nothing a static credential does: the
    supervisor swaps a placeholder wherever a request carries it (a whole header value, after a `Bearer `-style
    prefix, inside Basic's decoded `user:pass`, the path or the query; crates/openshell-core/src/secrets.rs

    `provider profile get` prints them, so the reviewed file's intent is visible in the gateway's own view. Rejected:
    leaving them out because they do nothing.

    expects KEY=VALUE"), with no bare `KEY` that reads the CLI's environment (as `provider create --credential KEY`

    The exec's other `--env` names are unchanged (`NON_SECRET_ENV_KEYS`, the git helper, `HOME`). Rejected: a provider
    for them (the agent would hold placeholders, useless for a value it must use itself: an HMAC key, a PEM, a
    database URL). The env file, rejected at first as a job-image change, is what review round 1 chose:
  - **The file channel (review round 1, H1)**: the stage writes the plain variables as one JSON object to

    `openshell-bundle-endpoint-not-allowed`: the host is not EXACTLY an endpoint host of the generated policy (a reviewed file may not widen egress),

    every HTTP MCP server's host the job names (its headers may carry a run.secrets value). Gaps left, each refused
    loudly at run time by the supervisor's 403 and never a leak: a model whose `baseUrl` cannot be composed (no
    catalog entry, no overlay definition) adds no host; an agent switching to another overlay model whose `baseUrl`
    is a bundle host, on a trigger with no allowed-model list (the callable set is then open, so it cannot be listed;
    `run.models` or `PI_ALLOWED_MODELS` closes it); and a stdio MCP server's own HTTP calls with a secret to a bundle
    host (its destinations are its own, not in its configuration).
    `openshell-bundle-endpoint-unknown`: an `endpoints` name the bundle did not deliver (and no run.secrets value
    shadowed): a typo would otherwise send the real variable in PLAIN while the file reads as holding it as a
    placeholder. `openshell-bundle-name-taken`: the `PI_` prefix (the worker's and the runner's own, final review round), a
    name the sandbox sets itself (`USER`, `SHELL` and `TERM` for every exec, crates/openshell-sandbox/src/process.rs and
    boundary_exec.rs, and `LOGNAME` beside them), the `OPENSHELL_` prefix (common.rs
    `parse_env_pairs`; crates/openshell-server/src/grpc/validation.rs `validate_env_entries_inner`;
    crates/openshell-sandbox/src/process.rs `RESERVED_ENV_PREFIX`), the CA variables
    (crates/openshell-sandbox/src/child_env.rs `tls_env_vars`), the proxy variables (process.rs `PROXY_ENV_VARS`), `HOME` and the git helper's
    `GIT_CONFIG_*` (`OPENSHELL_SET_ENV_NAMES`). `openshell-bundle-unpassable`: what the gateway would refuse
    (`OPENSHELL_LIMITS`, from crates/openshell-server/src/grpc/mod.rs and validation.rs): a placeholder value over 8 KiB
    (`MAX_MAP_VALUE_LEN`), more than 32 placeholders for one host (`MAX_PROVIDER_CREDENTIALS_ENTRIES`), more than 31
    bundle hosts (`MAX_PROVIDERS` 32 per sandbox, one is the job's); the plain-value limits it first had (32 KiB, no
    line break, the exec's) are gone with the exec path. `openshell-bundle-image-too-old`: plain variables on an image
    without `bundleEnvFile`. The wildcard check ignores ports (an allowlist wildcard is 443, a model endpoint may not
    be) and errs toward refusing, as its any-depth suffix match does (review round 1, L3). **A shadowed endpoint name**
    (review round 1, M2): a trigger's run.secrets value for a name the bundle's `endpoints` declare goes into THAT host's
    provider, since it is the value that wins and the reviewed file binds the name to the host; it counts among the
    placeholders. A
    source the gate cannot read retries. A plan the stage still cannot build (a key in two places, a bundle host
    without an endpoint) is a defect refused as infrastructure (`openshell_bundle_collision`,
    `openshell_bundle_host_unbound`), never run around.
  - **Read-back**: `expectedPolicies(policy, { providers })` adds one `_provider_<name>` layer per attached provider and
    nothing else, read at the pin (crates/openshell-policy/src/compose.rs `provider_rule_name`, `compose_effective_policy`:
    each layer under its own key, a numeric suffix only on a clash these names cannot have;
    policy.rs `provider_policy_context_from_records`: an endpointless profile's layer is the measured `{ name }`).
    `--full` is kept rather than `--base`: the base alone would no longer see a layer this job did not attach, the one
    difference a read-back exists for. A missing or an extra layer never starts the job (unit-tested).
  - **Lifecycle**: teardown deletes every provider the attempt created, after the sandbox, by #684's bounded retry,
    and every profile it imported; an attempt removes its earlier attempt's leftovers by name first; the boot sweep
    deletes owner-labelled providers named like a job's or a bundle host's (`isJobProviderName`, `BUNDLE_PROVIDER_NAME`
    `pi-job-s<11 hex>-b<n>`, sandboxes first since a provider still attached is refused deletion), then (review round
    1, L4) every profile named in the job namespace, which a provider never created for (an import, then a crash)
    would otherwise leave: `provider profile list -o json` is the whole catalog as one array
    (crates/openshell-cli/src/commands/provider.rs `provider_list_profiles_text`,
    crates/openshell-providers/src/profiles.rs `profiles_to_json`), and a failed listing leaves the sweep's answer as it is; the gone-check deletes a
    gone sandbox's bundle providers too. Still one set per job, never shared (`OQ-047`).
  - **The record** gains `bundle.placeholders` and `bundle.plain` on both venues (`INT-RUN-HISTORY-FILE-CONTRACT`).
    The redactor still holds every placeholder variable's real value (it is in the job's env as every secret is), so a
    value that came back some other way is still masked.
  - **CI** (advisory lane): the copy pass binds a bundle variable to the stand-in's second alias (`host.docker.internal`)
    and reads from inside: the placeholder in the env and `/proc/self/environ` and no process holding the value, the
    plain value in `/sandbox/job/bundle-env.json` with `PI_BUNDLE_ENV=1` and on no process's command line, neither value
    in the gateway's log (the probe replaces the runner, so the runner's own read is `verify-image.sh`'s `bundleEnvFile`
    check), the real value received by the stand-in at that host, the same placeholder refused at the
    first alias (the job provider's endpoint) and the job's model key refused at the bundle's host; then a worker
    process SIGKILLed while its bundled sandbox runs, and the reaper's sweep leaving neither the sandbox nor its two
    providers. The bind pass repeats the inside reads and the swap. Only that lane, on Linux with a gateway, can prove
    them; the unit tests drive the adapter against a fake CLI.
  - **Code evidence**: worker/src/backend-openshell.mjs -> judgeBundle, bundleProviderPlan, bundleAuthFields,
    providerProfileFor, credentialHostsOf, OPENSHELL_LIMITS, OPENSHELL_SET_ENV_NAMES, BUNDLE_PROVIDER_NAME,

- **Recorded run facts (#712 part D, AMENDED 2026-10-21)**: a run on either OpenShell venue records `openshell`, `{ mode,
  ruleHosts, ruleHostCount, providers, placeholders }` (`INT-RUN-HISTORY-FILE-CONTRACT`), so a run's page can say
  which box it ran in after the sandbox is gone:
  - **Where it comes from.** The stage sets the facts once every provider of the attempt exists (`at.facts`, after the
    bundle hosts' providers are made), from what it just built: the mode, the hosts of the written policy's endpoints,
    `at.providers.length` (the job's own provider, made only when the job has a secret and the policy a rule, and one
    per bundle host), and the keys those providers bind (the job provider's secrets plus each bundle host's
    variables; a plain bundle variable is a value by file and is not counted). `collectRun` puts them on every result it
    returns, aborted runs, a failed download and bind mode's early return included, and the processor's settle carries
    them to the record as it carries `liveSkipped`. None is carried for an attempt that never reached the exec: a stage that throws or is stopped before the exec, or a detached run (a never-started exit found still running), carries none,
    a sandbox create that fails after the providers exist included (that attempt never started,
    `container-never-started`). The record rebuilds them and keeps them only when `mode` is the
    mode of the venue the record's `backend` names.
  - **Why the host names may be recorded.** They are operator config: the policy is generated from
    `egress-allowlist.conf`, `model-endpoints.json` and the forge's fixed web host (`networkPolicyFor`), and a bundle
    host must already be one of its endpoints (`judgeBundle`). Nothing from a webhook payload, an issue, a branch or a
    repository reaches one: the repository is a PATH in the push rule, and the rule's paths are not read. Each host is
    held to the host-name charset again (an optional leading `*.` for a dot entry), at most 32 listed and the total
    counted, so the record stays PII-free by construction.
  - **Counts, never names, for credentials.** The record already names a bundle's variables (`bundle.variables`); the
    job's own secrets are the provider key, the forge token and `run.secrets`, whose names `doctor` prints and the
    trigger view counts, so a count is what the run page needs and a name list would add nothing it can act on.
  - **Not recorded**: MCP connection state. #684 made the venue's MCP preflight and the sandbox's policy admit the
    servers, and records nothing of a server's connection on any venue; the run record's MCP facts are the runner's
    refusal reasons alone (`MCP_RUNNER_REASONS`). Nothing is invented for it here.
  - **Read by** the console's run page ("Sandbox policy", "Rule hosts") and the panel's RUN_DETAIL ("policy", "rule
    hosts", wrapped at most four lines and the rest counted), and by the model-callable `dispatch_runs`: a run read by
    its `jobId` carries the record's host names and counts (operator config, the class `backend` and `host` already
    are), a list of runs only `ruleHostCount` and the counts (`modelRunRecord`'s `list`).
  - **CI** (advisory lane): the copy pass's bundle run and the bind pass's bundle run each put the real result's
    `openshell` through `buildRecord` and require, exactly: the venue's mode; `ruleHosts` equal to the sorted endpoint
    hosts of `networkPolicyFor` run over the script's own sources (its allowlist, the endpoints that case reads, the
    job's forge and repository), and `ruleHostCount` equal to their number; 2 providers (the job's and the bundle
    host's); 4 placeholders in copy mode (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, the bundle's endpoint
    variable) and 2 in bind mode (no token is passed there); and no bundle value anywhere in the record.
  - **Code evidence**: worker/src/backend-openshell.mjs -> stageRun (`at.facts`), collectRun (`withFacts`);
    worker/src/index.mjs -> carryLiveSkip (`openshellRan`); worker/src/run-history.mjs -> recordedOpenshell,
    OPENSHELL_RULE_HOSTS_MAX, buildRecord; admin/src/read-model.mjs -> recordOpenshell, openshellCountsText,
    openshellHostsText, modelRunRecord; admin/src/console/panels.mjs -> openshellRows; admin/src/dashboard.ts ->
    renderRunDetail; worker/test/run-record-openshell.test.mjs, backend-openshell.test.mjs,
    backend-openshell-bind.test.mjs; admin/test/secret-profiles-view.test.mjs; .github/scripts/openshell-conformance.mjs,
    openshell-bind-conformance.mjs.

## DES-OOM-CONFIRMED-BY-AN-IN-IMAGE-SUPERVISOR

- **Decision** (issue #596, phase 0): each run records what its container used, and a job killed for memory is
  `policy` / `oom-killed`, not retried, only when the kill is CONFIRMED inside the container. The runner reads its own
  cgroup just before its exit line and puts `resources` on it, through the one writer every exit path uses. A small
  **supervisor** (`image/runner/supervise.mjs`, an entry file that always calls `image/runner/src/supervise.mjs`) runs
  between the container's init and the runner, under the same exec-only node and, like the runner, with
  `--disable-sigusr1`: it passes the exit key on, raises the runner tree's `oom_score_adj` to 1000 (through a shell
  that then execs the runner), forwards a stop, exits with the runner's own code when the runner exits, and writes the
  signed exit line itself only when the runner was killed by a signal, naming `oom-killed` for a SIGKILL with
  `oom_kill` above 0, and marking every line it writes `by: "supervisor"` inside the signed bytes. The worker
  classifies an OOM only from that line, verified under the run's key, beside a container exit `137` it did not cause,
  and only when the line's `memPeak` reached 90% of the `--memory` the worker gave the container. A supervisor line
  that follows a line the runner wrote is ignored by every exit-line scanner (`decisiveExitLine`): that runner
  finished and was killed afterwards. No container limit changes in this phase (`INT-CONTAINER-RUNTIME-CONTRACT`).
  The supervisor is not free: it holds about 8 MB of anonymous memory inside the job's own limit (an RSS of about
  46 MB, most of it the node binary's text, shared with the runner), so a job's headroom is that much lower than
  before it. Measured on Docker Desktop: the smallest limit at which the offline smoke job still reached its own exit
  moved up by 8 to 16 MB, from about 72 MB. The `resources` block carries `swapPeak` (`memory.swap.peak`) beside
  `memPeak`, which cannot see swap: while a job may swap as much as its memory (today's default), a job at its limit
  swaps instead of dying, and only the swap peak tells one that fit from one that needed more.
- **Why**: the same size is killed the same way on every retry, so retrying an OOM pays twice for nothing, and an
  unclassified `137` recorded no reason at all. The worker cannot look after the fact: `--rm` is a fixed isolation
  flag, so the container's state is gone when `docker run` returns. The process that can see the cgroup at the moment
  the runner dies has to live in the container and outlive the runner, and its report has to be one a job's tool
  cannot forge, which the exit-line key already provides (`INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`).
- **Rejected**:
  - **Docker's `oom` event stream** (`docker events --filter event=oom`, one per worker, matched by the cidfile's
    ID). Built first and removed in the same pull request: the event fires also when only a CHILD was killed and the
    job exited 0 (measured on Docker Desktop and Docker 29), so it needs the exit code beside it anyway, and Podman
    (4.9 and 5.8, rootful and rootless) emits no `oom` event at all, so the podman venue would have had no answer. The
    supervisor answers on every venue with one mechanism. What only the event covered, an image without the
    supervisor on Docker, retries as it always did.
  - **`docker inspect` `State.OOMKilled`**: impossible under `--rm`, and Podman 4.9 rootless never set it (measured).
  - **The runner reading its own cgroup at exit to classify itself**: a runner killed for memory runs no more code.
  - **No score bump**: on Fedora's 6.19 kernel a second OOM in one cgroup killed even a 1 MB main shell while the
    first victim's memory was being freed (measured), so the supervisor would die with the runner. With the bump it
    survived 15 of 15 kills on three venues.
  - **Reading `oom` or `max` from `memory.events`**: under crun the limit sits on the parent scope and the job's leaf
    shows `oom 0` beside `oom_kill 1` (measured); only `oom_kill` is charged to the job's own cgroup everywhere.
  - **`oom_kill` above 0 as the whole proof** (the first cut, refuted in its review): the counter also counts a kill
    by the HOST's OOM killer, and the score of 1000 makes the runner that killer's first choice when the machine is
    short, so a host shortage would be recorded as "this job's size is too small" and never retried. A cgroup OOM
    happens only at the limit, so its `memory.peak` sits there (the bound exactly, or just under, on every venue
    measured); the worker reads the limit off the argv it built (`--memory=`, the job's size since phase 1) rather than off its
    environment, and wants the peak at 90% of it or more.
  - **The LAST verified line, whoever wrote it** (the first cut, refuted in its review): a runner can be SIGKILLed
    after its own decided line (a tool can do it, the kernel can too), and the supervisor then signs a second line.
    Read last, it relabelled a finished run `oom-killed` and dropped its tokens, usage and session, an undercharge
    and a token cap that missed the spend. One picker for every scanner, so they cannot disagree again.
  - **A main-module guard in the supervisor** (`import.meta.url` against `argv[1]`): when it read false, node ran
    nothing and exited 0, which the worker records as a completed run. The image runs an entry file with no guard.
- **Residuals**: a supervisor killed for memory itself (never seen with the bump) leaves no line, and the `137`
  retries as before. A job can still FORGE `oom-killed`: let a child grow to the limit until the kernel kills it
  (`oom_kill` above 0, the peak at the limit), then SIGKILL the runner (same uid) BEFORE the runner writes its own
  line (after it, the supervisor's line is ignored). The job then ends `oom-killed`, not retried, its dollars settled
  at the floor and its tokens unknown, as a run with no line always was: the job can only stop itself, which it could
  already do, and gains no money (the floor is an overcharge, never an undercharge). A HOST OOM that strikes a job
  already at 90% of its own limit (page cache included: `memory.peak` counts a job's file cache, so a job that read
  large files can sit near its bound without using that much) reads as the job's own, and so does one that strikes
  after the job touched 90% earlier in the run, because the peak is a high-water mark. Every `resources` number is
  produced inside the container and can be inflated by the job; it is advisory (`docs/insights.md`), and a later phase
  that suggests sizes from it must clamp it and never apply one by itself. `--disable-sigusr1` on both key holders
  closes only the route from OUTSIDE a holder (`INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`): code loaded into the runner itself
  (the serviced repo's `/workspace/.pi/extensions`, imported after the key was read, `image/runner/src/loader.mjs`)
  can open `node:inspector` in process, and an operator-set `NODE_OPTIONS` (a trigger's secret named so, or
  `PI_FORWARD_ENV`) reaches both holders. Both predate #596 and stay outside the key's guarantee; no environment name
  is reserved against the second.
- **Evidence**: the issue #596 lab (five venues, zero spend), and the shipped image on Docker Desktop: at
  `--memory=64m` 3 of 3 runs ended on a signed `oom-killed` line with exit `137`, at 96m the runner reached its own
  exit; a `docker stop` still ends on the runner's own `terminated` line (the supervisor forwards it). The image job in
  `pi-upgrade-check.yml` checks both on every pull request: the real runner at 4g for the `resources` block, and, for
  the kill, the real entrypoint and supervisor with a stand-in runner that fills anonymous memory past 64m, because
  near its limit with a cold page cache the real runner thrashed on its own files instead of being killed (rootless
  Podman on Fedora still running at 100 s, Docker Desktop stopped at 90 s, review round 2). The stand-in's line must
  say `oom-killed` by the supervisor with `memPeak` at 90% of the limit, and the check fails on an image whose
  entrypoint skips the supervisor (measured). After the review: a tool's
  `process._debugProcess` opened the inspector of the supervisor (and of the runner) on the pre-review image and
  opens neither on the fixed one, which `verify-image.sh` now probes on every image that declares `exitAuth`, finding
  every holder by its executable (`/opt/pi-dispatch/runner-node` as argv[0]) and wanting at least two. Code:
  image/runner/supervise.mjs, image/runner/src/supervise.mjs, image/entrypoint.sh,
  image/runner/src/cgroup-usage.mjs, image/runner/src/exit-line.mjs, worker/src/run-history.mjs
  (`decisiveExitLine`, `parseExitResources`, `parseExitOomKilled`), worker/src/container-spec.mjs (`memoryBytes`),
  worker/src/run-container.mjs, worker/src/processor.mjs (`peakReachedLimit`), image/verify-image.sh.

## DES-OPERATOR-CONSOLE

- **Status**: issue #640, the security model and hardened skeleton of the console epic (#650); issue #641, the
  screens, the live updates and `/api/state` (the bullets from "The screens" to "Wiring" below); issue #642, the
  writes and actions (the bullets from "The action table" to "The sandbox, shown and not run" below, and the four
  rejected options marked #642); issue #643, the live transcript on the run page (the bullet "The live transcript"
  below, over `DES-LIVE-TRANSCRIPT-STREAM`); issue #644, run progress (the bullet "Run progress" below, over
  `DES-RUN-PROGRESS`); issue #646 part 3, steering (the bullet "Steering a running job" below, over
  `DES-STEER-VIA-READONLY-INBOX-MOUNT`); issue #647 part 1, run chat (the bullet "Run chat" below, over
  `DES-TERMINAL-CHAT`). This entry supersedes three of the
  rejected options of `DES-ADMIN-VIA-PI-EXTENSION` (a served graph page, the web panel with Bull Board) where they
  stand, and keeps its fourth: mounting admin on the receiver stays rejected.
- **Decision**: an operator console served over HTTP by a **separate process**, the bin `pi-dispatch-console` of the
  admin package (`@edgehero/pi-dispatch-admin`, `admin/src/console/cli.mjs` bundled to `dist/console.mjs` beside the
  extension), on `node:http` alone. The pi extension is unchanged and still binds no port; the console is a second
  surface over the same read model (`admin/src/read-model.mjs`), never a second write path. The property that
  replaces "binds no network port" has five parts, each held by a lettered clause of `REQ-CONSOLE-SECURITY`:
  1. **It listens on loopback or on a private socket.** `PI_CONSOLE_LISTEN` takes `127.0.0.1:4790` (the default),
     `[::1]:<port>` or `unix:/abs/path`. Only IP literals are accepted, because a hostname can resolve somewhere else;
     loopback is 127.0.0.0/8 and ::1, and any other literal is refused unless `PI_CONSOLE_BIND_PUBLIC=1`, on which
     doctor warns. A unix socket's parent directory must exist, belong to the console's account and give nothing to
     group or other; the socket is created under umask 077 and then set to 0600. A stale socket is removed only when
     `lstat` says it is a socket AND a connect to it fails, so a running console's socket is never taken over, and a
     path longer than the platform's `sun_path` (104 bytes on macOS, 108 on Linux) is refused before the bind, by
     name, because the kernel would otherwise truncate it to a different path.
  2. **Every request needs a named token's session.** Apart from `GET /healthz` (no data, `ok`) and the login routes,
     a request needs a session, and a session comes only from a token in the tokens file
     (`INT-CONSOLE-TOKENS-FILE-CONTRACT`) or from a one-time login code that `pi-dispatch-console link --name <n>`
     mints as the deployment's own account (since issue #708 the panel's `/dispatch console --link` mints one too, as
     the same account: "The panel as a second minter" below). Two roles: `operator` (reads and writes) and `viewer` (reads). Sessions
     live in the process (a restart signs everyone out), the id is 32 random bytes, a new one at every login (no
     fixation), in the cookie `pdc_session` with `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Path=/`. An idle limit
     (`PI_CONSOLE_IDLE_MINUTES`, default 60, 5 to 1440) and an absolute one (`PI_CONSOLE_MAX_HOURS`, default 12, 1
     to 168) bound it, and every request re-reads the tokens file: a session whose token was revoked or rotated, whose
     role changed, or whose `generation` is older than the file's (`sessions end-all`) ends on that request. Each
     token holds at most `PI_CONSOLE_MAX_STREAMS` (default 4) live streams across its sessions, for #641's event
     streams.
  3. **A write is same-origin, JSON, and confirmed by a single-use ticket bound to its diff.** A write route is a POST
     whose `Content-Type` is `application/json`. When the request carries `Sec-Fetch-Site` (every current browser sends it),
     the write is refused unless it says exactly `same-origin`; without that header (an older browser, a script) the
     `Origin` must equal `http://<Host>`, and a write with no `Origin` at all is refused. A write also needs the
     operator role and a console that is not read-only (`PI_CONSOLE_READ_ONLY=1` answers every write route 403). A
     config write is two requests: a preview, which answers the diff and a ticket, and a confirm, which carries only
     the ticket. The ticket is random, held by the server, bound to the session and the action, deleted on any
     attempt to redeem it (single use, refused or not) and good for 5 minutes. It holds the snapshots the preview was
     built from, and the confirm hands them to the funnel's existing `expect` parameter, so a confirm applies exactly
     the change it showed or refuses with "changed after this change was built from it", and writes nothing. A paid
     action (from #642) carries the reservation the page shows before its confirm. Every write goes through the
     read model's funnels: in #640 that is `writePauseWindows`, which gains the `expect` parameter its money-file
     siblings (`writeScopedLimits`, `writeProjects`) already had; since #642 it is every funnel in the action table
     below, `writeTriggers` and `writeSettings` gaining `expect` too. The console adds no write path of its own.
  4. **Every response carries the same headers, and every page escapes.** One function, applied to every response
     including refusals and 404s, sets a CSP of
     `default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self'; form-action 'self'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`,
     `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`,
     `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin`, `Cache-Control: no-store` and a `Permissions-Policy` that denies
     every feature. No response carries an `Access-Control-*` header, so no cross-origin script can read one, and
     a cross-origin JSON write never passes its preflight. Every page is built by one tagged template that escapes
     every interpolated value after the panel's control-byte scrub (`scrubControls`, then `escapeHtml` from
     `graph-html.mjs`); only an already-built fragment can be inserted raw, so raw interpolation of a value is
     impossible by construction. The page's script is a file served from `/static/console.js`, never inline. Run
     text (titles, transcripts, tool output) reaches the page only for the operator role, and always escaped.
  5. **Every write and every guard's refusal is audited, in a hash chain.** Each write, each refused write (Host,
     origin, content type, read-only, auth, role), each login, failed login, used login code and logout, each token change made
     with the CLI, and each `serve` start appends one row to `PI_LOGS_DIR/console-audit/YYYY-MM.jsonl`
     (`INT-CONSOLE-AUDIT-LOG`), whose `prev` is the sha256 of the row before it. An append that fails refuses the
     write it would have recorded (fail loudly, as the allocation audit does). No row holds a token, a login code, a
     cookie value or a request body. A refusal of a request that carries no session costs its sender nothing, so
     those rows are rate limited (60 a minute, burst 120) and the rest counted into one row written with the next
     allowed one: one row per request would let anyone who reaches the port grow the log, and the chain's verify
     time, without bound. A refusal from a signed-in session, every sign-in and every write is
     always its own row. Since #642 a signed-in write whose body is refused as too large or as not JSON is a row too
     (the session's actor, a fixed `body:` reason, nothing of the body); a change the preview refuses as invalid is
     answered without a row, since it got no further than the preview.
  The guards come from one route table, `{method, path, auth, write, handler}`, applied by one dispatcher in a fixed
  order: security headers, the Host check, the route lookup (404, 405), the write guards (origin, content type,
  read-only, role), the session (401 JSON for `/api/*`, a 303 to `/login` for a page), the handler. A new route
  cannot skip a guard, and the tests iterate the table rather than a hand list. Login is a write for origin and
  content type and needs no session, and read-only mode and the viewer role do not refuse it. The server's own limits:
  `headersTimeout` 10 s, `requestTimeout` 30 s, a 64 KiB body (413), 64 connections, and a login rate limit that is
  one global token bucket (5 a minute, burst 10, 429), global because every peer is loopback and a per-address
  bucket would be one bucket anyway. Each failed login is audited. The limit delays; it never locks anyone out.
- **Why**: the issue's decisions (full management from the first version, writes included; loopback, an SSH tunnel
  for remote use, a long random token) make the console the most powerful surface this project has after a shell on
  the host, and put it on a socket. "Loopback only" does not mean "the operator only": every local account, every
  page the operator's browser opens, and, on Docker Desktop, the job container itself can reach a loopback port. So
  no single control carries the model. The socket narrows who can connect; the token says who is asking; the Host
  check defeats DNS rebinding; same-origin plus JSON defeats a hostile page that rides the operator's cookie; the
  ticket makes a confirm mean "this diff" and nothing newer; the funnels keep every write inside the validation the
  pi extension's writes already pass; and the audit says afterwards who did what. Per-person tokens answer the
  issue's first open question: the audit names a person, and one person's access is revoked without rotating
  everyone's.
- **The six threats found while surveying, beyond the issue's text, and what answers each**:
  1. **The job container can be a client of the console.** On Docker Desktop `host.docker.internal` reaches the
     host's loopback listeners (measured from the egress proxy on 2026-09-30, Docker Desktop 4.37.2, `docs/backends.md`).
     So "loopback only" does not keep the untrusted side out. The Host check always refuses `host.docker.internal`, `host.containers.internal` and
     `gateway.docker.internal`, and the console refuses to start when `PI_CONSOLE_ALLOWED_HOSTS` names one; a job
     that reaches the port still needs a token; and unix-socket mode removes the path. Measured on 2026-10-14
     with `ghcr.io/edgehero/pi-job:4.3.0` and a listener bound to `127.0.0.1`: on Docker Desktop 27.4.0 (macOS) a
     container on the default bridge (the `PI_EGRESS=0` posture) reached it through `host.docker.internal` with a
     200, and the server saw the peer as `127.0.0.1` with `Host: host.docker.internal:<port>`, so the peer address
     cannot tell a job from the operator. The Host header tells them apart only for a client that keeps the name it
     dialled (a browser, `curl`, an SDK); a program in the job can send `Host: localhost` and pass the Host check,
     which is why the Host refusal is a defence against browsers and careless clients, the token is the barrier
     against a job, and the unix socket is the recommended mode on Docker Desktop. A listener on `::1` was not
     reached. On the
     `--internal` network of the armed posture the name did not resolve (`EAI_AGAIN`) and the gateway addresses were
     unreachable (`ENETUNREACH`); there the egress proxy is the only way out, and it reaches the host's loopback only
     for an operator who allowlisted `host.docker.internal` (`docs/backends.md`). On native Linux (Docker 27.5.1, the
     `docker:27-dind` lab) a bridge container with `--add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway` was refused, as was
     the bridge gateway address, and an `--internal` container got "network unreachable". A unix socket has no
     address a container can name, and no job mount carries it. Podman is unmeasured.
  2. **An SSH tunnel changes the port.** With `ssh -L 8080:127.0.0.1:4790` the browser sends `Host: localhost:8080`,
